one_line: Open-vocabulary dense scores carry a hidden BPE-token-count bias: multi-token class names are scored on a different scale than single-token names
problem: Open-vocab detectors and segmenters compare similarity scores across class names as if the text encoder placed all names on one commensurable scale, but nobody checks whether tokenization length alone shifts score distributions.
core_hypothesis: Pooled text embeddings for names that fragment into many BPE pieces have systematically different norms and neighborhood densities than single-token names, so pixel-text similarity distributions are keyed to token count rather than visual evidence, biasing cross-class comparisons and thresholds.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a large query vocabulary, the mean and variance of per-pixel similarity scores will regress significantly on BPE token count after controlling for class frequency and visual size, and re-normalizing scores per token-count stratum will change which class wins at a nontrivial fraction of pixels.
why_important: If token count is a confound, every fixed-threshold open-vocab deployment and every cross-class score comparison is silently biased against long-named (often rare, fine-grained) categories, exactly the classes open-vocab methods exist to serve.
why_possibly_novel: Token-length artifacts are discussed for text-only tasks, but a stratified audit of dense similarity scores by tokenization length, with a correction applied at the pixel level, does not appear to be standard practice in dense VLM evaluation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a frozen open-vocab segmenter, build a 500-name vocabulary spanning 1 to 6 BPE tokens, run on a few hundred images, and regress per-class score statistics on token count with frequency and object-size covariates; then apply per-stratum z-normalization and measure the change in per-pixel argmax decisions.
main_risk: Token count is strongly correlated with word rarity, so the bias may be a frequency effect in disguise and the correction may just relabel a known long-tail problem.
default_community_belief: Text embeddings from a shared encoder are directly comparable across class names, so one confidence threshold and one softmax over the vocabulary are meaningful.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive pretraining normalizes embeddings onto the unit sphere and may wash out tokenization artifacts, leaving frequency as the only real driver.
fastest_falsification: One inference-only afternoon: 100 images, 200 queries stratified by token count, plot score distributions per stratum; overlapping distributions kill the idea.

one_line: Dense grounding of polysemous words follows the dominant web sense, not the image: the picture rarely overrides the text prior
problem: Queries like 'bat', 'mouse', 'crane', or 'jack' are ambiguous in text but unambiguous given the image; dense VLMs are assumed to use image context to select the sense, but this is never measured.
core_hypothesis: The text embedding of a polysemous word is a frequency-weighted mixture of its senses, and dense heads inherit the dominant-sense direction, so pixels of the minority sense receive systematically depressed similarity even when the image contains only the minority sense.
falsifiable_prediction: On images containing only the minority sense of a polysemous word, similarity maps will show depressed scores relative to a monosemous synonym of the same object (e.g. 'computer mouse' vs 'mouse'), and adding a disambiguating modifier will recover most of the gap; matched non-polysemous control words will show no such gap.
why_important: Open-vocab interfaces expose raw words to users; a sense-prior failure means recall silently depends on lexical statistics of web text, which practitioners in robotics or retail (full of polysemous product words) cannot anticipate.
why_possibly_novel: Polysemy is studied for CLIP retrieval at image level, but a controlled dense-prediction audit comparing minority-sense recall against monosemous synonym controls appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 30 polysemous words with clearly imageable senses, collect 20 images per minority sense from existing datasets, query a frozen open-vocab segmenter with the bare word vs a disambiguated phrase vs a monosemous synonym, and compare mask recall across the three query forms.
main_risk: Disambiguated phrases change token count and syntax simultaneously, so the recovery effect could be a phrase-length artifact rather than sense selection.
default_community_belief: Given a clear image, the visual evidence dominates and the model grounds whatever object is present that matches the word.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive training pairs polysemous words with images of all senses, so the vision-conditioned similarity may genuinely re-weight senses per image, making the prior weak in practice.
fastest_falsification: Score 10 minority-sense images with word vs synonym queries on one frozen model in an hour; equal recall kills the hypothesis.

one_line: Trivial string variants (casing, articles, punctuation) move dense masks by more than most modeling improvements move benchmarks
problem: Benchmarks query models with canonical lowercase class strings, while deployed systems receive user text with arbitrary casing, articles, plurals, and trailing punctuation; the sensitivity of dense outputs to these semantically-null variations is unreported.
core_hypothesis: Because contrastive text encoders are trained on noisy web text without canonicalization, semantically identical query strings occupy measurably different embedding positions, and dense decoders amplify these differences into mask-level disagreement larger than typical method-to-method benchmark gaps.
falsifiable_prediction: Averaged over a standard referring or open-vocab benchmark, the mean IoU disagreement between masks from 'dog', 'Dog', 'a dog', 'the dog.', and 'dogs' variants of the same query will exceed the IoU gap separating adjacent published methods on that benchmark's leaderboard-style comparisons.
why_important: If true, a fraction of reported progress is within the noise floor of string canonicalization, and a zero-cost normalization layer is worth more than architecture work; it also defines a needed invariance metric for dense VLM evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is folklore for classification, but quantifying string-variant noise floors specifically for dense outputs and comparing them to leaderboard gaps appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one frozen referring-segmentation model and one open-vocab segmenter, run 5 canonical string variants per query over a full validation set, compute pairwise mask IoU disagreement, and compare the disagreement magnitude to inter-method gaps reported on the same split.
main_risk: Models trained with heavy text augmentation may already be invariant, making the audit a null result with limited publishable content beyond a sanity certificate.
default_community_belief: Trivial string variation is absorbed by the text encoder and is not a meaningful source of dense output variance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Subword tokenizations of case and article variants overlap heavily, so embedding drift may be tiny and the decoder may be contraction-stable rather than amplifying.
fastest_falsification: One hour: 50 queries, 5 variants each, one frozen model; if pairwise mask IoU stays above 0.95 the noise-floor claim dies.

one_line: Multilingual queries degrade localization before they degrade recognition: dense grounding is the weakest link of claimed multilinguality
problem: VLM systems inherit multilingual capability claims from their text encoders, but dense benchmarks are almost exclusively English; how localization quality (not just class recognition) degrades across languages is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Cross-lingual alignment in contrastive pretraining is dominated by image-level co-occurrence, so non-English queries retain coarse recognition (the right object region is warm in the similarity map) while precise boundary localization collapses, because the fine-grained pixel-text alignment was only ever supervised through English captions.
falsifiable_prediction: Translating queries of a referring benchmark into several languages will show boundary-quality metrics (boundary F-score) dropping proportionally more than region-level metrics (center-hit rate), and the drop will correlate with the language's share in the pretraining corpus proxy (e.g. web prevalence rank).
why_important: Products localize their UI strings but reuse one grounding model; a recognition-intact but boundary-broken failure mode is exactly the kind that passes demos and fails deployments, and it dictates whether translation-at-inference is a sufficient fix.
why_possibly_novel: Multilingual evaluation exists for retrieval and VQA, but a decomposition of dense degradation into recognition vs localization components across languages appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Machine-translate 500 referring expressions into 6 languages, run one frozen multilingual-encoder grounding model, and report center-hit rate vs boundary F-score per language; compare against an English-with-back-translation control to isolate translation noise.
main_risk: Machine translation errors confound the measurement; the control only partially removes them because back-translation does not preserve referential specificity.
default_community_belief: If the text encoder is multilingual, grounding quality transfers across languages roughly uniformly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cross-lingual embeddings may be tight enough that the dense decoder sees nearly identical conditioning vectors, making degradation uniform and small across metrics.
fastest_falsification: 100 expressions, 3 languages, one afternoon of inference; parallel drops in center-hit and boundary metrics falsify the differential-degradation claim.

one_line: A single typo makes dense grounding bimodal: either fully rescued or catastrophically lost, unlike the graceful degradation everyone assumes
problem: User-facing grounding systems receive typos constantly, but robustness studies focus on image corruptions; the behavior of dense outputs under character-level text noise is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: BPE tokenization makes typo damage discontinuous: some typos preserve dominant subwords (embedding barely moves, mask intact) while others fragment the word into unrelated pieces (embedding jumps to a semantically alien region, mask lands on an unrelated object), so per-query outcomes are bimodal rather than smoothly degrading with edit distance.
falsifiable_prediction: Across many single-character typos of grounding queries, the distribution of mask IoU against the clean-query mask will be strongly bimodal (modes near 1.0 and near 0.0) with the mode assignment predictable from subword overlap between clean and typo tokenizations, not from edit distance.
why_important: Bimodality means average-case robustness numbers are misleading and simple confidence checks will not catch failures; a cheap tokenization-overlap guard could flag exactly the dangerous typos before inference.
why_possibly_novel: Typo robustness is studied in NLP classification; connecting subword fragmentation to dense mask outcomes and proposing tokenization overlap as a deployable failure predictor appears new for grounding.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate 20 single-character corruptions for each of 100 queries, run a frozen grounding model, plot the IoU-to-clean distribution, and fit a classifier predicting failure from subword overlap alone; bimodality plus predictive overlap confirms, unimodal graceful decay falsifies.
main_risk: Context tokens in longer referring expressions may rescue fragmented words via the text encoder's contextualization, collapsing the bimodality for realistic multi-word queries.
default_community_belief: Text-side noise causes proportional, roughly smooth degradation of grounding quality, and image-side robustness is the harder problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Character-level information may be partially recoverable by the encoder from subword composition, making most typos land in the rescued mode and the effect economically irrelevant.
fastest_falsification: One-hour inference sweep of 500 typo queries on one model; a unimodal IoU histogram kills the claim.

one_line: Domain jargon grounds with false confidence because subword sharing places technical terms near everyday words in text space
problem: Practitioners in medical, industrial, and scientific imaging query open-vocab models with jargon ('stenosis', 'spalling', 'chlorosis') and receive confident masks; whether those masks reflect the concept or a subword-neighbor of it is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Rare technical terms are fragmented into subwords shared with common words, so their embeddings land in the neighborhood of everyday concepts; dense heads then produce well-formed, confident masks of the wrong (everyday) concept, making jargon failure invisible to confidence-based monitoring.
falsifiable_prediction: For jargon terms absent from common web text, the produced masks will overlap significantly with masks of the jargon term's nearest common-word subword neighbors, and mask confidence will be statistically indistinguishable from confidence on common words, despite near-zero semantic correctness.
why_important: Silent, confident wrongness on jargon is the exact failure that makes open-vocab tools dangerous in specialized domains, and a subword-neighborhood audit would be a deployable pre-flight check requiring no domain labels.
why_possibly_novel: Out-of-vocabulary behavior is discussed for classification, but a mechanism-level account (subword neighbor capture) with a proposed no-label audit for dense prediction appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick 40 jargon terms from two specialized domains, compute their subword-decomposition neighbors in the text encoder, run dense queries for both jargon and neighbors on in-domain images, and measure mask overlap between jargon masks and neighbor masks plus confidence distributions.
main_risk: Some jargon may genuinely appear in web captions (medical stock photos), giving the model partial true knowledge that muddies the neighbor-capture signature.
default_community_belief: Low familiarity with a term shows up as low confidence, so thresholding protects against out-of-vocabulary queries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive encoders may map unfamiliar fragmented terms to low-norm or high-entropy conditioning vectors that visibly diffuse the similarity map, making failures detectable after all.
fastest_falsification: Ten jargon terms, one frozen model, compare masks against subword-neighbor queries in an afternoon; low overlap with neighbors falsifies the capture mechanism.

one_line: Compound-word form ('fire truck' vs 'firetruck' vs 'fire-truck') is an unmeasured nuisance variable that changes dense masks
problem: English compounds have multiple orthographic forms with identical meaning; queries and training captions mix them freely, yet dense evaluation always picks one canonical form per class.
core_hypothesis: The three orthographic forms of a compound tokenize differently and appear with different frequencies in pretraining text, so they condition the dense head differently; moreover the spaced form additionally activates the head noun ('truck') as a partial match, producing systematically larger or differently-shaped masks than the fused form.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a list of compounds, spaced forms will yield masks with higher recall on the head-noun's general category (more truck-like pixels included for 'fire truck') while fused forms yield tighter but lower-recall masks, and the disagreement between forms will exceed run-to-run noise by an order of magnitude.
why_important: Compound handling determines fair comparison across benchmark class lists and affects any user-facing system; if the spaced-form-head-noun leak exists, it is also a lens into how compositional the text conditioning really is.
why_possibly_novel: Orthographic-variant sensitivity for dense grounding, and the specific head-noun-leak prediction for spaced compounds, appear absent from the prompt-robustness literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 50 imageable compounds with all three attested forms, query one frozen open-vocab segmenter on images containing the compound referent among other head-noun instances (a fire truck among trucks), and measure per-form recall on the target vs false inclusion of non-target head-noun instances.
main_risk: Finding enough images with both the compound referent and same-head-noun distractors may be hard, weakening the statistical power of the head-noun-leak test.
default_community_belief: Orthographic variants of the same compound are interchangeable inputs and the encoder handles them equivalently.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-frequency compounds may have all forms well-anchored to the same visual concept, restricting any effect to rare compounds where it matters less.
fastest_falsification: Twenty compounds, three forms each, one model, one afternoon: if pairwise form-to-form mask IoU exceeds 0.95, the nuisance claim dies.

one_line: Synonym consistency is the missing invariance metric: open-vocab segmenters give materially different masks for 'couch' and 'sofa'
problem: Open-vocabulary is claimed as robustness to wording, yet no standard benchmark reports whether synonymous queries produce the same masks; per-class results are always keyed to one canonical name.
core_hypothesis: Because synonyms occupy distinct text-embedding positions shaped by different usage contexts and image-caption co-occurrences, dense outputs for synonym pairs disagree substantially, and the disagreement is largest exactly for the informal or regional variants users actually type.
falsifiable_prediction: On a curated synonym-pair list, mask IoU between synonym queries on identical images will average well below the model's self-consistency under image re-encoding noise, and disagreement will anti-correlate with the rarer synonym's web frequency; a synonym-consistency score will rank models differently than standard accuracy metrics.
why_important: A model that only works for canonical class names is closed-vocabulary in practice; a consistency metric would expose this and is trivially computable without new ground truth, since it compares model outputs to each other.
why_possibly_novel: Robustness metrics for dense VLMs focus on image corruption; an output-only, label-free synonym-invariance score for segmentation with a model re-ranking claim appears novel.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 100 synonym pairs, run 3 public open-vocab segmenters on a shared image set, compute cross-synonym mask IoU per model, and check whether the consistency ranking diverges from accuracy ranking on a standard benchmark split.
main_risk: Some synonym pairs carry genuine referential nuance (couch vs futon-adjacent usage), contaminating the pair list and overstating inconsistency.
default_community_belief: Text encoders map synonyms close together, so open-vocab models are approximately synonym-invariant and reporting one name per class is sufficient.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For high-frequency object nouns, contrastive training on billions of captions may have already collapsed synonyms onto the visual concept, leaving disagreement only on rare words with little practical impact.
fastest_falsification: Thirty synonym pairs, one model, two hours: cross-synonym IoU above 0.9 everywhere kills the metric's motivation.

one_line: Using the literal word 'background' as the negative class imports a real visual concept, structuring false negatives around what web captions call background
problem: Many open-vocab segmentation pipelines score pixels against class names plus a textual negative like 'background' or 'other', silently assuming these words denote visual absence rather than being real words with their own imagery.
core_hypothesis: The embedding of 'background' encodes what web captions describe as background (skies, walls, blurred bokeh regions, distant landscapes), so pixels of legitimate query objects that resemble caption-typical backgrounds (a wall being queried, sky, a distant building) are disproportionately captured by the negative class, creating a structured recall hole.
falsifiable_prediction: Recall for query classes that are caption-typical backgrounds (sky, wall, road, mountain) will drop significantly more when 'background' is in the negative set than recall for foreground-typical classes, and swapping the negative word to a nonsense token or an averaged null embedding will selectively recover recall on those classes.
why_important: The negative-class design is a two-line implementation detail that may dominate stuff-class performance; a principled null embedding could be a free, universal improvement to open-vocab segmentation pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: The background-logit problem is known in closed-set terms, but the specific claim that the lexical semantics of the chosen negative word structures dense errors, testable by word substitution, appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one open-vocab segmenter, evaluate stuff-class and thing-class recall under four negative-class designs (word 'background', word 'other', random rare token, mean-of-vocabulary embedding) and compare per-class recall deltas between background-typical and foreground-typical classes.
main_risk: Pipelines may already learn the negative logit end-to-end rather than using the raw word embedding, in which case the lexical-import mechanism does not apply to the strongest baselines.
default_community_belief: The textual negative class is a harmless calibration trick; what word is used for it does not matter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Softmax competition against strong positive classes may dominate the outcome, making the negative embedding's direction nearly irrelevant in practice.
fastest_falsification: Swap the negative word across four variants and re-run validation inference in one afternoon; identical per-class recall profiles falsify the lexical-import claim.

one_line: Similarity-map sharpness tracks word frequency, not visual distinctiveness: rare words get diffuse maps regardless of how salient the object is
problem: Dense similarity maps are treated as evidence maps whose sharpness reflects visual difficulty, but the text side contributes its own frequency-keyed geometry that nobody separates out.
core_hypothesis: Frequent words develop tight, high-norm, well-separated embedding neighborhoods during contrastive training while rare words remain in diffuse regions, so the peakedness of a pixel-text similarity map is substantially a function of lexical frequency, independent of how visually distinctive the referent is.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlling for object size, contrast, and category (using synonym pairs where one member is frequent and one rare for the same referent in the same image), the rare synonym's similarity map will show measurably higher entropy and lower peak-to-background ratio than the frequent synonym's map on identical pixels.
why_important: If map sharpness is lexically driven, all downstream uses of sharpness (thresholding, pseudo-labeling, uncertainty estimation, mask NMS) inherit a language bias, and pseudo-label pipelines will systematically under-train rare vocabulary, compounding the long tail.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency effects on classification accuracy are known; isolating frequency's effect on the spatial statistics of dense similarity maps via same-image synonym controls appears to be a new measurement.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 60 frequent/rare synonym or hypernym pairs denoting the same visible referent, compute similarity-map entropy and peak ratios for both members over the same images with a frozen model, and test the paired difference.
main_risk: Rare synonyms often carry subtle sense differences or register (formal/informal) that could change what the model attends to for legitimate semantic reasons.
default_community_belief: Diffuse similarity maps indicate genuine visual ambiguity or model uncertainty about the image content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Final-layer normalization and the contrastive temperature may equalize effective peakedness across the vocabulary, leaving frequency effects only in pathological tails.
fastest_falsification: Twenty same-referent pairs, one model, entropy comparison in two hours; no paired entropy gap falsifies.

one_line: Classification prompt templates are wrong for dense tasks: 'a photo of a {}' optimizes image-level alignment while region-level alignment wants different words
problem: Dense open-vocab pipelines inherit prompt templates that were tuned to improve zero-shot classification, assuming template quality transfers from global image matching to pixel or region matching.
core_hypothesis: Templates like 'a photo of a {}' bias the text embedding toward whole-scene, subject-centric alignment learned from photo captions, whereas region-level matching benefits from part-like and context-free phrasings ('a cropped photo of', 'a close-up of', bare noun), so the classification-optimal template is measurably suboptimal for localization.
falsifiable_prediction: Ranking a fixed template set by zero-shot classification accuracy and separately by dense segmentation quality with the same frozen encoders will produce discordant rankings, with rank correlation substantially below 1 and at least one template pair whose ordering flips between the two tasks.
why_important: Template choice is a zero-parameter design decision applied to every query; if dense tasks need their own template science, there is free accuracy currently left on the table in most open-vocab dense pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: Template engineering has been studied for classification; a systematic, controlled discordance analysis between classification-optimal and localization-optimal templates appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 20 templates on a zero-shot classification set and on an open-vocab segmentation set using the same text and vision encoders, compute the two quality rankings, and test rank correlation with confidence intervals from bootstrap over classes.
main_risk: Template effects may be small relative to class-level variance in dense metrics, requiring many classes to detect discordance and limiting practical significance.
default_community_belief: Good classification templates are good templates in general; reusing them for dense tasks is safe and standard.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both tasks may depend on the same dominant embedding direction per class, with templates only rescaling it, in which case rankings agree and the transfer assumption holds.
fastest_falsification: Five templates, one segmenter, one classification set, one dense set, half a day; concordant rankings falsify.

one_line: Prompt ensembling helps recognition but can hurt localization: averaging template embeddings blurs the direction that localizes
problem: Averaging text embeddings across many templates is a default trick assumed to be a strict improvement, but its effect on the spatial precision of dense predictions has not been isolated from its effect on recognition.
core_hypothesis: Different templates align to different visual support (whole scene vs object vs close-up); averaging them produces a conditioning vector aligned with the union of supports, which improves class recognition robustness while systematically enlarging and blurring the spatial extent that dense heads ground, degrading boundary metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: On open-vocab segmentation, template ensembling relative to the single best template will improve class-presence metrics (image-level recall of the class) while degrading boundary F-score or mask compactness, and the boundary degradation will grow with the diversity of the ensembled templates.
why_important: If ensembling trades boundary quality for recognition, dense pipelines should ensemble at the score-map level or select templates per task, a simple change affecting nearly every CLIP-based dense system.
why_possibly_novel: The recognition benefit of ensembling is well known; a decomposition showing an opposite-signed effect on localization precision appears to be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare single-template, embedding-averaged, and score-map-averaged inference for one frozen open-vocab segmenter across a validation set, reporting image-level class recall and boundary F-score separately, with ensemble diversity varied from 2 to 30 templates.
main_risk: Boundary effects may be dominated by the mask decoder's own priors, leaving little measurable difference attributable to the conditioning vector.
default_community_belief: Prompt ensembling is a free win inherited from classification and should always be enabled.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Embedding averaging may act as noise reduction that sharpens rather than blurs dense alignment, in which case both recognition and localization improve together.
fastest_falsification: One model, 1 vs 30 templates, boundary metrics on one split in an afternoon; if boundary quality improves with embedding averaging, the trade-off claim dies.

one_line: Determiners are not noise: 'the dog' vs 'a dog' presuppose different scene structures, and models that ignore this fail on multi-instance and empty scenes
problem: Referring pipelines strip or ignore determiners, assuming 'a' and 'the' carry no groundable information, yet definite articles presuppose unique identifiable referents while indefinites do not.
core_hypothesis: Because referring-expression training data overwhelmingly uses definite descriptions for unique targets, models have learned neither the uniqueness presupposition of 'the' nor the non-uniqueness tolerance of 'a'; their outputs are determiner-invariant, which is itself a measurable linguistic deficit that predicts specific errors when uniqueness fails (multiple matches) or existence fails (no match).
falsifiable_prediction: Model outputs for 'the X' and 'a X' will be nearly identical (IoU near 1) on all scene types, including scenes with multiple X instances where a human would treat 'the X' as infelicitous and 'a X' as licensing any instance; no current public grounding model will modulate its output distribution by determiner.
why_important: Determiner semantics is a cheap probe of whether models represent referential structure at all; systems for robotics instruction-following need the uniqueness presupposition to detect ambiguous commands rather than guessing.
why_possibly_novel: Ambiguity in referring expressions is studied, but using determiner minimal pairs as a controlled probe of presupposition sensitivity in dense grounding appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct minimal-pair queries over scenes stratified into unique-instance, multi-instance, and zero-instance conditions; measure output divergence between determiner variants and whether any output statistic (entropy over instances, confidence) tracks the presupposition-violating conditions.
main_risk: Demonstrating a deficit without a repair may be received as low-impact unless paired with a fine-tuning fix that instills determiner sensitivity.
default_community_belief: Articles are stop-words for grounding; stripping them is harmless preprocessing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instruction-tuned VLM-LLM hybrids may already modulate behavior by determiner due to language-model pretraining, showing the deficit only in pure dual-encoder models.
fastest_falsification: Fifty minimal pairs across the three scene conditions on two models in an afternoon; if outputs already diverge appropriately by determiner, the deficit claim dies.

one_line: Query format (imperative, declarative, interrogative) is an unreported condition that shifts dense outputs across the same referent
problem: Deployed grounding systems receive 'segment the dog', 'the dog', 'where is the dog?', and 'find dog' interchangeably; papers evaluate exactly one format and never report cross-format variance.
core_hypothesis: Training data for grounding-capable models pairs each format with different supervision styles (imperatives from instruction tuning, bare noun phrases from referring datasets, questions from VQA), so the syntactic frame of the query selects different internal pathways and yields systematically different masks, with bare noun phrases best for dual-encoder models and imperatives best for instruction-tuned models.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-format mask IoU on identical referents will be substantially below self-consistency noise, the best-performing format will differ by model family in the predicted direction, and format-induced variance will be comparable to several points of benchmark metric, enough to reorder similar methods.
why_important: Cross-paper comparisons silently mix formats, and practitioners have no guidance on how to phrase queries; a format-sensitivity report per model would fix both cheaply.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-format sensitivity is documented for LLM text tasks; a quantified cross-format grounding study with the model-family interaction prediction appears missing for dense outputs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run 4 query formats over one referring benchmark on a dual-encoder grounding model and an instruction-tuned segmenting VLM, report per-format metrics and cross-format IoU, and test the predicted family-by-format interaction.
main_risk: The interaction may be swamped by per-model idiosyncrasies, showing format sensitivity without the clean family-level pattern that makes the finding actionable.
default_community_belief: Query phrasing is a cosmetic choice; models ground the noun phrase and ignore the syntactic wrapper.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instruction tuning may have taught models to normalize all formats to the same internal query representation, making cross-format variance negligible on modern systems.
fastest_falsification: One hundred referents, four formats, two models, one afternoon; cross-format IoU above self-consistency levels falsifies.

one_line: Fine-tuning grounding models on templated pseudo-expressions collapses language understanding into template matching
problem: Scaling dense-grounding data is often done by generating expressions from templates ('the {class} on the {position}'); the assumption is that more grounded pairs always help language-conditioned localization.
core_hypothesis: Training on template-generated expressions teaches the model to key on template slots rather than to parse language, so free-form paraphrase performance degrades as templated training proceeds even while templated-format performance improves, with the gap growing monotonically with the templated fraction of training data.
falsifiable_prediction: Holding data volume fixed and varying the templated fraction from 0 to 100 percent, in-template accuracy will rise while paraphrased-query accuracy on the same referents will fall beyond some fraction, producing a crossing point that quantifies safe template usage.
why_important: Synthetic expression generation is the cheapest way to scale grounding data, and everyone uses it; knowing the safe mixing ratio and the collapse signature would directly change data recipes for dense VLM training.
why_possibly_novel: Template overfitting is folklore in NLP, but a dose-response curve for template fraction in dense grounding fine-tuning, with paraphrase-gap as the outcome, appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune a small grounding model at 5 template-fraction levels on the same referent set, evaluate on templated and human-paraphrased versions of held-out referents, and plot both curves against fraction.
main_risk: The effect may depend heavily on template diversity, so a result with one template family may not generalize to modern pipelines that use LLM-generated diverse expressions.
default_community_belief: More grounded text-region pairs are better, and synthetic templated expressions are an unambiguous win for scaling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even rigid templates vary the slot fillers, which may provide enough lexical diversity to keep the language pathway general, making the collapse negligible below extreme fractions.
fastest_falsification: Two fine-tunes (0 and 90 percent templated) of a small model, evaluate both on paraphrases, roughly a day of GPU time; no paraphrase gap falsifies.

one_line: Learned continuous prompts for dense tasks overfit annotation style, transferring worse across datasets than hand-written prompts
problem: Prompt tuning optimizes continuous text-side vectors on a target dense dataset and reports in-distribution gains, assuming the learned prompts encode task semantics rather than dataset quirks.
core_hypothesis: Continuous prompts have enough capacity to absorb dataset-specific annotation conventions (mask tightness, boundary style, which pixels count as the object), so their in-dataset gains come substantially from style matching; under cross-dataset transfer with identical classes, learned prompts will underperform plain hand-written prompts.
falsifiable_prediction: Prompts tuned on dataset A will beat hand-written prompts on A but lose to them on dataset B for the same class vocabulary, and the size of the reversal will correlate with measurable annotation-style distance between A and B (e.g. boundary tightness statistics).
why_important: If prompt tuning mostly buys style adaptation, its reported gains mislead method comparison, and practitioners deploying across domains should prefer hand-written prompts or style-regularized tuning.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-dataset fragility of prompt tuning is documented for classification; attributing dense-task prompt-tuning gains specifically to annotation-style absorption, with a style-distance correlate, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Tune prompts for a fixed open-vocab segmenter on one segmentation dataset, evaluate on a second dataset sharing classes, compare against hand-written prompts both ways, and regress transfer gaps on annotation-style statistics computed from ground-truth masks.
main_risk: Class-distribution differences between datasets could confound the style attribution despite the shared-vocabulary control.
default_community_belief: Learned prompts capture task-relevant semantics and are a robust upgrade over hand-written templates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The prompt vector is low-dimensional relative to the decoder, so style may be absorbed by the decoder during any fine-tuning instead, leaving prompts genuinely semantic.
fastest_falsification: One tuning run plus two cross-evaluations, about a GPU-day; if tuned prompts transfer as well as hand-written ones, the overfitting claim dies.

one_line: Benchmark queries phrased like pretraining captions inflate dense scores: a template-shift evaluation would deflate open-vocab claims
problem: Dense VLM benchmarks query models with phrasings drawn from the same distribution as web caption text, so reported zero-shot numbers conflate visual grounding ability with phrasing familiarity.
core_hypothesis: A meaningful share of open-vocab dense performance is contingent on the query matching caption-like register; re-expressing the same referents in registers rare in captions (technical, colloquial, telegraphic) will drop performance well beyond paraphrase noise, revealing register overfitting as a hidden benchmark inflation.
falsifiable_prediction: Semantically-equivalent register shifts of benchmark queries will reduce dense metrics by a margin several times larger than the variance across caption-register paraphrases, and models with larger text encoders will show smaller but still significant drops.
why_important: Zero-shot claims drive adoption; if numbers are register-inflated, deployment estimates are systematically optimistic for users who do not write like alt-text, which is most users.
why_possibly_novel: Paraphrase robustness is occasionally reported, but organizing the perturbation by register distance from caption text, and framing it as benchmark inflation with a correction factor, appears new for dense tasks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Produce register-shifted versions (telegraphic, formal-technical, conversational) of 500 benchmark queries with human verification of meaning preservation, run 3 public models, and compare drops against within-register paraphrase baselines.
main_risk: Register shifting without meaning drift is hard; residual semantic drift in the rewrites could account for part of the measured drop.
default_community_belief: Zero-shot dense benchmarks measure grounding of meanings, and phrasing effects are second-order noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive text encoders trained on billions of diverse captions may already cover most registers, making the shift penalty genuinely small.
fastest_falsification: Rewrite 100 queries into telegraphic register, run one model in an afternoon; a drop within paraphrase noise falsifies the inflation claim.

one_line: Right-truncation of long queries deletes exactly the disambiguating clause: English puts restrictive modifiers last, and token limits eat them silently
problem: Text encoders in dense pipelines have fixed token budgets and silently truncate long referring expressions from the right; nobody audits what information the truncation removes.
core_hypothesis: English referring expressions place head nouns early and restrictive material (relative clauses, spatial phrases) late, so right-truncation preferentially deletes the disambiguating constraints while preserving the noun, converting specific referring expressions into generic category queries that confidently ground the wrong instance.
falsifiable_prediction: For expressions near or above the token limit in multi-instance scenes, accuracy will collapse toward the accuracy of the bare head noun, errors will be overwhelmingly wrong-instance rather than wrong-category, and left-truncation (an unnatural control) will produce a different, category-level error profile.
why_important: Long queries arise exactly in cluttered scenes where disambiguation matters most; a silent truncation policy converts the hardest cases into confident wrong answers, and the fix (clause-aware compression or warning) is cheap.
why_possibly_novel: Token limits are a known engineering detail, but the linguistic asymmetry argument (restrictive material is right-heavy in English) and the wrong-instance error signature appear unanalyzed for grounding.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct multi-instance scenes with expressions of graded length crossing the encoder's limit, measure accuracy and error type (wrong instance vs wrong category) as a function of tokens-beyond-limit, and compare right- vs left-truncation.
main_risk: Modern pipelines with LLM text towers have long budgets, limiting the finding's applicability to dual-encoder systems with short limits.
default_community_belief: Queries rarely exceed the token budget, and when they do, truncation degrades performance gracefully.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Referring datasets favor short expressions, and users may naturally write short queries, making the regime rare enough to be practically irrelevant.
fastest_falsification: Fifty over-limit expressions in multi-instance scenes on one short-budget model, one afternoon; graceful degradation without the wrong-instance signature falsifies.

one_line: Dense grounding exhibits primacy bias: information in the first sentence of a multi-sentence prompt dominates the mask, regardless of relevance
problem: Instruction-tuned segmenting VLMs accept multi-sentence prompts (context plus request), and the assumption is that the model weights content by relevance rather than by position.
core_hypothesis: Attention and contrastive pooling over text favor early tokens, so referential constraints stated in the first sentence dominate constraints stated later; reordering the same constraint set changes the produced mask, with early-position constraints satisfied at systematically higher rates.
falsifiable_prediction: For prompts containing two independent constraints (category and spatial relation) in both orders, the satisfied-constraint rate will be higher for whichever constraint appears first, producing a measurable order effect on identical constraint sets that no order-invariant grounding model should show.
why_important: Prompt order is invisible in benchmarks (single-sentence queries) but pervasive in real instruction use; an order effect means output correctness depends on how users happen to arrange sentences, a silent reliability issue.
why_possibly_novel: Positional biases are documented for LLM in-context learning; measuring constraint-satisfaction order effects in dense grounding outputs appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 200 two-constraint referring prompts in both orders, run an instruction-tuned segmenter, and compare per-constraint satisfaction rates (category correctness vs relation correctness) across orders with paired tests.
main_risk: Constraint satisfaction must be scored automatically from masks, which requires reliable relation-checking code and clean scenes, restricting stimulus diversity.
default_community_belief: Models integrate all prompt content; sentence order within a short prompt does not meaningfully change dense outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cross-attention over short prompts may be effectively order-insensitive because every token attends to every image region, leaving no room for primacy effects at this scale.
fastest_falsification: Fifty prompt pairs on one model in an afternoon; symmetric constraint satisfaction across orders falsifies.

one_line: Default test-time augmentation silently breaks spatial language: horizontal-flip TTA averages 'left' with 'right' and nobody guards against it
problem: Dense prediction toolkits apply horizontal-flip test-time augmentation by default because it helps class-only segmentation; language-conditioned models are dropped into these pipelines without anyone reconciling flips with lateral spatial terms.
core_hypothesis: For queries containing lateral spatial language, flip-TTA averages a correct prediction with a systematically wrong (mirrored) one, so TTA degrades exactly the query subset containing 'left' or 'right', while improving or preserving the rest, creating a hidden per-query-type regression that aggregate metrics mask.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying a referring benchmark by presence of lateral terms, flip-TTA will reduce accuracy on the lateral stratum (toward the average of correct and mirrored answers) while not harming the non-lateral stratum, and the aggregate metric will show near-zero change, hiding the regression.
why_important: This is a concrete, checkable deployment bug class affecting any language-conditioned model dropped into standard dense-inference tooling; the fix (text-aware TTA that flips spatial words with the image) is trivial once the failure is demonstrated.
why_possibly_novel: TTA is treated as task-agnostic plumbing; an analysis of TTA-language interaction and a text-aware TTA fix appear absent from grounding literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one grounding model with and without flip-TTA on a referring split stratified by lateral terms, measure per-stratum deltas, then implement word-swapping flip-TTA and verify it recovers the lateral stratum.
main_risk: Some pipelines already disable TTA for referring tasks, making the finding an audit of sloppy configurations rather than of published methods.
default_community_belief: TTA is harmless plumbing that at worst does nothing; augmentation choices need no coordination with query text.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Grounding failures on lateral language may already be so common that mirror-averaging changes little, making the bug real but immaterial.
fastest_falsification: One model, one split, TTA on vs off, stratified metrics in two hours; no lateral-stratum regression falsifies.

one_line: Grounding models commit silently to a viewer-centric frame of reference and cannot represent the ambiguity of 'left of the car'
problem: Spatial expressions like 'left of the car' are ambiguous between the viewer's frame and the object's intrinsic frame, yet dense models output one mask with no representation of frame ambiguity, and benchmarks score whichever frame the annotator happened to use.
core_hypothesis: Web and referring data overwhelmingly encode viewer-centric usage, so models resolve every lateral relation in the viewer frame; performance on intrinsic-frame referents (natural for objects with canonical fronts, like cars and chairs) will be at or below chance, and no output statistic will signal the frame conflict.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes where viewer-frame and intrinsic-frame interpretations pick different objects, model choices will align with the viewer frame at a rate far above 50 percent regardless of the relatum's orientation, and accuracy against intrinsic-frame ground truth will be near the inverse of that rate.
why_important: Robotics and AR instructions routinely use intrinsic frames ('to the left of the chair' meaning the chair's left); a silent viewer-frame commitment is an actionable safety-relevant failure with a measurable signature.
why_possibly_novel: Frame of reference is classic in spatial cognition, but a quantified frame-commitment audit for modern dense grounding models with orientation-controlled scenes appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or render scenes with oriented relatum objects and candidate targets on both frame interpretations, query several grounding models with lateral relations, and tabulate frame choice as a function of relatum orientation visibility.
main_risk: Constructing unambiguous orientation cues in natural images is hard; rendered scenes may introduce a domain gap that changes model behavior.
default_community_belief: Lateral relations are handled adequately and frame choice is a linguistic nicety irrelevant to benchmark performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may not use any consistent frame at all, instead exploiting dataset-specific position priors, in which case the viewer-frame commitment story is too generous.
fastest_falsification: Forty two-interpretation scenes on two models in a day; near-random frame choice falsifies the systematic-commitment claim (and reveals something worse).

one_line: Depth prepositions are grounded as 2D image statistics: 'behind' is answered by 'higher and smaller in the image', not by 3D relations
problem: Models score well on 'behind/in front of' queries in standard data, and this is read as 3D relational understanding, ignoring that projective geometry makes 2D proxies (vertical position, size, occlusion) highly predictive in typical photos.
core_hypothesis: Dense models implement depth prepositions as learned 2D correlates, so their accuracy tracks the reliability of those correlates rather than actual 3D layout; on scenes where the 2D proxies are decorrelated from true depth order (elevated platforms, overhead views, size-inverted objects), performance will collapse to chance.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy on 'behind/in front of' queries will be high when 2D proxies agree with depth and near chance when proxies are adversarially decorrelated, and a trivial classifier using only 2D box statistics will reproduce most of the model's decisions on both subsets.
why_important: Depth-relation grounding gates household robotics and driving applications; knowing it is proxy-based tells us it will break precisely in atypical viewpoints, and it defines what supervision (3D-grounded pairs) is actually missing.
why_possibly_novel: Shortcut learning is a known theme, but a proxy-decorrelation stress test specific to depth prepositions in dense grounding, with the proxy-mimicry analysis, appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble proxy-congruent and proxy-incongruent scene sets (using depth maps from existing RGB-D data to verify true depth order), run grounding models on relation queries, and fit a 2D-statistics-only classifier to compare decision agreement.
main_risk: Proxy-incongruent natural scenes are rare and may be visually odd in other ways, introducing confounds beyond the decorrelation of interest.
default_community_belief: Reasonable accuracy on depth-preposition queries demonstrates emergent 3D relational understanding in VLMs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large-scale pretraining may have induced genuine coarse depth features (from motion parallax in video-derived data or depth-correlated textures), letting models survive proxy decorrelation.
fastest_falsification: Sixty incongruent scenes verified with RGB-D ground truth, one model, one day; preserved accuracy falsifies the proxy story.

one_line: Ordinal reference ('the second cup from the left') fails beyond position two because it requires serial scanning that parallel decoders cannot do
problem: Ordinal referring expressions require establishing an ordering and indexing into it; dense decoders process the image in parallel and are simply assumed to handle ordinals like any other spatial phrase.
core_hypothesis: Grounding ordinals requires a sequential counting-and-ranking computation that single-pass cross-attention approximates only for the first and last positions (which reduce to extremal detection); accuracy will be high for 'first/leftmost' and 'last/rightmost', degrade sharply for middle ordinals, and be near chance by the third or fourth position independent of instance count.
falsifiable_prediction: Plotting accuracy against ordinal position across scenes with 4 to 8 aligned instances will show an extremal-position advantage and a steep monotone drop for interior ordinals, and errors will concentrate on off-by-one neighbors, a counting-failure signature distinct from random guessing.
why_important: Ordinals are ubiquitous in natural instructions (pick the third one); a principled account of which spatial indexing operations single-pass architectures can express informs both benchmark design and architectural fixes like iterative decoding.
why_possibly_novel: Counting limits of VLMs are studied for 'how many' questions; transferring the analysis to ordinal dense grounding with the extremal-vs-interior and off-by-one signatures appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct scenes with 4 to 8 near-identical aligned objects (natural shelf and parking images plus rendered controls), query all ordinal positions, and analyze the accuracy-by-position curve and error adjacency matrix on 3 public models.
main_risk: Near-identical aligned instances may already break the models' instance separation for non-ordinal reasons, contaminating the ordinal-specific attribution.
default_community_belief: Ordinal expressions are just another spatial constraint that current grounding models handle with moderate reliability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instruction-tuned VLMs with LLM decoders can perform serial computation across tokens and may genuinely count, showing no interior-position collapse.
fastest_falsification: Rendered 6-object rows, all positions, two models, one afternoon; flat accuracy across positions falsifies.

one_line: Proximity words are grounded in absolute pixels: 'next to' has a fixed pixel radius, so resolution and object scale flip its truth value
problem: 'Near', 'next to', and 'beside' are scale-relative in human usage (near for a building differs from near for a fork), but models process resized fixed-resolution inputs where learned proximity may be a pixel-distance template.
core_hypothesis: Dense models implement proximity terms as an absolute pixel-distance kernel calibrated to training resolution and typical object scales, so judgments will not rescale with object size or image resolution; the same physical scene resized or reframed will flip 'next to' groundings.
falsifiable_prediction: Holding the scene constant and varying capture framing (zoom levels) or input resolution, the pixel distance at which the model transitions between grounding and not grounding a 'next to' relation will stay near-constant in pixels rather than constant relative to object size, an unambiguous absolute-kernel signature.
why_important: Scale-invariance of relational language is assumed by every downstream user; an absolute kernel means silent behavior changes with camera choice and preprocessing, and it suggests a concrete fix via scale-normalized relational features.
why_possibly_novel: Resolution sensitivity is studied for recognition accuracy; measuring the psychophysics-style transition threshold of a relational term as a function of scale appears novel for dense VLMs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build image series with a target-relatum pair at parametrically varied separations, rendered or photographed at multiple zooms, query the relation, and estimate the grounding transition threshold in pixels vs in object-widths across scales.
main_risk: Threshold estimation requires many inference points per scene and a clean binary readout, which some models blur with partial masks.
default_community_belief: Models pick up scale-relative meanings of proximity words from data because captions use them scale-relatively.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Multi-scale feature pyramids may naturally implement object-relative distance coding, giving approximate scale-invariance without anyone designing it.
fastest_falsification: One rendered scene series at three zooms, threshold curves on one model in a day; object-relative constancy falsifies.

one_line: Benchmarks reward ignoring spatial words: deleting the spatial phrase from referring queries barely changes accuracy, exposing dataset leakage
problem: High referring-benchmark scores are cited as evidence that models parse spatial constraints, but if the target is usually identifiable from the noun and salience alone, spatial phrases are decorative and the benchmark cannot detect spatial parsing at all.
core_hypothesis: In standard referring data, the head noun plus dataset position priors suffice to identify the target for most samples, so models achieve their scores largely without using spatial words; a deletion audit (removing spatial phrases at test time) will change predictions on only a small minority of samples, quantifying how little spatial parsing benchmarks actually measure.
falsifiable_prediction: Test-time deletion of spatial modifiers will preserve the original prediction on a large majority of benchmark samples, and the samples where deletion changes the answer will be flagged as the only genuinely spatial subset, on which measured accuracy will be dramatically lower than the headline number.
why_important: This reframes reported spatial-grounding competence as an artifact of benchmark composition, and the deletion-sensitive subset provides an immediately usable hard split for honest evaluation without collecting new data.
why_possibly_novel: Input-ablation audits exist in VQA (question-only baselines); the specific deletion-sensitivity split for dense referring benchmarks, with re-scored spatial competence, appears not to be standard.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Automatically strip spatial phrases from a full referring validation split via dependency parsing, re-run 3 models, compute prediction-change rate and accuracy on changed vs unchanged subsets, and release the split protocol.
main_risk: Parser errors could strip semantically-load-bearing material, overstating the unchanged fraction; manual verification of a subsample is needed.
default_community_belief: Referring benchmark scores measure the ability to resolve spatial constraints expressed in language.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For heavily curated multi-instance benchmarks the noun alone is genuinely insufficient, so deletion may change most predictions and vindicate the benchmarks.
fastest_falsification: Strip-and-rerun on 500 samples with one model in an afternoon; a high prediction-change rate falsifies the leakage claim.

one_line: Square-resize preprocessing distorts the meaning of shape and position words: 'wide', 'tall', and relative positions are judged in squished coordinates
problem: Most dense VLM pipelines resize arbitrary aspect ratios to a square input, and everyone treats this as a benign normalization even though it changes the geometry that shape-and-position language refers to.
core_hypothesis: Models judge dimensional adjectives and positional relations in post-resize coordinates, so a panorama squeezed 2:1 makes genuinely wide objects appear square to the model; grounding of 'the wide X' and fine positional comparatives will systematically err in the direction predicted by the resize distortion, and the error will be a deterministic function of the aspect ratio.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy for dimensional-adjective queries will degrade as source aspect ratio departs from square, with errors biased exactly as the distortion predicts (wide objects missed, tall objects over-selected in landscape sources), and aspect-preserving padding will remove the bias at identical resolution.
why_important: This is a pure preprocessing bug class with a zero-cost fix, and it corrupts any application processing panoramas, documents, or vertical phone video with shape-referential language.
why_possibly_novel: Aspect-ratio effects on accuracy are known generally; connecting them causally to the semantics of dimensional and positional language with a direction-of-error prediction appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take scenes with ground-truth wide/tall objects, evaluate dimensional-adjective grounding under square-resize vs aspect-preserving padding at matched pixel budgets across source aspect ratios, and test for the predicted directional error.
main_risk: Padding changes the effective object resolution and adds border artifacts, so the comparison must control pixel area on the object rather than just input size.
default_community_belief: Square resizing is a standard, harmless preprocessing step whose distortion the model learns to compensate for.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training with the same square-resize means the model may interpret language in post-resize space consistently during training too, partially compensating for the distortion on distorted data.
fastest_falsification: Fifty panorama-derived scenes with wide/tall targets under two preprocessing modes, one model, one afternoon; no directional error difference falsifies.

one_line: Person-deixis breaks dense grounding: 'my left hand' in egocentric video is grounded as the viewer's left, not the camera-wearer's
problem: Egocentric applications (AR assistants, surgical guidance) issue queries with first-person deixis and body-relative frames, but grounding models are trained almost exclusively on third-person web imagery with viewer-centric language.
core_hypothesis: Models lack a representation of the camera-wearer as a referent-anchoring agent, so possessives and body-relative terms in egocentric footage are resolved with third-person heuristics: 'my left hand' will be grounded to the hand on the image's left side (the wearer's right hand), a systematic mirror error with a precise signature.
falsifiable_prediction: On egocentric frames with both hands visible, 'my left hand' queries will select the image-left hand at a rate far above chance, exactly the mirrored-answer signature, and performance will invert (become correct) when frames are horizontally flipped, a manipulation that would not affect a model with true wearer-anchored representation.
why_important: Egocentric grounding is the deployment mode for wearable assistants; a predictable mirror error is both a safety issue and an easy patch (deixis-aware flip) once demonstrated.
why_possibly_novel: Egocentric vision work focuses on activity and hand detection; a deixis-resolution audit for language-conditioned dense models with the flip-inversion test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample a few hundred egocentric frames with both hands visible from existing egocentric datasets, query body-relative referents on grounding models, score against wearer-frame ground truth (derivable from hand-side annotations), and run the flip-inversion control.
main_risk: Hand-side ground truth from datasets may itself be annotated in image frame, requiring careful relabeling to wearer frame.
default_community_belief: Grounding models generalize to egocentric viewpoints, and possessive or body-relative phrasing is a minor lexical variation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Egocentric data in modern pretraining mixes (first-person video with narration) may have taught wearer-anchored deixis already, at least for hands.
fastest_falsification: Fifty two-hand egocentric frames, 'my left/right hand' queries plus flipped controls, one model, two hours; correct wearer-frame answers falsify.

one_line: Vertical spatial language is reliable but lateral language is broken, because horizontal-flip augmentation in vision pretraining erased chirality
problem: Left/right and above/below are treated as interchangeable difficulty in spatial evaluation, but the vision towers inside dense VLMs were pretrained with pervasive horizontal-flip augmentation and none with vertical flips.
core_hypothesis: Flip augmentation forces the visual representation toward mirror invariance, destroying the chirality information that lateral language needs while preserving verticality; therefore dense models will show a stable, architecture-independent asymmetry: above/below grounding substantially more accurate than left/right grounding on matched constructions, and vision towers pretrained without flips will show a smaller gap.
falsifiable_prediction: On relation queries matched for distance, object category, and salience, the vertical-relation accuracy will exceed lateral-relation accuracy by a large margin across model families, and the gap will shrink for models whose vision towers were pretrained without horizontal flips or with flip-aware objectives.
why_important: This attributes a whole class of spatial-grounding failures to a single default augmentation choice, giving pretraining teams a concrete, testable lever (chirality-preserving augmentation) rather than vague 'spatial reasoning is hard' explanations.
why_possibly_novel: The vertical-lateral asymmetry has been noticed anecdotally in VQA settings; the causal attribution to flip augmentation, with the pretraining-recipe comparison as the discriminating test, appears untested for dense grounding.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate matched vertical vs lateral relation grounding across models whose vision-tower augmentation recipes are documented and differ in flip usage; if feasible, fine-tune two small towers (with and without flips) and compare downstream lateral grounding.
main_risk: Pretraining recipes covary with many other factors across public models, so the correlational cross-model comparison may not isolate flips without the controlled fine-tune.
default_community_belief: Spatial relation difficulty is roughly isotropic, and lateral failures reflect general relational weakness rather than a specific augmentation artifact.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Language-side asymmetries (left/right confusability in text corpora) could produce the same behavioral gap without any visual chirality loss, which the controlled fine-tune must disentangle.
fastest_falsification: Matched vertical vs lateral query sets on three models in a day; no consistent vertical advantage falsifies the premise before any causal work.

one_line: 'Without' is invisible: dense models ground 'person without a hat' onto hatted people at near-baseline rates
problem: Negated modifiers are common in real queries (find the door without a lock, the person without a badge), but referring benchmarks contain almost no negation, so the behavior is unmeasured and assumed to be a mild weakness rather than a systematic inversion.
core_hypothesis: Contrastive text encoders represent 'person without a hat' in a region dominated by the tokens 'person' and 'hat', so the negated attribute acts as a positive attractor; dense outputs will not merely ignore the negation but will preferentially select instances that possess the negated attribute when both types are present.
falsifiable_prediction: In scenes containing both an attribute-positive and an attribute-negative instance, negated queries will select the attribute-positive instance at a rate at or above the rate for the un-negated query, demonstrating attraction rather than mere ignorance; scrambled-token controls will show the effect is driven by the attribute word's presence.
why_important: Attraction (not just ignorance) means negated safety queries actively retrieve the wrong instances, the worst possible polarity for filtering and compliance applications, and it dictates that fixes must restructure text conditioning rather than just add negation data.
why_possibly_novel: Negation blindness is documented for image-text retrieval; the attraction-vs-ignorance distinction measured at instance level in dense grounding, with paired-scene controls, appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate 150 paired scenes (instances with and without a target attribute co-present), query negated and affirmative forms on 3 grounding models, and compare selection rates across the three logical possibilities (correct, ignore, attract).
main_risk: Attribute detectability itself may be weak (hats may be low-salience), muddying whether failures come from negation handling or attribute grounding.
default_community_belief: Models are somewhat weak at negation but roughly ignore it, defaulting to the head noun; explicit negation failures are a text-encoder detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instruction-tuned segmenters with LLM text processing may genuinely parse negation, showing correct behavior and limiting the finding to dual-encoder architectures.
fastest_falsification: Thirty paired scenes, negated vs affirmative queries, one model, two hours; correct-selection dominance falsifies.

one_line: Grounding models cannot say 'not present': under empty-target queries they emit confident masks, and no benchmark penalizes it
problem: Standard referring and open-vocab segmentation evaluation assumes the queried object exists in the image, so the abstention behavior of dense models under absent referents is both untrained and unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Because training never presents empty-target examples with an abstain label, dense decoders implement a normalized selection over image regions (pick the best match) rather than a detection decision (is there a match), so under absent referents they produce well-formed masks whose confidence distribution overlaps heavily with correct predictions, making post-hoc thresholding fundamentally weak.
falsifiable_prediction: On an empty-target suite built by querying objects verified absent, mask-emission rate will be near 100 percent, and the best achievable abstention operating point using any output statistic (max score, mask area, entropy) will be far worse than the same statistic's discrimination on presence-matched hard positives, quantifying an architecture-level gap.
why_important: Every real deployment faces absent referents (users ask for things not in the image); quantifying the selection-vs-detection gap converts a folklore weakness into a measured architectural requirement for dense heads with calibrated null hypotheses.
why_possibly_novel: Absence handling is known to be weak anecdotally; a systematic operating-characteristic analysis comparing abstention statistics against matched hard positives for dense models appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 1000 empty-target queries by pairing images with verified-absent categories (using existing exhaustive-annotation datasets to guarantee absence), run 3 models, and compute abstention ROC curves for every available output statistic against matched present-object controls.
main_risk: Verifying true absence requires exhaustively annotated images, restricting the domain diversity of the suite.
default_community_belief: Low confidence scores identify absent targets well enough, so thresholding solves the abstention problem in practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For some model families the background logit or a no-object query token may already provide a usable null hypothesis, making thresholded abstention respectable.
fastest_falsification: Two hundred absent-target queries on one model, ROC of max-score abstention in an afternoon; strong separability falsifies the gap claim.

one_line: Hallucinated masks are scene-conditional: absent-but-plausible objects get grounded at high rates while absent-and-implausible ones do not
problem: Dense hallucination is reported as a single rate, hiding whether the driver is visual mismatch or the language prior of scene-object co-occurrence.
core_hypothesis: The hallucination rate for an absent object is primarily a function of its co-occurrence prior with the scene context (keyboards in offices, gulls at beaches), not of low-level visual similarity; models fill in expected objects at contextually canonical locations, so hallucination is a structured scene-completion behavior rather than noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-query hallucination rates on (a) scene-object co-occurrence statistics estimated from public caption corpora and (b) visual similarity of the best-matching region to the queried class, the co-occurrence term will dominate, and hallucinated masks will cluster at the spatial locations where the object typically appears in scenes of that type.
why_important: If hallucination is prior-driven and spatially canonical, then it is predictable before inference from text statistics alone, enabling cheap query-level risk scoring, and it implicates training-data statistics rather than visual features as the fix target.
why_possibly_novel: Object hallucination is heavily studied for captioning and VQA; decomposing dense-mask hallucination into co-occurrence vs visual-similarity drivers with spatial-canonicality analysis appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Query verified-absent objects spanning high and low co-occurrence with each scene across an exhaustively-annotated dataset, record mask emission and locations, and fit the two-factor regression plus a spatial concentration analysis against typical-location priors.
main_risk: Co-occurrence and visual similarity are themselves correlated (offices contain keyboard-like laptops), demanding careful covariate control.
default_community_belief: Hallucination reflects insufficient visual grounding and is best reduced by better visual features or more data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask emission may be driven mostly by whatever region weakly matches the query visually, with context priors contributing little once a lookalike exists.
fastest_falsification: Fifty high-prior and fifty low-prior absent queries on one model in a day; equal hallucination rates falsify the prior-driven account.

one_line: The score margin between a query and its negation is a free, label-free mask-quality estimator nobody uses
problem: Dense predictions ship without reliable quality estimates; existing confidence scores are miscalibrated, and quality estimation is treated as requiring extra heads or ensembles.
core_hypothesis: Even though models handle negation poorly for grounding, the difference between the mask score under the original query and under contrast queries (negated attribute, swapped relation, shuffled words) carries usable information: correct masks are more contrastive-sensitive than hallucinated or wrong-instance masks, so a counterfactual-margin statistic will predict mask IoU better than raw confidence at zero training cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a referring benchmark, the rank correlation between counterfactual margin and actual mask IoU will exceed that of raw confidence, and combining margins over a small battery of automatic counterfactuals will further improve selective-prediction risk-coverage curves without any learned parameters.
why_important: A label-free quality signal upgrades every deployed grounding model immediately (flagging low-margin outputs for review) and provides a new model-diagnostic axis: which counterfactuals a model is insensitive to reveals what it ignores.
why_possibly_novel: Counterfactual probing is used for interpretability and for training-time contrastive losses; repurposing inference-time counterfactual margins as a selective-prediction score for dense outputs appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement 5 automatic counterfactual generators (attribute negation, relation swap, noun hypernym, word shuffle, distractor noun), compute margins on a validation split with 2 models, and compare risk-coverage curves against confidence baselines.
main_risk: If models are globally insensitive to text perturbations, margins will be uniformly small and noisy, providing no discrimination.
default_community_belief: Mask confidence or IoU-prediction heads are the way to estimate output quality; text-side perturbations are for robustness testing, not quality estimation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Margin informativeness presupposes partial compositional sensitivity, which the same research agenda shows is weak; the signal may exist only for the easiest samples where confidence already works.
fastest_falsification: One model, one counterfactual type, 500 samples, correlation with IoU in an afternoon; no advantage over confidence falsifies.

one_line: Complement queries ('everything except the people') expose whether models compose set operations in language or only retrieve positives
problem: Real editing and safety workflows need complements (blur everything except faces, segment all but the road), yet dense grounding is evaluated exclusively on positive retrieval, and it is unknown whether any model composes complementation internally.
core_hypothesis: Text-conditioned dense heads implement similarity-to-referent, not logical operations over referents; complement queries will therefore produce either the positive mask itself (negation ignored), a generic salience mask, or degenerate full-image masks, and no current public model will produce reliable complements even though the operation is trivially computable from its own positive output.
falsifiable_prediction: Complement-query IoU against true complements will be far below the IoU obtained by simply inverting the model's own positive-query mask, an internal-inconsistency gap that quantifies missing compositionality; the gap will persist across phrasings ('except', 'other than', 'not including').
why_important: The inversion gap is a rare case where the ceiling is computable from the model's own outputs, making it a sharp, self-normalizing benchmark of language-side compositionality that does not depend on model quality on positives.
why_possibly_novel: Set-theoretic query composition (complement, union, difference expressed in words) as a measured capability for dense models, benchmarked against self-inversion ceilings, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 300 scenes, run positive queries and complement phrasings on 3 models, compute complement IoU vs inverted-positive IoU per model, and report the inconsistency gap and its phrasing sensitivity.
