main_risk: Instruction-tuned segmenters may have seen 'except' patterns during instruction tuning, splitting model families into haves and have-nots and complicating a single headline claim.
default_community_belief: Complement handling is a niche linguistic capability that will arrive automatically with better instruction tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some models may map 'everything except X' onto background-of-X representations learned from panoptic-style data, performing surprisingly well and closing the gap.
fastest_falsification: Thirty scenes, three complement phrasings, one model in two hours; complement IoU near the inversion ceiling falsifies.

one_line: Large query vocabularies self-poison: false-positive rates per query grow with the semantic density of the vocabulary, not just its size
problem: Practitioners scale open-vocab detectors by querying ever-larger vocabularies, assuming per-class behavior is independent of what else is in the query list.
core_hypothesis: As vocabulary density increases (more classes per unit of embedding space), each absent class gains close semantic neighbors that are present, and score competition plus near-neighbor confusion drives absent-class false positives up superlinearly; the operative variable is local embedding crowding, not raw vocabulary size.
falsifiable_prediction: Holding image set and vocabulary size fixed, vocabularies constructed to be semantically dense will show materially higher absent-class false-positive rates than sparse vocabularies of equal size, and per-class FP rates will regress on local crowding (distance to nearest co-queried neighbor) more strongly than on vocabulary size.
why_important: This changes deployment guidance from 'bigger vocabulary is free recall' to 'vocabulary composition is a tunable precision knob', and motivates crowding-aware score normalization as a simple fix for open-vocab dense systems.
why_possibly_novel: Vocabulary-size effects are occasionally noted; isolating semantic crowding as the causal variable with density-controlled vocabulary construction appears unstudied for dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct equal-size dense and sparse vocabularies via embedding-space sampling, evaluate absent-class FP rates on exhaustively-annotated images with one open-vocab detector and one segmenter, and fit the crowding regression.
main_risk: Dense vocabularies are also harder for annotation verification (fine-grained absence is harder to guarantee), risking label noise in the FP measurements.
default_community_belief: Query lists are independent probes; adding classes to the vocabulary does not change behavior on other classes beyond softmax renormalization trivia.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sigmoid-scored (non-competing) architectures may show no crowding effect, localizing the problem to softmax pipelines and reducing generality.
fastest_falsification: Two 200-class vocabularies (dense vs sparse) over one annotated split, one model, one day; equal FP rates falsify.

one_line: 'Present but small' and 'absent' are inseparable in open-vocab score space, making abstention on small objects fundamentally unreliable
problem: Thresholding is the universal abstention mechanism for open-vocab dense models, implicitly assuming score distributions for absent targets and hard-to-see present targets are separable.
core_hypothesis: The dense score for a small present object is generated by the same weak-evidence regime as the best spurious match for an absent object, so their score distributions converge as object size shrinks; below some size, no threshold can trade precision for recall acceptably, defining a computable abstention floor that is a property of the representation, not the threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: Plotting the overlap between absent-target and present-target score distributions as a function of true object size will show monotone convergence to full overlap below a characteristic size (in patch units), and this characteristic size will track the vision tower's patch size across models rather than their benchmark accuracy.
why_important: An abstention floor keyed to patch size gives deployment engineers a concrete spec (below N patches, do not trust presence decisions) and redirects research from threshold tuning to representation changes for the small-object regime.
why_possibly_novel: Small-object weakness and abstention are studied separately; unifying them as a size-indexed separability analysis with a patch-size scaling law appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On exhaustively-annotated data, bin present targets by size, collect score distributions for present bins and matched absent queries across 3 models with different patch sizes, and estimate the size at which distribution overlap crosses a fixed level.
main_risk: Score distributions depend on the scoring head, not just the representation, so cross-model comparison must normalize scoring mechanisms carefully.
default_community_belief: Better thresholds or calibration can always buy usable abstention; small-object failures are a recall problem, not an abstention problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-resolution multi-scale architectures may keep distributions separable well below one patch of the nominal grid via learned upsampling, breaking the patch-size law.
fastest_falsification: One model, size-binned overlap curves from a single annotated split, one day; no size-dependent convergence falsifies.

one_line: Negated attributes attract: 'the cup that is not red' selects the red cup more often than chance, inverting the query's meaning
problem: Attribute negation inside referring expressions is assumed to at worst be ignored, defaulting to noun-level behavior; whether it actively inverts selection is untested at instance level.
core_hypothesis: Because the attribute token contributes a positive similarity component regardless of the negator, in scenes with multiple same-category instances the negated-attribute query concentrates probability on instances bearing the attribute, so accuracy falls below the noun-only baseline, the signature of active inversion rather than passive ignorance.
falsifiable_prediction: In controlled multi-instance scenes, accuracy for 'the X that is not A' will be significantly below accuracy for the bare 'the X' query (which is at chance among instances), while accuracy for 'the X that is A' is above chance, yielding the strict ordering affirmative > bare > negated that only the attraction account predicts.
why_important: The strict ordering distinguishes two mechanistic accounts (ignoring vs attraction) with different fixes: data augmentation might fix ignoring, but attraction requires architectural handling of polarity in text conditioning, informing where effort should go.
why_possibly_novel: Negation weakness is well known; the three-way ordering test that separates ignorance from inversion in dense instance selection appears not to have been run.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 200 scenes with 2 to 4 same-category instances differing in one attribute, run affirmative, bare, and negated queries on 3 models, and test the predicted accuracy ordering with paired statistics.
main_risk: Attribute salience imbalance (red things are more salient) could mimic attraction, requiring salience-controlled counterbalancing across attribute values.
default_community_belief: Negation is ignored, so negated queries behave like the noun-only query and land at chance among instances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Salience confounds and dataset quirks might produce apparent attraction without any systematic text-side mechanism, which the counterbalanced design must rule out.
fastest_falsification: Forty counterbalanced scenes, three query forms, one model, two hours; negated accuracy at the bare-noun level falsifies attraction.

one_line: Plural queries collapse instances into blobs: 'the dogs' returns one connected mask whose topology depends on instance spacing, not on countability
problem: Referring segmentation treats plural expressions as a mask-union problem, and evaluation with region IoU cannot see whether the model represents the plurality as distinct individuals or as a single texture-like region.
core_hypothesis: Dense decoders trained with single-region supervision produce plural masks via spatial smoothing rather than instance enumeration, so mask topology (number of connected components) will track instance spacing (merging when gaps fall below a feature-map-resolution threshold) instead of true instance count, revealing that plurality is rendered, not represented.
falsifiable_prediction: Across scenes with fixed instance count but varied spacing, the number of connected components in plural-query masks will fall from N toward 1 as spacing shrinks, with the merge threshold predicted by feature-map stride; component count will be a poor estimator of true count even when region IoU is high.
why_important: Downstream users routinely extract instances from plural masks by connected components; if topology is spacing-driven, all such pipelines silently miscount in crowded scenes, and region-IoU benchmarks cannot detect it.
why_possibly_novel: Plural referring is evaluated with region overlap; a topology-vs-spacing analysis with a stride-derived merge threshold prediction appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compose or select scenes with controlled instance spacing at fixed counts, run plural queries on 3 models, and plot connected-component count against normalized spacing, testing the stride-threshold prediction.
main_risk: Ground-truth plural masks in existing data are themselves unions, so training-data topology may explain merging independent of decoder resolution limits.
default_community_belief: High plural-query IoU means the model handles plurality; mask topology is an irrelevant detail of rendering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Query-based instance decoders (one query per instance) may genuinely enumerate and only merge at rendering, in which case component collapse reflects output rasterization rather than representation failure.
fastest_falsification: One spacing-series of 20 scenes, one model, component counts in two hours; spacing-independent topology falsifies.

one_line: Universal quantifiers are dropped: 'every dog' and 'the dog' produce the same single-instance mask because referring data taught one-expression-one-object
problem: Referring datasets pair each expression with exactly one region, embedding a hidden one-referent prior into every model trained on them; quantified expressions that demand exhaustive selection have no representation in this training distribution.
core_hypothesis: Models trained under the one-referent prior treat quantifiers as stop-words, so 'every/all X' queries will return masks covering approximately one salient instance rather than the full set, and coverage will not improve with the number of quantifier words, demonstrating a data-inherited structural bias rather than a capacity limit.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-instance scenes, recall of 'every X' queries against the full instance set will be close to the recall of 'the X' (single-instance behavior) and far from union coverage; models additionally trained on grounded-caption or panoptic-style data (exposure to exhaustive sets) will show measurably higher quantifier recall, tracking training exposure.
why_important: Exhaustive selection is the semantics behind many practical commands (redact all faces, count all products); attributing its failure to a specific dataset convention identifies the exact data intervention needed, rather than blaming model scale.
why_possibly_novel: Quantifier handling is studied in VQA text answers; measuring exhaustive-mask coverage as a function of training-data referent cardinality conventions appears new for dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 'the X' vs 'all X' vs 'every X' coverage on multi-instance scenes across models with documented training mixtures, and correlate quantifier recall with whether their training included exhaustive-set supervision.
main_risk: Training mixtures of public models are only partially documented, weakening the exposure correlation without controlled fine-tuning experiments.
default_community_belief: Bigger and better-instruction-tuned models progressively acquire quantifier semantics; failures are generic capability gaps.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instruction tuning may already include enough 'segment all' phrasing to teach exhaustive selection, decoupling the behavior from referring-data conventions.
fastest_falsification: Fifty multi-instance scenes, three query forms, one model, two hours; near-union coverage for quantified queries falsifies.

one_line: Numerals in queries are decorative: 'three cats' neither selects three nor signals conflict when the image shows five
problem: Numerically-quantified referring expressions presuppose a count match between query and scene; models are assumed to use the numeral for selection or at least to be perturbed by count conflicts.
core_hypothesis: Dense models treat numerals as unweighted tokens: the produced mask's instance coverage will be statistically identical whether the query says two, three, or five, and count-conflicting queries (asking for three when five are present) will produce neither an error signal nor a principled subset, exposing that cardinality is absent from the text-conditioning interface.
falsifiable_prediction: A numeral-swap test (same scene, numerals two through six) will produce near-identical masks (pairwise IoU close to self-consistency), and a numeral-deletion test will show no significant output change, jointly demonstrating numeral invisibility; subset selection under conflict will match salience order rather than any count-aware strategy.
why_important: Numeral invisibility means any pipeline trusting counted requests (grab two items, verify four bolts) gets arbitrary subsets with full confidence; the deletion test also gives a clean, cheap diagnostic for whether future models acquire cardinality.
why_possibly_novel: Counting is studied as answer generation ('how many'); cardinality as an input constraint for dense selection, measured by swap and deletion invariance, appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On scenes with 4 to 8 instances, run numeral-varied and numeral-deleted queries across 3 models, compute swap-invariance and deletion-invariance statistics, and characterize which subsets are returned under conflicts.
main_risk: Some instruction-tuned models emit textual complaints about count conflicts without changing masks, requiring a decision about what counts as using the numeral.
default_community_belief: Models partially use numerals, and count handling improves steadily with instruction tuning and scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: LLM-decoder segmenters that emit one mask token per instance may genuinely condition mask count on the numeral, breaking swap invariance.
fastest_falsification: Ten scenes, numerals two through six, one model, one hour; masks that scale with the numeral falsify.

one_line: Collective vs distributive reference is unrepresented: 'the team' and 'the players' get the same mask though they demand different topologies
problem: Language distinguishes collective entities (the team, the pile, the crowd) from distributed pluralities (the players, the boxes, the people), but dense outputs are evaluated only by pixel overlap, where the two are indistinguishable when spatially coincident.
core_hypothesis: Models learned both phrasings against similar union-style masks, so they encode no topological distinction: collective queries will not produce more merged, hull-like masks, and distributive queries will not produce more instance-separated masks; the linguistic distinction is measurable only in mask topology, and it will be absent.
falsifiable_prediction: Across scenes containing groups, topological statistics of masks (component count, convexity, hull-fill ratio) will not differ between collective and distributive phrasings of the same group, while human annotators asked the same two questions produce robustly different mask topologies on identical scenes.
why_important: The collective-distributive distinction is the semantic backbone of group-level commands (move the pile vs move each box); knowing models lack it, and that pixel-IoU evaluation cannot see it, motivates topology-aware metrics for grounding evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Group reference appears in linguistics and in crowd analysis separately; a topology-based behavioral test of collective vs distributive grounding appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect 100 group scenes, obtain human masks for both phrasings as topology ground truth, run 3 models on both phrasings, and compare model topology deltas against human topology deltas.
main_risk: Human annotators may also disagree on collective boundaries (does the team include the coach), inflating human variance and weakening the contrast.
default_community_belief: Pixel-level evaluation captures what matters about plural grounding; topology is a rendering detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instruction-tuned models may produce different verbal framings but identical masks for good reason: many downstream uses genuinely need only the union.
fastest_falsification: Twenty scenes, both phrasings, one model, topology statistics in two hours; significant topology modulation by phrasing falsifies.

one_line: Group grounding has a density phase transition: below a crowding threshold models return instances, above it they return stuff-like regions, with a hysteresis nobody has mapped
problem: Queries like 'the crowd' or 'the flock' require treating many things as one mass; models handle sparse groups and dense masses differently, but the transition between instance-mode and mass-mode outputs is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Dense models switch between two learned regimes (thing-like instance masks and stuff-like texture masks) as a function of instance density in the image, with an abrupt transition at a characteristic density set by feature-map resolution; near the transition, outputs are unstable and small image changes flip the regime, explaining erratic behavior on mid-density groups.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping instance density continuously (by cropping or compositing), output statistics (component count, boundary roughness, per-instance recall) will show a sharp sigmoidal transition rather than a linear trend, and near-threshold images will show maximal output variance under small perturbations, the instability signature of a regime boundary.
why_important: Mid-density groups (queues, shelves, herds) are common in surveillance, retail, and agriculture; locating the unstable regime tells practitioners which scenes need special handling and gives architects a target (smooth interpolation between regimes).
why_possibly_novel: Crowd analysis and instance segmentation are separate literatures; identifying and measuring a density-driven regime transition inside language-conditioned dense models appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build density sweeps for 3 group categories via controlled compositing, run group queries at each density on 2 models, fit transition curves to output statistics, and measure perturbation variance versus density.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts could themselves drive output changes, requiring natural-image density series as a control.
default_community_belief: Group segmentation quality degrades smoothly with crowding; there is no qualitative regime change to worry about.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The transition may be gradual and architecture-dependent, showing up as a boring monotone trend rather than a sharp, general phenomenon.
fastest_falsification: One 10-step density sweep, one model, output statistics in three hours; a linear trend without variance peak falsifies.

one_line: 'Both' is broken asymmetrically: dual quantification selects one or all, revealing that the two-instance case falls between learned regimes
problem: The word 'both' presupposes exactly two referents and demands selecting exactly that pair, a minimal test of cardinality-aware selection that no dense benchmark isolates.
core_hypothesis: Because referring data teaches single selection and quantifier data (when present) teaches exhaustive selection, the dual case has no training regime: 'both X' in scenes with exactly two X will underperform 'the two X' and 'all X' phrasings, and in scenes with three or more X the presupposition violation will go unnoticed, with the model returning an arbitrary-cardinality set.
falsifiable_prediction: Coverage of exactly-two ground truth under 'both X' will be significantly lower than under 'all X' in two-instance scenes (a phrasing gap unexplainable by semantics, since they coincide there), and 'both' in three-instance scenes will return one or three instances at high rates without any conflict signal.
why_important: The two-instance case is the smallest possible cardinality test, cheap to construct at scale and diagnostic: a model that cannot select exactly two on demand cannot be trusted for any counted selection, whatever its benchmark scores.
why_possibly_novel: Dual quantification and its presupposition seem never to have been used as a probe for dense grounding; the phrasing-gap design ('both' vs 'all' where they coincide) is a clean novel control.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate 200 two-instance and 100 three-instance scenes, run 'both/all/the two' phrasings on 3 models, and compare exact-pair coverage and cardinality distributions across phrasings and scene types.
main_risk: Tokenizer treatment of 'both' inside longer expressions may vary across models, adding text-side noise to a small phrasing effect.
default_community_belief: 'Both' is an easy high-frequency word; if a model handles 'all', the two-element case is trivially included.
why_it_might_be_wrong: 'Both' may be frequent enough in instruction-tuning data to be well-grounded, making the phrasing gap negligible on modern models.
fastest_falsification: Forty two-instance scenes, two phrasings, one model, ninety minutes; equal coverage for 'both' and 'all' falsifies.

one_line: Attribute binding fails silently in dense grounding: 'the red cup next to the blue cup' picks a cup by salience because attributes are pooled bag-of-words style
problem: Scenes with attribute-swapped distractors (red cup and blue cup) are the minimal test of whether text conditioning binds attributes to nouns, but standard referring metrics average over mostly-unambiguous scenes and hide binding failures.
core_hypothesis: Contrastive text encoders pool token information with weak syntactic structure, so the conditioning vector for 'red cup next to blue cup' is nearly symmetric to its attribute-swapped counterpart; dense selection in swap scenes will hover near chance, and the model's similarity gap between the two readings will be a small fraction of its gap on non-compositional controls.
falsifiable_prediction: On a swap-scene suite, instance-selection accuracy will fall from high (unambiguous controls) to near 50 percent (swap scenes), and the drop will be far larger for dual-encoder grounding models than for LLM-decoder segmenters, tracking text-side compositional capacity rather than visual capability.
why_important: Binding is the difference between grounding language and matching keywords; a per-model binding score would let practitioners predict failure on any query with multiple same-category instances, one of the most common real-world configurations.
why_possibly_novel: Binding is well studied for text-to-image generation and retrieval; a controlled instance-selection binding benchmark for dense grounding with the architecture-contrast prediction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compose 300 swap scenes across 10 attribute pairs and 15 categories (natural where possible, composited otherwise), run 4 models spanning both architecture families, and report binding accuracy alongside matched non-compositional controls.
main_risk: Composited swap scenes may introduce artifacts that models key on; natural swap scenes are rarer and less controlled.
default_community_belief: Referring models handle attribute-noun composition adequately, as evidenced by strong benchmark scores on expressions containing attributes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmark expressions with attributes may already include enough swap-like distractors that high scores genuinely certify binding, making the suite redundant.
fastest_falsification: Forty swap scenes, one dual-encoder model, two hours; above-80-percent selection accuracy falsifies the near-chance claim.

one_line: Size adjectives are grounded in absolute pixels, not category norms: 'the small dog' means small-in-image, so distance masquerades as size
problem: Human size adjectives are category-relative (a small building dwarfs a large dog) and viewing-distance invariant, but dense models see only projected pixel extents, and nobody has separated the two computations behaviorally.
core_hypothesis: Models implement 'small X' as a rank over pixel areas of X-instances in the image, without correcting for category norms or depth-induced scaling, so a distant large dog will be selected for 'the small dog' over a nearby small dog whenever projected areas invert the true sizes.
falsifiable_prediction: In scenes where projected area and physical size disagree (verified via depth or scene geometry), size-adjective selections will follow projected area at a rate near ceiling, and cross-category size queries ('the small animal' between a small elephant and a large cat) will follow raw pixel area rather than category-relative size.
why_important: Size language is pervasive in disambiguation; knowing it is a projected-area rank tells users precisely when it breaks (depth variation, cross-category comparison) and specifies the missing ingredient as category-norm or metric-depth integration.
why_possibly_novel: Size-term grounding has psychophysics literature for humans; a mechanistic determination of which size variable dense VLMs actually rank appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble scenes with depth-verified size inversions from RGB-D datasets plus cross-category comparisons, query size adjectives on 3 models, and fit choice models comparing projected-area, physical-size, and category-relative predictors.
main_risk: Depth-verified natural inversions are uncommon, and rendered scenes may not transfer, limiting sample size in the critical cells.
default_community_belief: Size adjectives are handled sensibly because size is a simple visual attribute that contrastive pretraining captures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web captions describe physical size, not projected size, so text-image pairing may have taught partial depth-corrected size after all.
fastest_falsification: Twenty inversion scenes, one model, two hours; physical-size-consistent choices falsify the projected-area account.

one_line: There is a stable attribute hierarchy in dense grounding: color > material > state > relational, and it mirrors caption statistics rather than visual difficulty
problem: Attribute grounding is reported as one aggregate number; whether different attribute types fail at systematically different rates, and why, is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: Attribute-type grounding quality follows the frequency and reliability with which each type is captioned in web data (color is captioned often and reliably, states like 'open' or 'wet' rarely and noisily), producing a stable cross-model hierarchy that is predicted by caption statistics and not by human visual discriminability of the attribute.
falsifiable_prediction: Across models, per-attribute-type accuracy on a controlled disambiguation suite will rank color highest and relational or state attributes lowest, the ranking will correlate strongly with attribute-mention frequencies estimated from public caption corpora, and will correlate weakly with human reaction-time-based discriminability of the same attributes on the same images.
why_important: The hierarchy converts anecdotal attribute failures into a predictable map, and the caption-statistics attribution redirects data collection toward under-captioned attribute types instead of undirected scaling.
why_possibly_novel: Attribute studies exist for classification-style probing; a dense-grounding attribute-type hierarchy with a dual regression against caption statistics and human discriminability appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build disambiguation scenes for 8 attribute types (20 scenes each), evaluate 3 models, estimate attribute-mention frequencies from a public caption corpus, and run the two correlations.
main_risk: Constructing equally-hard scenes across attribute types is difficult; hardness imbalance could masquerade as a hierarchy.
default_community_belief: Attribute grounding difficulty reflects visual difficulty; models fail on subtle attributes and succeed on obvious ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Visual and caption-statistical difficulty are correlated (people caption what is visually obvious), so the discriminating power between the two accounts may be low in practice.
fastest_falsification: Four attribute types, ten scenes each, one model, one afternoon; a ranking that tracks visual discriminability rather than caption frequency falsifies.

one_line: Compositional queries degrade multiplicatively: each added attribute multiplies error odds, revealing independent per-constraint filtering with no joint parsing
problem: Queries stack constraints ('the small red cup on the left'), yet accuracy is only reported per benchmark, never as a function of constraint count, leaving the scaling law of compositional grounding unknown.
core_hypothesis: Dense models apply constraints as approximately independent soft filters over instances rather than parsing a joint description, so the odds of correct selection decompose approximately multiplicatively over constraints; deviations below multiplicative (subadditive accuracy) will appear exactly when constraints must interact (relational constraints referencing another constrained object).
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes constructed so each constraint alone has measurable selectivity, observed accuracy at k constraints will match the product of single-constraint accuracies for independent constraints, and fall significantly below the product for interacting constraints, yielding a two-regime scaling law.
why_important: A validated scaling law lets practitioners predict reliability of complex queries from cheap single-constraint measurements, and the independent-filter mechanism explains why more descriptive queries often hurt rather than help.
why_possibly_novel: Compositional evaluation exists for VQA and retrieval; a quantitative odds-decomposition test distinguishing independent filtering from joint parsing in dense grounding appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Design factorial scenes where constraint selectivities are individually measurable, query all constraint subsets on 3 models, and compare observed accuracy at k constraints against the product-model prediction with interaction terms.
main_risk: Single-constraint selectivities vary per scene, requiring careful per-scene normalization before the product model can be tested.
default_community_belief: More descriptive queries help models find the target; added constraints are additional signal, not additional failure surface.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention over text may create constraint interference even for logically independent constraints, breaking the product model in a direction the two-regime story does not predict.
fastest_falsification: One factorial scene set (3 constraints, all subsets), one model, one day; accuracy that stays flat or improves with constraint count falsifies.

one_line: Evidence hierarchy under conflict: when the attribute contradicts the image ('the wooden dog'), the noun wins and the conflict leaves no trace in output confidence
problem: Real queries contain errors and mismatches; how dense models arbitrate between contradicting textual constraints and visual evidence, and whether the arbitration is visible in any output signal, is unstudied.
core_hypothesis: Text conditioning contributes a fixed-precedence evidence hierarchy (head noun strongest, then attributes, then relations), so conflicting attributes are overridden by noun matching without any confidence penalty; the model will ground 'the wooden dog' on an ordinary dog with confidence indistinguishable from 'the dog', making query-image mismatch undetectable downstream.
falsifiable_prediction: Across conflict types, selection will follow the hierarchy (noun overrides attribute overrides relation) with high consistency, and output confidence distributions under conflict will be statistically indistinguishable from no-conflict controls, failing every conflict-detection test at fixed false-alarm rates.
why_important: Conflict-blindness means user typos or stale queries produce confident wrong masks with no detectable signature; establishing the hierarchy also gives a compact behavioral spec of what current text conditioning actually encodes.
why_possibly_novel: Conflict arbitration between language components in dense grounding, and the claim that confidence carries no conflict information, appear unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct conflict suites (wrong attribute, wrong relation, wrong noun with right attributes) over natural scenes, run 3 models, tabulate override directions, and test confidence separability between conflict and control queries.
main_risk: Some conflicts create genuinely ambiguous references where override behavior is arguably correct, requiring careful annotation of expected behavior per item.
default_community_belief: Mismatched queries produce degraded confidence that downstream thresholds can catch.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive scoring may genuinely subtract for contradicted attributes, giving measurable confidence dips that make conflict detection feasible after calibration.
fastest_falsification: Fifty conflict queries vs matched controls, confidence histograms on one model, two hours; separable distributions falsify conflict-blindness.

one_line: Grounding accuracy falls off a cliff at one level of syntactic embedding: 'the cup on the tray' works, 'the cup on the tray near the sink' collapses
problem: Referring expressions in the wild embed clauses recursively, but benchmarks skew shallow, so the depth at which models stop parsing and start keyword-matching is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Dense models resolve one level of head-plus-modifier structure through learned co-attention patterns but have no mechanism for recursive attachment, so accuracy as a function of parse depth will show a cliff between depth 1 and depth 2 rather than gradual decline, and depth-2 errors will concentrate on attachment mistakes (grounding the inner relatum's match) rather than random errors.
falsifiable_prediction: On a depth-controlled suite with distractors forcing correct attachment at every level, accuracy will drop disproportionately from depth 1 to depth 2 across model families, and the modal error at depth 2 will be selection of the intermediate object (the tray or the sink region), a diagnostic attachment-failure signature.
why_important: A depth cliff with attachment-error signatures tells builders exactly which query complexity is safe, and points to iterative or structured decoding as the necessary fix rather than more data at shallow depths.
why_possibly_novel: Query complexity is usually measured in word count; controlling syntactic depth with attachment-forcing distractors and analyzing the error type appears new for dense grounding.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate depth-0 through depth-3 expressions over curated scenes with distractors that punish wrong attachment, evaluate 3 models, and plot accuracy and attachment-error rates by depth.
main_risk: Longer expressions also add token count and rare constructions, so length- and frequency-matched controls at each depth are essential.
default_community_belief: Accuracy declines gradually with expression complexity; there is no qualitative parsing limit at a specific depth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: LLM-based segmenters can parse recursively in principle, so the cliff may exist only for dual-encoder models and be misattributed as universal.
fastest_falsification: Twenty scenes with depth-1 and depth-2 variants, one model, three hours; smooth decline without attachment-error concentration falsifies.

one_line: Restrictive and non-restrictive clauses are conflated: 'the dog, which is brown,' and 'the dog that is brown' produce identical grounding when they should diverge under distractors
problem: Restrictive clauses select among candidates while non-restrictive clauses merely comment on an already-identified referent; this distinction changes the correct answer when the comment is false or when distractors exist, and models are assumed (without test) to ignore it.
core_hypothesis: Models treat both clause types as identical soft constraints, so in scenes where a non-restrictive reading licenses grounding a unique salient dog despite a false comment, and a restrictive reading demands abstaining or switching, model behavior will not vary with clause type, revealing that punctuation-borne and complementizer-borne semantics are lost in text conditioning.
falsifiable_prediction: Behavioral divergence between minimal-pair clause types will be near zero across scene conditions where human interpretations reliably diverge (measured with human annotators on the same stimuli), quantifying a specific, previously-unmeasured semantic blind spot.
why_important: Clause type is a proxy for a broader capability: using linguistic structure (not just words) to determine what is being asked; a clean negative result defines a capability boundary and a training-data target for grounded syntax.
why_possibly_novel: Restrictive vs non-restrictive semantics appears entirely absent from grounding evaluation; the human-divergence-normalized design is a novel way to score such blind spots.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 100 minimal pairs over scenes with unique-salient and multi-candidate conditions, collect human interpretations as divergence ground truth, run 3 models, and compare model divergence to human divergence per condition.
main_risk: Comma-based cues may be stripped by tokenization or normalization in some pipelines, making the null result partly an artifact of preprocessing rather than model semantics.
default_community_belief: Such fine-grained syntax is irrelevant to practical grounding and safely ignorable by models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The distinction may matter so rarely in practice that even humans diverge weakly on natural scenes, leaving nothing measurable to be blind to.
fastest_falsification: Thirty minimal pairs on one model with human comparison, one day; model divergence tracking human divergence falsifies the blind-spot claim.

one_line: Action modifiers are grounded through co-occurring objects, not pose: 'the man riding' finds men near horses, and fails when the horse is out of frame
problem: Verbal modifiers in referring expressions (riding, eating, holding) are assumed to be grounded via human pose and interaction cues, but co-occurring object context provides a cheaper shortcut that standard benchmarks never decorrelate from the action itself.
core_hypothesis: Dense models implement action words primarily as detectors of the action's typical object context, so masking or cropping out the interacting object (keeping the person's pose fully visible) will collapse action-based selection toward chance, while pose-preserving context removal should not matter to a genuinely pose-based mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: Selection accuracy for action-modified queries will drop by a large margin when the interacting object is occluded or out of frame despite unchanged body pose, and a context-only classifier (object detections without the person) will reproduce a majority of model selections on the original scenes.
why_important: Action-based reference is central to human-robot interaction and surveillance retrieval; a context-shortcut mechanism predicts exactly when these systems fail (interaction partner occluded) and shows that apparent action understanding is object co-occurrence.
why_possibly_novel: Contextual bias is known for object recognition; a decorrelation test isolating pose from interacting-object context for action words in dense grounding appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate scenes with visible interactions, create context-removed variants via cropping and inpainting that preserve the agent's pose, run action-modified queries on 3 models, and compare accuracy plus fit the context-only mimic classifier.
main_risk: Inpainting artifacts may perturb model behavior independently of context removal; camera-cropped natural variants are cleaner but harder to collect at scale.
default_community_belief: Grounding of action words reflects learned human-object interaction understanding, including pose cues.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Video-pretrained or pose-augmented models may genuinely encode pose signatures for common actions, surviving context removal for actions with distinctive kinematics.
fastest_falsification: Twenty-five interaction scenes with cropped-context variants, one model, half a day; preserved accuracy under context removal falsifies.

one_line: Superlatives are grounded by salience, not comparison: 'the tallest player' picks the most prominent one when height and salience are decorrelated
problem: Superlative expressions require comparing a property across all candidate instances, an operation qualitatively different from matching; benchmarks rarely decorrelate the superlative dimension from visual salience, so apparent superlative competence may be salience retrieval.
core_hypothesis: Dense models lack a cross-instance comparison mechanism, so superlative queries are answered by a salience prior weakly modulated by the property word; when the truly-superlative instance is made less salient than a competitor, selections will follow salience, and accuracy will be near chance on salience-balanced stimuli.
falsifiable_prediction: On stimuli where the superlative dimension (height, size, brightness) is decorrelated from salience (centrality, sharpness, contrast), accuracy will drop toward chance and selections will regress on salience features rather than the queried property; comparative phrasings ('taller than the one next to it') will fail equally, confirming absent comparison machinery.
why_important: Superlatives are frequent in natural disambiguation and in analytics queries (largest defect, brightest lesion); demonstrating salience capture with a controlled decorrelation design would redefine what current benchmarks certify.
why_possibly_novel: Superlative handling is studied in text-only NLP and some VQA work; a salience-decorrelated instance-selection test for dense grounding appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 150 scenes with measured salience and property values decorrelated by design, run superlative and comparative queries on 3 models, and fit selection models with property and salience predictors.
main_risk: Salience is multi-dimensional and imperfectly measurable; residual salience-property correlation could hide genuine comparison ability or fake its absence.
default_community_belief: Reasonable benchmark performance on superlative expressions indicates emergent cross-instance comparison in grounding models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: LLM-decoder models could implement comparison through iterative attention over candidate regions, genuinely succeeding on decorrelated stimuli.
fastest_falsification: Thirty decorrelated scenes, one model, three hours; property-consistent selection falsifies salience capture.

one_line: Knowledge-dependent referents fail along a measurable gradient: perceptual paraphrases ground, functional and cultural descriptions do not
problem: Users often refer through function or role ('the thing you open bottles with', 'the goalkeeper') rather than category names; models are marketed as knowledge-rich, but which knowledge types actually reach the dense output is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: Grounding quality for knowledge-dependent referents decays along a gradient of abstraction: perceptual descriptions (shape, color paraphrases) ground best, functional descriptions worse, and social or cultural role descriptions worst, because contrastive pretraining aligns perceptual language directly while functional and cultural language reaches images only through weak indirect co-occurrence.
falsifiable_prediction: On a suite where the same referents are described perceptually, functionally, and by role, per-type accuracy will show the predicted monotone gradient across model families, and the gap between perceptual and functional grounding will shrink in models with LLM text towers, tracking language-side knowledge integration.
why_important: The gradient specifies which user phrasings a deployed system supports, and localizes the bottleneck: if functional descriptions fail in dual-encoder models but pass in LLM-decoder models, the fix is architectural (route language through reasoning) rather than data volume.
why_possibly_novel: Knowledge probing exists for VQA; a typed-description gradient measured at dense-output level with the architecture-interaction prediction appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 100 objects, write three description types validated by humans for identifiability, run 4 models across families, and compare per-type accuracy and the family-by-type interaction.
main_risk: Human validation must ensure all three descriptions are equally identifying, otherwise type differences reflect description quality rather than model knowledge routing.
default_community_belief: Modern VLMs bring world knowledge to grounding uniformly; a referent described any identifiable way can be found.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gradient could be flat-low (everything but category names fails), making the typed structure uninteresting compared to the general paraphrase weakness.
fastest_falsification: Twenty-five objects, three description types, one model, three hours; a flat accuracy profile across types falsifies the gradient.

one_line: Printed words hijack masks: rendering 'dog' on a box makes grounding models segment the box, a spatial typographic attack surface for dense prediction
problem: Typographic attacks are known to flip CLIP classifications, but dense prediction adds a spatial dimension: where the attack text sits determines which pixels get stolen, and this attack surface is uncharacterized for grounding models.
core_hypothesis: Pixel-text similarity inherits CLIP-style text-region sensitivity, so scene text matching the query acts as a super-stimulus that outcompetes actual object evidence; mask theft will succeed at high rates, scale with rendered-text size and contrast, and persist even when a genuine instance of the queried object is present elsewhere in the image.
falsifiable_prediction: Composited scenes with query-matching text on distractor objects will divert masks to the text-bearing object at rates far above attribute-matched control text, the diversion rate will grow with text prominence, and OCR-capable instruction-tuned segmenters will be more vulnerable than pure dual-encoder models, not less.
why_important: Grounding outputs feed robotic manipulation and content moderation; a printable sticker that steals masks is a physically-realizable attack, and the architecture-vulnerability ordering (OCR strength increasing vulnerability) would upend the assumption that more capable readers are safer.
why_possibly_novel: Typographic attacks are documented for classification; systematic mask-theft characterization with prominence dose-response and the capability-vulnerability ordering appears new for dense models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite query words onto distractor objects at varied sizes and contrasts across 200 scenes containing genuine query referents, run 4 models, and measure mask-diversion rates and dose-response curves.
main_risk: Compositing realism may matter; physical-world validation (printed labels photographed) is needed before claiming a practical attack.
default_community_belief: Typographic vulnerability is a classification quirk; dense models grounded in spatial features are less exposed, and stronger models are more robust.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense heads may weight shape and texture evidence enough that scene text only wins when the genuine object is absent, reducing the attack to the already-known hallucination case.
fastest_falsification: Thirty composited scenes with genuine referents present, one model, two hours; diversion at control-text rates falsifies.

one_line: 'The sign that says STOP' is grounded by sign-ness, not by reading: content-conditioned reference fails whenever multiple signs are present
problem: Queries referring to objects by their written content (the jersey with number 10, the door marked exit) require reading text and matching it to the query; whether dense models actually read or just match object category plus salience is untested.
core_hypothesis: Dual-encoder grounding models match 'sign' semantics and ignore the quoted content entirely, while instruction-tuned VLMs read text globally but fail to route the read content into spatial selection; both will perform near chance among multiple same-category text-bearing objects, a shared failure with different mechanisms.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-sign scenes, content-conditioned selection will be near chance for both model families, content-word deletion from the query will barely change outputs for dual-encoder models (proving the content was unused), and instruction-tuned models will correctly answer what each sign says in text while still mis-grounding, demonstrating a read-ground routing gap.
why_important: Content-conditioned reference is everywhere in navigation and retail; the routing-gap finding (models that read but cannot ground what they read) identifies a specific integration failure invisible to both OCR benchmarks and grounding benchmarks separately.
why_possibly_novel: Scene-text understanding and referring segmentation are mature separately; the dissociation test showing reading without grounded routing appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate 150 scenes with 2 or more legible same-category text objects, run content-conditioned queries plus deletion controls and separate reading probes on both model families, and tabulate the read-versus-ground dissociation.
main_risk: Text legibility at model input resolution may bottleneck everything, requiring resolution-stratified analysis to avoid conflating reading failure with routing failure.
default_community_belief: OCR-capable VLMs can ground text-content references; scene-text reading and localization compose naturally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some grounding-tuned VLMs trained with document and UI data may have learned the routing, performing well and confining the gap to older models.
fastest_falsification: Twenty multi-sign scenes, one instruction-tuned model, reading probe plus grounding query, three hours; correct grounding falsifies the routing gap.

one_line: Caption-subject bias shapes dense grounding: categories that web captions mention first ground better, independent of size and frequency
problem: Dense grounding quality differs across categories in ways not explained by size, frequency, or visual difficulty; the syntactic role that categories typically occupy in pretraining captions is an unexamined predictor.
core_hypothesis: Contrastive alignment is dominated by caption subjects (first-mentioned, agentive nouns), so categories that typically appear as subjects acquire strong pixel-text alignment while equally-frequent categories that appear as objects or in prepositional phrases (tables, walls, backgrounds of actions) acquire weak alignment; grammatical-role statistics will predict per-category dense performance after controlling for frequency, size, and concreteness.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-category open-vocab segmentation quality on subject-position rate estimated from a public caption corpus will yield a significant positive coefficient after controls, and categories with high frequency but low subjecthood will be systematic underperformers across unrelated model families.
why_important: If grammatical role in pretraining text is a hidden driver of dense performance, data curation gains a new lever (rebalancing caption syntax, augmenting object-position mentions) that is far cheaper than collecting new images.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency effects are established; syntactic-role statistics as an independent predictor of dense grounding quality appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Parse a large public caption corpus for per-category subject rates, evaluate per-category segmentation quality for 3 models on standard benchmarks, and fit the controlled regression with bootstrap confidence intervals.
main_risk: Subjecthood correlates with animacy and salience, which also affect visual learnability, so the causal claim needs careful covariates and ideally a controlled fine-tuning experiment.
default_community_belief: Per-category performance is explained by data frequency and visual difficulty; caption syntax is irrelevant to visual grounding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern pretraining mixes include region-level and detection-style supervision that bypasses caption syntax, potentially washing out the subject bias in recent models.
fastest_falsification: Subject-rate vs per-class quality correlation using existing per-class benchmark numbers and one corpus parse, two days of mostly CPU work; a null controlled correlation falsifies.

one_line: Prompt length leaks into mask area: padding a query with redundant words systematically grows the predicted mask
problem: Longer captions in pretraining tend to describe larger or more central scene content, and longer referring expressions in training data correlate with bigger, more complex targets; whether models internalized a length-to-size prior that acts independently of content is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Dense decoders learned a spurious correlation between text length and expected mask statistics, so semantically-redundant query padding (adding true but uninformative words) will shift predicted masks toward larger areas and softer boundaries even though the referent is unchanged, a pure nuisance pathway from token count to geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: Across referents, padded queries will produce masks with systematically larger area and lower boundary sharpness than minimal queries for the same referent, the effect will scale with padding length, and it will persist when padding consists of content-free hedges, isolating length from added meaning.
why_important: A length-to-geometry leak means verbose users and terse users get different segmentations of the same object, and it contaminates every study that varies query detail while believing content is the only variable.
why_possibly_novel: Length effects on retrieval scores are known; a causal test of length on output mask geometry with content-free padding appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 300 referents, construct minimal, medium, and heavily-padded queries with human-verified constant meaning, run 3 models, and test monotone trends in mask area and boundary sharpness against padding length.
main_risk: Content-free padding is hard to make truly neutral; hedging words might shift formality register, which could affect outputs through a different pathway.
default_community_belief: Redundant words are harmless; mask geometry is determined by image evidence and referent identity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention normalization over longer text may dilute all token contributions equally, leaving conditioning effectively unchanged and geometry stable.
fastest_falsification: Fifty referents, three padding levels, one model, two hours; flat area and sharpness trends falsify.

one_line: Rare-word queries return the frequent cousin: 'ocelot' produces cat-shaped masks because open vocabulary regresses to taxonomic neighbors
problem: Open-vocab systems are pitched on rare and fine-grained categories, yet what actually happens when the query word is rare (correct grounding, refusal, or silent substitution by a frequent co-hyponym) has not been characterized.
core_hypothesis: For rare category words, the text embedding lands near its frequent taxonomic neighbors, and dense outputs inherit the neighbor's selection behavior: masks will cover instances of the frequent cousin with confidence resembling the cousin's, making rare-word outputs indistinguishable from silent substitution rather than degraded versions of correct behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes containing a frequent cousin but not the rare category, rare-word queries will produce masks over the cousin at rates far above unrelated-word controls, and the effect will strengthen as text-embedding distance to the cousin shrinks; on scenes containing both, the rare word will select the cousin over the true referent at a nontrivial rate.
why_important: Silent substitution is worse than failure for fine-grained applications (biodiversity monitoring, retail SKUs) because outputs look plausible; an embedding-distance early-warning score could flag substitution-prone queries before deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Long-tail performance drops are documented; characterizing the failure as structured taxonomic substitution with an embedding-distance predictor at dense-output level appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select 60 rare-frequent category pairs from fine-grained taxonomies, evaluate rare-word queries on cousin-only and both-present scenes across 3 models, and regress substitution rates on text-embedding distances.
main_risk: True rare-category images with verified labels are scarce for the both-present condition, limiting that cell's statistical power.
default_community_belief: Rare-word performance is a milder version of frequent-word performance, degrading in accuracy but not changing in kind.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some rare words are compositionally transparent (spider monkey), letting models ground them via parts and defeating the substitution story for a visible subset.
fastest_falsification: Fifteen cousin-only scenes per 10 rare words, one model, three hours; substitution at control-word rates falsifies.

one_line: Hallucinated masks are placed at dataset position priors: querying an absent object yields a mask where that object usually appears in training data
problem: When dense models hallucinate a mask for an absent object, the spatial placement of that mask is treated as arbitrary noise, leaving unexamined whether it encodes learned position priors that could identify the training-data origin of the hallucination.
core_hypothesis: Dense decoders internalize per-category spatial priors from training data (skies on top, keyboards at bottom-center, faces upper-middle), and under absent-object queries with weak visual evidence, these priors dominate placement; hallucinated masks will cluster at category-specific canonical locations, reproducible across images and models trained on similar data.
falsifiable_prediction: Aggregating hallucinated-mask centroids per category over many absent-object queries will produce spatial distributions significantly more concentrated than chance and significantly correlated with the category's ground-truth position distribution in common training datasets, and this correlation will hold across independently trained models sharing data sources.
why_important: Position-prior hallucination gives a forensic tool (inferring training-data statistics from output behavior) and a practical detector: masks landing at canonical positions with weak local evidence are probable hallucinations, enabling a spatial-prior-aware confidence penalty.
why_possibly_novel: Hallucination rates are studied; the spatial forensics of where hallucinated dense outputs land, and its use as a detection signal, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run absent-object queries for 30 categories over 500 verified-absent images on 2 models, map hallucinated centroid distributions, and compare against category position statistics computed from public detection datasets.
main_risk: Image composition itself constrains placement (floors are always at the bottom), requiring scene-geometry-matched null distributions rather than uniform chance.
default_community_belief: Hallucinated masks attach to whatever region weakly resembles the query; placement is image-driven and carries no systematic information.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Lookalike-region matching may dominate priors entirely, making placement fully image-dependent and the forensic signal empty.
fastest_falsification: Ten categories, 50 absent-query images, one model, centroid concentration test in half a day; scene-matched-null-level dispersion falsifies.

one_line: Domain shift flips the evidence balance: on out-of-distribution images, dense predictions rely measurably more on language priors and less on pixels
problem: Robustness studies report accuracy drops under domain shift but never decompose whether the surviving predictions are still vision-driven or have quietly become prior-driven guesses that happen to score.
core_hypothesis: As visual features move off-distribution, their contribution to the dense output shrinks faster than the text prior's contribution, so the prior-reliance ratio (output similarity between intact and evidence-destroyed inputs) will rise with domain shift; models will increasingly return canonical-location, canonical-shape masks that ignore the actual pixels.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring output agreement between original and patch-scrambled (or heavily blurred) versions of the same image under identical queries, agreement will be low in-domain and rise substantially on sketches, thermal, or medical imagery, quantifying prior takeover; the rise will predict which domains suffer silent failure rather than loud failure.
why_important: Prior takeover explains why OOD dense outputs look plausible while being unmoored from evidence, the most dangerous failure mode for clinical or industrial imagery, and the scramble-agreement metric is a deployable, label-free domain-risk probe.
why_possibly_novel: Prior-vs-evidence decompositions exist for VQA (question-only baselines); an image-evidence-destruction agreement metric for dense outputs across domain shift appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 4 domains of increasing shift, compute query-conditioned output agreement between intact and evidence-destroyed images on 2 models, and correlate the agreement rise with silent-failure rates measured against ground truth where available.
main_risk: Evidence destruction methods (scrambling, blurring) also change global statistics that could suppress outputs entirely, requiring emission-rate-matched comparisons.
default_community_belief: Domain shift degrades dense accuracy uniformly; predictions remain evidence-driven, just with noisier evidence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Outputs on destroyed inputs may collapse to no-mask or full-image degenerate answers rather than canonical priors, making the agreement metric measure degeneracy instead of prior reliance.
fastest_falsification: One shifted domain, 100 images, intact-vs-scrambled agreement on one model in a day; no agreement rise over in-domain baseline falsifies.

one_line: Contrastive pretraining's salience bias caps dense recall: objects that captions rarely mention are unfindable regardless of decoder quality
problem: Pixel-text alignment is learned from image-caption pairs where captions describe the photographic subject, yet open-vocab segmenters are expected to find any visible object; the ceiling this caption-salience mismatch imposes on non-salient objects is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Alignment strength per category-instance is governed by the probability that such an instance would be mentioned in a caption of that image (a salience-mention prior), so recall for small, peripheral, or background instances is bounded by caption-mention statistics; decoder improvements shift precision but cannot lift this recall ceiling without re-aligned pretraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-instance recall across sizes and positions will track an independently-estimated mention probability (from human quick-captioning of the same images) more closely than it tracks pixel area alone, and models sharing pretraining data but differing in decoders will show near-identical non-salient-instance recall, revealing the shared ceiling.
why_important: If the bottleneck is mention probability rather than resolution or architecture, the field's decoder-centric effort cannot fix non-salient recall, and data interventions (dense re-captioning, region-level pairing) become the only path, a significant redirection.
why_possibly_novel: Salience bias is acknowledged qualitatively; operationalizing a mention-probability ceiling and testing decoder-invariance of the recall floor appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect quick captions for 300 images to estimate per-instance mention rates, evaluate multiple decoders on shared frozen alignment backbones, and compare recall curves against mention probability and against pixel-size baselines.
main_risk: Mention probability is expensive to estimate well and confounded with size and centrality, requiring careful regression rather than raw correlation.
default_community_belief: Recall of small and peripheral objects is a resolution and architecture problem, steadily fixable with higher-res features and better decoders.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern pretraining mixtures include detection-derived region-text pairs that break the caption-salience link, so newer models may not exhibit the ceiling.
fastest_falsification: Two decoders on one shared backbone, recall on the same non-salient instance set, one day; large decoder-driven recall differences falsify the ceiling claim.

one_line: Patch tokens are contaminated by scene context: a grass patch near a dog scores high for 'dog', setting a floor on open-vocab boundary precision
problem: Dense open-vocab methods read pixel-text similarity off patch embeddings, assuming each patch represents its own content, but ViTs trained with global objectives mix information across the image, and the spatial leakage of category evidence into neighboring patches is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Global attention distributes object evidence into surrounding patches (context contamination), so similarity maps bleed beyond true object boundaries by a characteristic distance set by the backbone's attention statistics rather than by the decoder; boundary precision of all decoder-based methods on a shared backbone will be limited by this common contamination floor.
falsifiable_prediction: Similarity for the object's category measured on background patches will decay with distance from the boundary following a profile that is stable across images, predictable from the backbone's average attention kernel, and unchanged by swapping decoders; inpainting the object away will leave elevated category similarity in the previously-neighboring patches (a residual-context signature).
why_important: A backbone-level contamination floor explains why boundary metrics saturate across method papers and identifies the effective intervention point (pretraining objectives or feature de-mixing) rather than more decoder engineering.
why_possibly_novel: Context effects on classification are known; a quantitative contamination-profile measurement with the decoder-invariance and inpainting-residual tests appears new for dense VLMs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure category-similarity decay profiles around boundaries for 2 backbones and 2 decoders each, compare profiles against attention-kernel predictions, and run the object-inpainting residual test on 200 objects.
main_risk: True boundary ambiguity in annotations could mimic contamination, requiring high-quality boundary ground truth (matting-grade) for the profile measurement.
default_community_belief: Boundary softness comes from decoder resolution limits and annotation noise; patch features are essentially local descriptors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Windowed or register-token architectures may confine mixing enough that contamination is negligible compared to decoder blur, breaking the backbone-floor account.
fastest_falsification: Decay profiles on 50 objects with one backbone and two decoders, one day; decoder-dependent profiles falsify the shared-floor claim.

one_line: Text-driven attention grounds the discriminative part, not the object: animate queries systematically over-weight heads and faces, distorting mask shape
problem: Cross-attention maps are treated as object evidence, but contrastive training only requires locating features that discriminate the caption, so attention may concentrate on identity-bearing parts and the resulting masks inherit a part-biased shape distortion that aggregate IoU conceals.
core_hypothesis: For animate categories the discriminative evidence is concentrated in heads and faces, so text-conditioned attention peaks there and mask decoders grow regions outward from these seeds, producing systematic over-inclusion of head-adjacent areas and under-inclusion of extremities, a shape bias that is category-predictable and absent for texture-uniform categories.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-part recall of predicted masks for animate categories will show a stable head-to-extremity gradient across models (feet, tails, and hands missing at multiples of the head miss-rate), while inanimate texture-uniform categories show flat part recall; seeding decoders with uniform attention will flatten the gradient, confirming attention concentration as the cause.
why_important: Part-biased masks silently corrupt downstream measurement (animal morphometrics, human pose regions, garment segmentation), and the head-seeded growth mechanism suggests specific fixes such as part-coverage losses or attention-spreading regularizers.
why_possibly_novel: Attention concentration is known qualitatively; a quantitative part-recall gradient analysis with an intervention that flattens it appears new for language-conditioned segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use part-annotated datasets to compute per-part recall of predicted masks for 10 animate and 10 inanimate categories over 3 models, then run the uniform-seed intervention on one open decoder to test causality.
main_risk: Extremities are also thin and low-resolution, so part recall must be normalized by a geometry-matched baseline (e.g. recall of equally-thin inanimate parts).
default_community_belief: Masks fail at extremities because thin structures are hard at low resolution, a purely geometric limitation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Geometry may fully explain the gradient, with attention concentration adding nothing once thinness is controlled, in which case the intervention will not flatten anything.
fastest_falsification: Part-recall gradient on one part-annotated dataset and one model with thinness controls, one day; a geometry-explained gradient falsifies.

one_line: Open vocabulary is nearest-neighbor retrieval in disguise: novel-word masks inherit the shape statistics of the closest seen class
problem: Open-vocab segmenters produce plausible masks for words never seen with dense supervision, which is celebrated as generalization without checking whether the produced geometry is genuinely evidence-driven or a copy of the nearest trained concept's mask prior.
core_hypothesis: Dense decoders learn per-concept shape priors keyed to text embeddings, and for novel words they interpolate priors from embedding neighbors; predicted masks for unseen categories will exhibit shape statistics (compactness, aspect ratio, boundary complexity) regressing toward those of their nearest seen neighbors, deviating measurably from the true category geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: For unseen categories whose true shape differs sharply from their embedding neighbors (e.g. elongated tools embedded near compact objects), predicted masks will be biased toward neighbor geometry (too compact, wrong aspect ratio) in proportion to embedding proximity, and this bias will shrink when dense supervision for the category is added, confirming the prior source.
why_important: If open-vocab geometry is neighbor interpolation, the failure cases are predictable from embedding space alone (a free audit for deployments), and claims of open-world generalization need shape-aware evaluation, not just region overlap.
why_possibly_novel: Zero-shot performance is measured by IoU; a shape-statistics regression-to-neighbor analysis as evidence of retrieval-style generalization appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Choose 30 held-out categories with shape-divergent embedding neighbors, compare predicted vs true shape statistics across 2 models, and regress the geometric bias on embedding distance to the nearest supervised class.
main_risk: Disentangling shape prior from genuine visual difficulty requires categories where evidence is clear but geometry is unusual, a delicate curation task.
default_community_belief: Plausible zero-shot masks demonstrate that dense evidence, not category-specific priors, drives segmentation for unseen words.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask decoders conditioned on strong image evidence may override text-keyed priors whenever boundaries are visible, confining the effect to low-contrast objects.
fastest_falsification: Ten shape-divergent unseen categories, shape-statistic comparison on one model, half a day; unbiased geometry falsifies.

one_line: Small-object grounding fails at the fusion stage, not the vision stage: language is injected at scales too coarse to address small instances
problem: Small-object failures in open-vocab dense prediction are attributed to the vision backbone, yet many architectures fuse text at a single coarse feature scale, and the specific contribution of fusion-scale mismatch has not been isolated.
core_hypothesis: Vision features often retain small-object evidence at fine pyramid levels, but text conditioning applied only at coarse levels cannot select it; small-object recall will therefore be limited by the fusion scale rather than feature content, and models will show a recall cliff at the object size corresponding to their coarsest-fusion receptive field.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear probes on fine-scale vision features will detect small instances that the full model misses (proving evidence exists past the fusion bottleneck), and architectures differing only in fusion scale will shift their small-object recall cliff accordingly, while backbone swaps at fixed fusion scale will not move it.
why_important: Correctly locating the bottleneck redirects effort from ever-higher-resolution backbones to multi-scale language fusion, a cheaper architectural change with a concrete testable payoff.
why_possibly_novel: Small-object weakness is universally noted; a probe-based evidence-exists-but-unselected demonstration pinpointing fusion scale appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train lightweight probes on fine-scale features of a frozen open-vocab segmenter to detect small instances it misses, then compare small-object recall cliffs across model variants with documented fusion scales.
main_risk: Probes introduce their own supervision, so probe success must be carefully bounded against what zero-shot fusion could plausibly achieve without new training.
default_community_belief: Small-object dense failures reflect missing visual evidence at low resolution; the fix is higher-resolution backbones and inputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-scale features may carry class-agnostic edges but not category evidence, in which case probes fail and the vision-stage account stands.
fastest_falsification: Probe fine-scale features for 20 missed small instances on one model, one day; probe failure falsifies the fusion-bottleneck claim.

one_line: Frozen deep features have already discarded locality: mid-layer features ground texture-defined referents better than final layers everyone uses
problem: Dense adaptations of contrastive VLMs default to final-layer features on the assumption that deeper is better, ignoring that the final layers are optimized for global pooling and may have irreversibly discarded the spatial specificity dense tasks need.
core_hypothesis: There is a layer-wise trade-off between semantic alignment and spatial fidelity: final layers maximize text alignment but spatially smear evidence, while mid layers retain localized texture and boundary information with adequate alignment; grounding quality per referent type will peak at different depths (mid layers for texture- and boundary-defined referents, late layers for semantic-category referents).
falsifiable_prediction: A layer sweep on frozen backbones will show boundary-quality metrics peaking several layers before the final block while category-recall metrics peak at the end, and simple two-layer feature mixing will beat final-layer-only baselines on boundary metrics without hurting recall, across at least two backbone families.
why_important: If a free layer-choice change improves dense outputs, every frozen-backbone open-vocab pipeline is leaving quality on the table, and the referent-type-dependent peak explains conflicting anecdotes about which layers work.
why_possibly_novel: Layer choice is studied for self-supervised backbones in unsupervised segmentation; a referent-type-resolved layer analysis for language-conditioned dense prediction with the mixing prescription appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep feature layers on 2 frozen contrastive backbones for a fixed lightweight decoder, evaluate boundary and recall metrics stratified by referent type, and test the two-layer mixture against the default.
main_risk: Decoder capacity could compensate for layer choice when trained per layer, shrinking the effect to initialization noise unless decoders are kept minimal.
default_community_belief: Final-layer features are the right representation for language-conditioned dense tasks; earlier layers are too raw to align with text.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Text alignment may collapse so quickly below the final blocks that mid-layer similarity maps are unusable despite better locality, killing the trade-off.
fastest_falsification: One backbone, four layers, one small decoder, boundary metrics in a GPU-day; monotone improvement toward the final layer falsifies.

one_line: Bimodal similarity maps predict grounding failure before it happens: multi-peak structure is the error budget of dense VLMs
problem: Dense pipelines threshold or argmax similarity maps assuming a unimodal peak over the referent, but the topological structure of these maps (number and separation of modes) is never measured or exploited.
