core_hypothesis: Most grounding errors pass through a specific intermediate state: the similarity map develops two or more comparable modes (true referent and a distractor), and the decoder commits to the wrong one; therefore the mode structure of the raw map predicts final-mask correctness better than any confidence score, and the fraction of multi-modal maps bounds the achievable error rate for decoder-side improvements.
falsifiable_prediction: Classifying outputs by raw-map mode structure, the multi-modal subset will contain the large majority of wrong-instance errors, mode-gap (score difference between top modes) will predict correctness with higher AUC than output confidence, and decoder variants will only redistribute errors within the multi-modal subset rather than reduce it.
why_important: A pre-decoder failure predictor enables selective escalation (asking clarifying questions or running expensive models only on multi-modal cases), and the decoder-invariance claim would show where dense grounding progress must come from (the map, not the decoder).
why_possibly_novel: Confidence-based failure prediction is standard; using raw similarity-map topology as a mechanistic bottleneck measurement with decoder-invariance analysis appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract raw maps from 2 open models, compute mode statistics, relate them to error types on a referring split, and compare error composition across decoder variants on the same maps.
main_risk: Mode detection needs scale-space care (small spurious peaks), so results may be sensitive to the mode-extraction procedure.
default_community_belief: Grounding errors are diffuse failures of alignment quality, best predicted by output confidence and best fixed by better decoders.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decoders may integrate context that genuinely resolves multi-modal maps, making the multi-modal fraction an overestimate of the error bound rather than a tight budget.
fastest_falsification: Mode statistics vs error on 300 samples of one model, half a day; equal error rates across mode classes falsify.

one_line: Register-token artifacts create position-stable phantom detections: high-norm ViT tokens attract text similarity at consistent grid locations
problem: ViT backbones develop high-norm artifact tokens at certain patch positions, and dense pipelines read pixel-text similarity from all patch tokens uniformly, without auditing whether artifact positions systematically distort similarity maps.
core_hypothesis: Artifact tokens aggregate global information with abnormal norms, so after the usual normalization they exhibit atypical similarity to many text queries, producing weak phantom responses at characteristic grid positions that persist across unrelated images; a per-position audit will reveal a stable spatial fingerprint of false-positive rates keyed to the backbone, not the content.
falsifiable_prediction: Averaging similarity maps over thousands of unrelated images per query will show statistically-elevated responses at specific grid positions that match the backbone's high-norm token positions, these positions will contribute a disproportionate share of small false-positive fragments in final masks, and masking them out will measurably improve precision at no recall cost.
why_important: A content-independent spatial fingerprint of errors is both a cheap accuracy fix (position masking or renormalization) and a caution for any work that interprets similarity maps as pure evidence.
why_possibly_novel: Artifact tokens are documented for self-supervised ViTs and their attention maps; connecting them quantitatively to open-vocab dense false positives with a position-masking fix appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-position average similarity over a large image set for several queries on 2 backbones, locate elevated positions, verify norm correspondence, and evaluate precision with and without position-aware correction.
main_risk: Newer backbones trained with explicit register tokens may have exported artifacts out of the patch grid, restricting the finding to older but still widely-deployed models.
default_community_belief: Similarity-map noise is content-driven; patch positions are exchangeable and no location deserves special treatment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature normalization in specific pipelines may already neutralize norm outliers, leaving no measurable positional fingerprint downstream.
fastest_falsification: Per-position similarity averages over 2000 images for 5 queries on one backbone, a few hours; a flat positional profile falsifies.

one_line: The modality gap eats the signal: pixel-text similarity variance is a sliver riding on a large constant offset, so dense decisions run at tiny effective SNR
problem: Contrastive spaces exhibit a modality gap (image and text embeddings occupy separate cones), and dense pipelines compute pixel-text cosine similarities directly in this geometry without asking how much of each score is constant offset versus informative variation.
core_hypothesis: Because all image embeddings share a large component along the inter-modality direction, raw pixel-text similarities are dominated by terms that do not vary across pixels; the spatially-informative component is small relative to the offset, making dense decisions sensitive to tiny perturbations, and projecting out the gap direction (plus per-image recentering) will improve dense metrics with zero training.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing similarity into gap-aligned and residual components will show the pixel-varying share is a small fraction of total magnitude, and applying gap-removal projections will improve open-vocab segmentation metrics and score stability under image noise across multiple frozen backbones, with larger gains for backbones exhibiting larger measured gaps.
why_important: A training-free geometric correction that improves every CLIP-derived dense pipeline would be immediately adoptable, and the effective-SNR framing explains the notorious fragility of similarity thresholds in dense settings.
why_possibly_novel: The modality gap is studied for retrieval and classification calibration; a pixel-level SNR decomposition and gap-removal intervention for dense prediction appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure the gap decomposition on 3 backbones, implement projection and recentering variants, and evaluate on open-vocab segmentation and referring splits without any retraining.
main_risk: Softmax over classes already cancels shared offsets in some pipelines, so gains may be confined to threshold-based and single-query settings.
default_community_belief: Cosine similarity in the joint space is the right dense score; the modality gap is a curiosity that renormalization handles implicitly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-class softmax and learned temperatures may already absorb the offset everywhere it matters, making explicit gap removal redundant in practice.
fastest_falsification: Implement projection on one backbone and re-run one benchmark split in a few hours; no improvement in threshold-based settings falsifies.

one_line: Classification-tuned temperature saturates dense maps: the contrastive logit scale is wrong for pixels, and retuning it alone recalibrates boundaries
problem: Contrastive pretraining learns a temperature optimized for image-level discrimination among captions, and dense pipelines inherit it implicitly when converting similarities to probabilities, assuming a global scalar tuned for one task transfers to a task with radically different score statistics.
core_hypothesis: Pixel-level similarity differences are much smaller than image-level ones, so the inherited temperature places most pixels in saturated regions of the softmax or sigmoid, flattening boundary gradients and corrupting probability calibration; a single dense-specific temperature, fit on a handful of images, will materially improve boundary calibration and soft-mask quality without touching any weights.
falsifiable_prediction: Calibration curves of per-pixel probabilities will show characteristic saturation under the inherited temperature, the optimal dense temperature will differ from the pretraining value by a large factor and be stable across images and datasets for a given backbone, and applying it will improve expected calibration error and boundary F-scores on soft-threshold metrics.
why_important: A one-scalar fix improving every downstream consumer of dense probability maps (thresholding, matting, uncertainty) is the cheapest possible win, and the mismatch explains why dense confidence maps look binary when the task is ambiguous.
why_possibly_novel: Temperature is discussed in contrastive training; the claim that the pretrained value is systematically wrong for dense inference, with a transferability characterization of the corrected value, appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit dense temperature on 50 images for 2 backbones, evaluate calibration and boundary metrics on held-out splits against the inherited value, and test cross-dataset stability of the fitted scalar.
main_risk: Pipelines that only use argmax decisions are temperature-invariant, so the improvement is confined to soft-output consumers and calibration-sensitive applications.
default_community_belief: The pretrained logit scale is part of the model and appropriate wherever its similarities are used.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Many dense pipelines already fit thresholds per dataset, which may implicitly absorb the temperature error, leaving explicit retuning without additional benefit.
fastest_falsification: Fit and evaluate one temperature on one backbone in two hours; no calibration improvement falsifies.

one_line: Bilinear upsampling adds a signed boundary bias: dense VLM masks are systematically dilated outward, not just blurry, and the bias is correctable post hoc
problem: Coarse similarity maps are bilinearly upsampled to pixel resolution in most open-vocab pipelines; the error this introduces is treated as symmetric blur, and boundary evaluation with unsigned metrics cannot detect a directional component.
core_hypothesis: Because objects tend to be locally convex and their interiors score higher than exteriors, interpolation between interior and exterior grid points places the threshold crossing outside the true boundary on average, producing a signed outward dilation whose magnitude depends on local curvature and grid phase; measuring signed boundary error will reveal a nonzero mean offset that simple curvature-aware correction can remove.
falsifiable_prediction: Signed boundary-error distributions for upsampled dense predictions will have a significantly positive (outward) mean that grows with boundary curvature and with upsampling factor, and applying an analytic offset correction will improve boundary F-scores without retraining, while unsigned metrics alone would have classified the same errors as symmetric noise.
why_important: A systematic outward bias corrupts area estimates (agriculture, medical measurements) in one direction, which is worse than noise; a free post-hoc correction and a case for signed boundary metrics in dense VLM evaluation both follow.
why_possibly_novel: Upsampling blur is acknowledged; isolating and correcting a signed dilation component with curvature dependence appears unmeasured for language-conditioned dense models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute signed boundary errors against high-quality ground truth for 2 pipelines at multiple upsampling factors, fit the curvature dependence, and evaluate the analytic correction on held-out data.
main_risk: Annotation conventions (annotators drawing slightly inside or outside true edges) could contribute their own signed offset, requiring matting-grade ground truth to separate model bias from label bias.
default_community_belief: Upsampling error is symmetric blur, fully captured by unsigned boundary metrics and fixable only by higher-resolution features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned upsampling layers in some decoders may already compensate for the geometric bias, leaving nothing systematic to correct in the strongest models.
fastest_falsification: Signed boundary-error histogram for one model on 100 objects with high-quality masks, half a day; a zero-centered distribution falsifies.

one_line: The CLIP vision tower is the wrong default for dense tasks: self-supervised spatial features plus a thin text-alignment adapter should ground better than contrastive features
problem: Dense VLM pipelines default to contrastive vision towers because they come pre-aligned with text, silently accepting their weak spatial fidelity; the alternative decomposition (spatially-strong self-supervised features, aligned to text by a small learned map) is rarely treated as the null hypothesis to beat.
core_hypothesis: Text alignment is a low-rank, cheaply-learnable property while spatial fidelity is expensive and hard to retrofit; therefore pairing a self-supervised spatial backbone with a lightweight channel-space adapter trained on modest paired data will match contrastive towers on category recall while beating them decisively on boundary and small-object metrics, inverting the community default.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched compute and adapter budgets, the SSL-plus-adapter configuration will dominate the contrastive tower on boundary F-score and small-instance recall across two dense benchmarks while staying within a small margin on category-level recall, and the gap will persist when both use identical decoders.
why_important: If alignment is cheap and locality is dear, the field's investment logic reverses: dense pretraining should optimize spatial structure first and buy language alignment later, affecting every future dense VLM design decision.
why_possibly_novel: Hybrid systems exist, but a controlled matched-budget test framed as which property is cheaper to retrofit (alignment vs locality) appears not to have been run cleanly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train identical small decoders and adapters on one SSL backbone and one contrastive backbone at matched sizes with the same paired data budget, and compare recall, boundary, and small-object metrics on two dense benchmarks.
main_risk: Adapter capacity and paired-data volume choices could tilt the comparison either way, demanding careful budget-matching to make the verdict credible.
default_community_belief: Pre-aligned contrastive towers are the natural backbone for language-conditioned dense prediction; alignment from scratch is the expensive part.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Open-vocab breadth may depend on the enormous concept coverage of contrastive pretraining that a small adapter cannot transfer, causing rare-category collapse in the SSL configuration.
fastest_falsification: One matched pair of backbones, one decoder, one benchmark, a few GPU-days; contrastive tower winning boundary metrics falsifies.

one_line: One threshold per model is meaningless: per-prompt score distributions are incommensurable, and open-vocab precision quietly varies tenfold across queries
problem: Deployed open-vocab systems apply a single confidence threshold across all queries, assuming score scales are comparable across prompts; per-prompt operating characteristics are almost never reported.
core_hypothesis: Score distributions are prompt-specific (shaped by word frequency, embedding norm, and concept breadth), so a global threshold delivers wildly different precision-recall trade-offs per query; per-prompt precision at a fixed global threshold will span an order of magnitude, and simple per-prompt renormalization using score statistics on unlabeled images will compress this spread substantially.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring per-prompt precision at one global threshold across 200 queries will show a spread exceeding an order of magnitude, and a label-free calibration (z-scoring against each prompt's score distribution over a fixed unlabeled image pool) will reduce the interquartile spread of per-prompt precision by at least half without changing mean performance.
why_important: Threshold incommensurability is the direct cause of erratic open-vocab behavior in production; a label-free per-prompt calibration recipe is immediately deployable and would change how every open-vocab system is shipped.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration work focuses on closed-set classifiers; prompt-conditional score normalization for dense open-vocab outputs using unlabeled reference pools appears under-explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate per-prompt precision at fixed thresholds for 2 models over exhaustively-annotated data, implement the unlabeled-pool z-scoring, and compare per-prompt precision spreads before and after.
main_risk: The reference pool's domain must match deployment images, or the calibration itself becomes a new source of shift sensitivity.
default_community_belief: A single tuned threshold plus maybe per-dataset adjustment is adequate; score comparability across prompts is assumed by construction of the shared embedding space.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The shared-space geometry might make score scales more comparable than hypothesized, with per-prompt spread driven mostly by genuine difficulty differences that calibration cannot and should not remove.
fastest_falsification: Per-prompt precision spread for 50 queries on one model, half a day; a tight spread falsifies the incommensurability claim.

one_line: Paraphrase disagreement is the best free uncertainty signal for dense outputs: variance across reworded queries predicts mask error better than confidence
problem: Dense models ship one mask per query with a confidence that is known to be unreliable, while the cheap ensemble sitting in plain sight (the same referent under several paraphrases) is never systematically exploited or benchmarked as an uncertainty source.
core_hypothesis: Grounding errors are usually query-form-sensitive (a wrong instance wins under one phrasing but not all), while correct groundings are phrasing-stable; therefore cross-paraphrase mask variance is a strong correctness predictor, and paraphrase-ensembled masks (pixelwise majority) will beat single-query outputs, together forming a training-free reliability upgrade.
falsifiable_prediction: Across referring benchmarks, cross-paraphrase mask variance will predict per-sample IoU with higher rank correlation than model confidence, and majority-vote masks over 5 paraphrases will improve mean IoU over the canonical query on at least two model families, with gains concentrated on multi-instance scenes.
why_important: A label-free, architecture-agnostic reliability and accuracy upgrade that costs only extra inference passes would be adopted immediately in high-stakes deployments, and the variance decomposition doubles as a diagnostic of which queries a model understands robustly.
why_possibly_novel: Self-consistency is standard for LLM text answers; a quantitative paraphrase-consistency framework for dense masks, benchmarked against confidence baselines, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate 5 validated paraphrases for 500 referring queries, run 2 models, compute variance-IoU correlations and majority-vote gains against single-query and confidence baselines.
main_risk: Paraphrase generation may introduce subtle meaning drift, mixing genuine ambiguity into the variance signal and inflating apparent uncertainty on correct outputs.
default_community_belief: Uncertainty for dense predictions requires ensembles, dropout, or dedicated heads; the query text is a fixed input, not an uncertainty resource.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If models are text-insensitive (a documented tendency), paraphrases will produce near-identical outputs for wrong answers too, gutting the discrimination power of the variance signal.
fastest_falsification: Five paraphrases over 100 samples on one model, correlation analysis in half a day; variance uncorrelated with IoU falsifies.

one_line: AP hides the deployment gap: rank-based evaluation flatters open-vocab detectors whose cross-class score calibration is broken, and thresholded F1 tells the opposite story
problem: Open-vocab detection progress is measured by average precision, a per-class rank metric that never asks whether scores are comparable across classes, while every deployment thresholds scores globally, an operation AP is blind to.
core_hypothesis: Open-vocab detectors have systematically worse cross-class score calibration than closed-set detectors (text-embedding classifiers introduce per-class scale artifacts), so the gap between AP-based rankings and global-threshold F1 rankings is much larger for open-vocab models; method comparisons and even ordering among methods will change under deployment-faithful metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a set of open-vocab and closed-set detectors under both AP and best-global-threshold F1 will show open-vocab models losing disproportionately more performance under thresholding, and at least one pair of open-vocab methods will swap ranks between the two metrics, demonstrating that AP-based conclusions do not transfer to deployment.
why_important: If the community's headline metric systematically overstates open-vocab readiness, both research prioritization (calibration is undervalued) and practitioner expectations are miscalibrated; a deployment-faithful metric suite would realign incentives.
why_possibly_novel: AP's threshold-blindness is known in principle; quantifying the differential inflation for open-vocab versus closed-set detectors and demonstrating rank swaps appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 3 open-vocab and 2 closed-set detectors on the same benchmark under AP and global-threshold F1 with matched vocabularies, and report the per-model inflation gap and any rank changes.
main_risk: Best-global-threshold F1 is one of many deployment metrics; conclusions could depend on the specific operating-point choice, requiring a small family of threshold metrics for robustness.
default_community_belief: AP improvements translate to deployment improvements; calibration is a post-processing detail orthogonal to detector quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-class threshold tuning (feasible when classes are known in advance) may recover most of the gap, weakening the deployment-relevance argument for applications with fixed vocabularies.
fastest_falsification: Two detectors, both metrics, one benchmark, one day; equal inflation for open-vocab and closed-set falsifies.

one_line: Specific queries score lower: adding correct detail to a prompt depresses similarity scores, so fixed thresholds silently punish precise language
problem: Users are told that more specific queries improve grounding, yet raw similarity scores tend to shrink as prompts lengthen and specialize; the interaction between prompt specificity and fixed decision thresholds is undocumented.
core_hypothesis: Each added token dilutes the pooled text embedding's alignment with any single region (more constraints to satisfy, more embedding directions averaged), so correct-and-more-specific prompts produce lower absolute scores than vague ones; under a fixed threshold, recall therefore falls with specificity even as ranking quality improves, a perverse deployment interaction nobody warns about.
falsifiable_prediction: Holding the referent fixed and increasing prompt specificity through verifiably-correct detail, mean similarity of the true region will decline monotonically, and fixed-threshold recall will drop while rank-based selection (argmax over regions) improves or holds, demonstrating the score-vs-ranking divergence.
why_important: The finding yields a concrete deployment rule (thresholds must be specificity-conditioned, or scores length-normalized) and dissolves a class of contradictory anecdotes about whether detail helps or hurts grounding.
why_possibly_novel: Length effects on retrieval similarity are known in NLP; the threshold-interaction analysis for dense grounding, separating score-scale effects from ranking effects, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 200 referents, build 4-level specificity ladders with human-verified correctness, measure true-region score, fixed-threshold recall, and argmax accuracy across 2 models, and test the divergence pattern.
main_risk: Specificity ladders confound token count with rare-word introduction; length-matched controls with frequency-matched vocabulary are needed to isolate the dilution mechanism.
default_community_belief: More specific correct language can only help grounding; score scales are stable enough that thresholds need no adjustment to prompt form.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some architectures max-pool over token-region alignments rather than averaging, which would keep scores stable under added correct detail and break the dilution premise.
fastest_falsification: Fifty referents, four specificity levels, score trajectories on one model, three hours; flat or rising true-region scores falsify.

one_line: Dense probability maps are sharp even when language is vague: boundary confidence ignores lexical vagueness, hiding referential uncertainty the model should express
problem: Vague referents ('the bushes', 'the clutter', 'the shaded area') have genuinely uncertain extents, and a well-calibrated dense model should express that in its probability map; whether map softness tracks semantic vagueness at all is untested.
core_hypothesis: Mask decoders are trained with binary targets that punish soft outputs, so they produce uniformly sharp probability maps regardless of the query's semantic precision; the correlation between lexical vagueness (measured by human inter-annotator mask variance for the same query) and model boundary entropy will be near zero, meaning the maps carry no information about referential uncertainty.
falsifiable_prediction: Across queries spanning precise to vague referents, human inter-annotator boundary variance will vary widely while model boundary entropy stays in a narrow band, yielding near-zero correlation; fine-tuning with soft multi-annotator targets on a small set will restore a positive correlation, confirming the training-objective cause.
why_important: Downstream consumers read probability maps as uncertainty; if sharpness is an artifact of binary training rather than a statement about the world, decisions in mapping, agriculture, and content editing are being made on fictitious certainty.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration is studied against correctness; calibrating dense outputs against human referential variance (semantic vagueness) appears to be an unexplored axis.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect multi-annotator masks for 100 queries stratified by vagueness, compute annotator variance and model boundary entropy for 2 models, correlate, and run the small soft-target fine-tune to test the causal account.
main_risk: Annotator variance conflates vagueness with task misunderstanding; careful instruction design and screening are needed to keep the human signal clean.
default_community_belief: Probability maps reflect model uncertainty, and uncertainty from any source (visual or semantic) shows up as softness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some entropy may leak through for vague queries via conflicting feature evidence even under binary training, producing a weak but nonzero correlation that muddies the clean null.
fastest_falsification: Twenty queries across the vagueness range, entropy vs available multi-annotator variance on one model, one day including annotation; a clear positive correlation falsifies.

one_line: Global image-text score is a bad proxy for mask quality, yet pipelines use it to rank and filter dense outputs everywhere
problem: Cascaded systems (propose masks, score with a VLM) and pseudo-labeling pipelines rank dense outputs by an image- or crop-level text score, assuming this global agreement number tracks the geometric quality of the mask itself.
core_hypothesis: Crop-level VLM scores respond to category presence and salience inside the crop but are nearly blind to mask geometry (boundary tightness, leakage, missing parts), so their correlation with mask IoU is weak beyond the coarse present-vs-absent signal; a mask that leaks background or crops the object scores as well as a perfect one whenever the category remains visible.
falsifiable_prediction: Perturbing ground-truth masks with controlled geometric corruptions (dilation, erosion, truncation) while keeping the category visible will change crop-level VLM scores by amounts statistically indistinguishable from noise until corruption is extreme, and score-IoU rank correlation within the present class will be far below what filtering pipelines implicitly assume.
why_important: Every pseudo-label filter and mask-reranking step built on crop scoring inherits this blindness, systematically admitting geometrically-poor masks into training data and propagating boundary errors into the next model generation.
why_possibly_novel: Crop scoring is ubiquitous plumbing; a perturbation-based sensitivity audit quantifying its geometric blindness for dense pipelines appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply graded geometric corruptions to ground-truth masks on 500 instances, score crops with 2 VLMs, and map score sensitivity as a function of corruption type and severity against the present-vs-absent baseline sensitivity.
main_risk: Some scoring protocols use background-removed or outlined crops that may carry more geometric signal, so the audit must cover the main protocol variants to be conclusive.
default_community_belief: Higher crop-text agreement means a better mask; VLM scoring is a reasonable universal quality filter for dense outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For small objects, background leakage rapidly changes crop composition, possibly giving crop scores more geometric sensitivity than hypothesized in exactly the cases that matter.
fastest_falsification: Dilation and erosion sweeps on 100 instances with one scorer, three hours; strong monotone score response to geometry falsifies.

one_line: Under referential ambiguity the output distribution is confidently peaked on one instance: dense models are miscalibrated over referents, not just over pixels
problem: When an expression matches several instances equally well, a calibrated system should spread probability across them; dense grounding models are evaluated only on single-answer benchmarks, so their referent-level calibration under genuine ambiguity is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Training with single ground-truth regions teaches models to concentrate probability on one instance regardless of evidence symmetry, so under constructed referential ambiguity the output distribution over instances will be far more peaked than the evidence warrants, and which instance wins will be decided by salience and position priors rather than by any tie-breaking the user could predict.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes with verified symmetric candidates (matched size, salience, and attribute fit), the winning instance's share of output probability mass will vastly exceed the calibrated 1-over-N level, the winner will be predictable from salience features, and models will show no output statistic that flags the ambiguity to downstream consumers.
why_important: Referent-level overconfidence is invisible to pixel calibration studies and directly harms interactive systems, which should ask a clarifying question exactly when candidates tie; a referent-level calibration metric would make this capability measurable and optimizable.
why_possibly_novel: Pixel-level calibration and ambiguity in language are separately studied; defining and measuring referent-level calibration for dense grounding under constructed symmetry appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 150 symmetric-candidate scenes, extract per-instance probability mass from 3 models, compare against the symmetric ideal, and fit winner-prediction models on salience features.
main_risk: True symmetry is hard to construct in natural images; residual asymmetries could justify some peaking and must be bounded by human choice distributions on the same stimuli.
default_community_belief: Ambiguity handling is a dialogue-layer concern; the dense model's job is to output its best guess, and its confidence machinery covers the rest.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Query-based decoders may internally maintain multi-instance hypotheses whose probability mass, if extracted properly, is less peaked than the final rendered mask suggests.
fastest_falsification: Thirty symmetric scenes, per-instance mass on one model, three hours; near-uniform mass over candidates falsifies.

one_line: Boundary entropy should track lexical vagueness across words: 'forest edge' has fuzzier truth than 'car edge', and models encode none of this gradient
problem: Different category words carry intrinsically different boundary crispness in the world (crowd, forest, smoke vs car, bottle, sign), a lexical-semantic property that dense predictions could and arguably should reflect, but no measurement connects word-level vagueness norms to model boundary behavior.
core_hypothesis: Because binary mask training erases target softness, model boundary statistics will be driven entirely by image gradients and not by the queried word's semantic crispness; the rank correlation between per-category human vagueness norms (collected as word-level judgments) and model boundary entropy will be near zero, while human segmentations of the same scenes will show the expected strong correlation.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 40 categories spanning the crispness spectrum, human inter-annotator boundary variance will correlate strongly with word-level vagueness norms, model boundary entropy will not, and the model-human gap will be largest for high-vagueness stuff categories, quantifying a semantic calibration failure invisible to standard metrics.
why_important: Matching boundary uncertainty to lexical semantics is required for honest downstream area and change measurements (deforestation, crowd size), and the norm-based methodology gives dense evaluation a new, cheap semantic axis that needs no pixel annotation.
why_possibly_novel: Vagueness norms exist in psycholinguistics and boundary entropy exists in segmentation, but connecting them as a calibration criterion for language-conditioned dense models appears unattempted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect word-level crispness norms for 40 categories, measure model boundary entropy and human annotation variance on matched scenes for 2 models, and compare the two correlation structures.
main_risk: Image-gradient strength covaries with category crispness (fuzzy things also have fuzzy pixels), so partial correlations controlling for local gradient statistics are essential.
default_community_belief: Boundary softness is a perceptual and image-statistics matter; word semantics has no role in how sharp a mask should be.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The image-gradient covariance may be so strong that models incidentally track vagueness through pixels alone, producing a spurious pass on the correlation test.
fastest_falsification: Ten crisp and ten vague categories, entropy comparison on one model, one day; a strong vagueness-entropy correlation (after gradient controls) falsifies the null claim.

one_line: The patch grid is a hidden ceiling: boundary F-scores of dense VLMs plateau at a value predicted by patch size, and no amount of decoder capacity moves it
problem: Boundary quality differences between dense VLM methods are interpreted as modeling progress, without normalizing for the fact that all methods inherit the same coarse patch grid whose quantization may already determine the achievable boundary regime.
core_hypothesis: The information needed to place a boundary within a patch is largely destroyed by patch embedding, so achievable boundary F-score at tight tolerances is a function of patch size with only minor decoder-dependent variation; plotting method results against patch size will reveal a tight envelope, and within-envelope differences (the decoder contribution) will be small relative to between-patch-size jumps.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled sweep (same model family at multiple patch sizes vs multiple decoders at fixed patch size) will attribute the dominant share of tight-tolerance boundary variance to patch size, and an oracle experiment (perfect classification of each patch, ideal within-patch boundary recovery from raw pixels) will bound and predict the observed plateaus.
why_important: If the ceiling is grid-imposed, dozens of decoder papers are competing inside a fixed envelope; the community should be told which metric regimes are grid-limited and steer work toward patch-free or hybrid-resolution representations.
why_possibly_novel: Patch effects are folklore, but a variance-attribution study with oracle bounds separating grid-limited from decoder-limited regimes appears missing for language-conditioned dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one family at 3 patch sizes and 3 decoders at one patch size on boundary metrics at several tolerances, run the oracle-bound computation, and report the variance decomposition.
main_risk: Models at different patch sizes differ in training compute and data exposure, requiring careful matching or fine-tune-from-common-init protocols.
default_community_belief: Better decoders and losses steadily improve boundary quality; reported gains reflect genuine modeling progress rather than movement inside a fixed grid envelope.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-resolution hybrid decoders that re-inject raw pixels (matting-style refinement) may already escape the grid, making the envelope leaky enough to be uninteresting.
fastest_falsification: Boundary metrics at two tolerances for two patch sizes and two decoders, one day of inference; decoder variance rivaling patch-size variance falsifies.

one_line: Sliding-window inference decapitates language: tiles lack the global context that referring expressions quantify over, so window-based high-res grounding mis-resolves globally-scoped queries
problem: High-resolution dense inference is standardly done by tiling images through the model and stitching outputs, a scheme designed for class-wise segmentation and silently reused for language-conditioned tasks where queries reference global scene structure.
core_hypothesis: Expressions like 'the largest window', 'the car furthest from the camera', or 'the only red chair' are evaluated per tile without access to the comparison set, so each tile answers a different effective question; stitched outputs will contain multiple mutually-inconsistent local answers or miss referents whose qualifying evidence lies outside the tile, a structural failure invisible in class-wise tiling.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing whole-image versus tiled inference on globally-scoped queries will show tiling producing duplicate or contradictory positive regions at rates far above locally-scoped control queries (plain category names), and the failure rate will grow as tile size shrinks relative to the comparison set's spatial extent.
why_important: Remote sensing, pathology, and mapping all tile giant images and are adopting language-conditioned models; a query-scope-dependent failure mode means silent errors precisely on the comparative and unique-reference queries analysts most value.
why_possibly_novel: Tiling artifacts are studied for boundary seams; the interaction between tiling and the logical scope of language appears unanalyzed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build paired locally- and globally-scoped queries over large images, run tiled and whole-image (downsampled) inference on 2 models, and score scope-dependent inconsistency rates across tile sizes.
main_risk: Whole-image inference requires downsampling that hurts small referents, so the comparison must carefully separate resolution effects from scope effects.
default_community_belief: Tiling is a resolution workaround orthogonal to the query; whatever works for class segmentation works for language-conditioned segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Practitioners may already run global-then-local cascades in mature pipelines, confining the failure to naive integrations rather than the deployed state of the art.
fastest_falsification: Twenty globally-scoped queries, tiled vs whole-image on one model, three hours; equal consistency falsifies.

one_line: Positional-embedding interpolation degrades grounding anisotropically: accuracy falls fastest at image peripheries when models run above native resolution
problem: Running ViT-based dense models above pretraining resolution requires interpolating positional embeddings, universally treated as a benign trick validated by aggregate metrics that never resolve where in the image quality is lost.
core_hypothesis: Interpolation preserves the central, densely-sampled region of the positional manifold better than its extremes, so position-sensitive computations (relative spatial language, boundary placement) degrade non-uniformly, with errors concentrating near image borders and corners; aggregate metrics dilute this into a small average drop while border-region grounding suffers multiply.
falsifiable_prediction: Spatially-resolved error maps at 2x native resolution will show border-region grounding and boundary errors growing significantly faster than central-region errors relative to native resolution, the anisotropy will strengthen with interpolation factor, and models using relative or factorized position schemes will show flatter degradation profiles.
why_important: Peripheral objects are operationally critical (pedestrians entering the frame, findings at scan edges); knowing that resolution scaling buys central quality at peripheral cost changes how practitioners choose inference resolution and how architects pick positional schemes.
why_possibly_novel: PE interpolation is standard practice with aggregate validation; spatially-resolved degradation analysis keyed to positional scheme appears unreported for dense grounding.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate referring and open-vocab segmentation at native and scaled resolutions on 3 models with different positional schemes, compute error as a function of normalized image position, and test the border-vs-center interaction.
main_risk: Photographic composition places different object statistics at borders, so position-stratified analysis needs object-matched sampling to avoid content confounds.
default_community_belief: PE interpolation works; running at higher resolution is a strict quality upgrade wherever it fits in memory.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models fine-tuned at multiple resolutions may have learned interpolation-robust position codes, flattening the anisotropy below detectability.
fastest_falsification: Border-vs-center error at two resolutions on one model, one day; isotropic degradation falsifies.

one_line: There is a class of ungroundable geometries: thin, elongated referents (cables, poles, railings) fall below the text-fusion grid and no query phrasing can retrieve them
problem: Failure on thin structures is reported per dataset as a difficulty, but the stronger claim that current dense VLMs are architecturally incapable of grounding sub-grid geometry regardless of language has not been articulated or tested as a capability boundary.
core_hypothesis: Referents thinner than the feature-grid stride at fusion never form addressable units in the fused representation (their evidence is averaged into dominant background cells), so no textual specificity, prompt engineering, or decoder capacity can recover them; grounding recall for sub-stride-width structures will be near zero and completely insensitive to query improvements that measurably help super-stride referents.
falsifiable_prediction: Across models, recall as a function of structure width in stride units will collapse below width one with a sharp knee at the stride, query-enrichment interventions will improve super-stride referents while leaving sub-stride recall flat, and the knee will move with architecture stride, confirming the geometric mechanism.
why_important: Declaring a precise, architecture-derived incapability tells industrial inspection and infrastructure-mapping users what current dense VLMs cannot do at any prompt-engineering cost, and defines the exact spec (sub-stride evidence preservation) that a fix must meet.
why_possibly_novel: Thin-structure difficulty is known; framing and verifying it as a stride-derived absolute capability boundary with query-insensitivity as the signature appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a width-stratified thin-structure suite from existing datasets, run 3 models with basic and enriched queries, and plot recall against width-in-stride-units with the query-sensitivity interaction.
main_risk: Some pipelines add high-res parallel branches that partially preserve thin evidence, blurring the knee and requiring per-architecture stride accounting.
default_community_belief: Thin structures are hard but incrementally improvable with better prompts, more data, and stronger decoders within current architectures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aliasing may leave recoverable traces of thin structures in adjacent cells that a sufficiently trained decoder can decode, making the boundary soft rather than absolute.
fastest_falsification: Width-stratified recall on one model with two query styles, one day; substantial sub-stride recall or query sensitivity falsifies.

one_line: Coordinate-emitting VLMs snap to round numbers: numeric tokenization imposes a quantization prior that structures localization error
problem: VLMs that output boxes or points as text emit coordinates through a tokenizer whose numeric tokens have wildly different training frequencies, an interaction between text statistics and geometry that detection-style evaluation averages away.
core_hypothesis: Autoregressive coordinate generation inherits the corpus prior over numerals, biasing outputs toward frequent round values (multiples of 5, 10, 100); localization error will therefore be structured (histogram spikes at round coordinates, boxes gravitating to grid-like positions), degrading precisely the fine-alignment regime and inflating error for objects whose true extents sit between round values.
falsifiable_prediction: Coordinate histograms from text-emitting localizers will show significant excess mass at round values compared to the ground-truth coordinate distribution, per-sample error will correlate with the distance of true coordinates from the nearest high-frequency numeral, and models using dedicated coordinate vocabularies or regression heads will show flat histograms on identical data.
why_important: The round-number prior is an invisible systematic error affecting every text-interfaced localization model, matters for fine measurement uses, and adjudicates a live architectural question (text coordinates vs dedicated heads) with a clean, cheap measurement.
why_possibly_novel: Numeric-token artifacts are studied for arithmetic in LLMs; their geometric footprint in dense localization outputs appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect predicted coordinates from 2 text-emitting localizers over a large detection split, compare coordinate histograms against ground truth, fit the error-vs-roundness regression, and contrast with one regression-head baseline.
main_risk: Ground-truth annotations themselves contain human round-number bias, requiring the analysis to model annotation snapping separately from model snapping.
default_community_belief: Emitting coordinates as text is a benign interface choice; the model learns the numeric mapping well enough that tokenization details wash out.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Heavy fine-tuning on localization data may have flattened the numeral prior for coordinate contexts, leaving snapping only in under-trained models.
fastest_falsification: Coordinate histogram from one model over 10k predictions, two hours; no round-value excess relative to ground truth falsifies.

one_line: Detect-then-segment pipelines structurally cannot ground non-box-compact referents: 'the road markings' dies at the box stage before segmentation begins
problem: The dominant open-vocab segmentation recipe routes language through a box-proposal stage, silently assuming every referent is representable as a compact box, though many legitimate referents (markings, scattered debris, wiring, spilled liquid) are diffuse, multi-component, or extreme-aspect regions.
core_hypothesis: The box stage imposes a topology filter: referents whose ground-truth support has low box-fill ratio or many components are eliminated or fragmented before mask refinement, so pipeline failures on such referents are attributable to the interface geometry rather than to either component's quality, and end-to-end pixel-conditioned models will beat cascades specifically on this referent class while losing nowhere else.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying referents by box-fill ratio and component count, cascade performance will degrade sharply with both variables while direct dense models degrade mildly, and cascade errors will concentrate at the proposal stage (correct masks unreachable from surviving boxes), verifiable by oracle-box substitution.
why_important: Cascades dominate deployments because they compose off-the-shelf parts; a topology-conditioned failure law tells users exactly which query classes need a different architecture and quantifies what the composability convenience costs.
why_possibly_novel: Cascade weaknesses are discussed anecdotally; a referent-topology-stratified attribution with oracle-stage analysis appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a referent set stratified by fill ratio and component count from existing stuff and scattered-object annotations, evaluate one cascade and one direct dense model, and run oracle-box substitution to localize the failure stage.
main_risk: Direct dense models may be generally weaker, muddying the comparison unless matched on compact-referent performance first.
default_community_belief: Boxes are a harmless intermediate; whatever can be segmented can be boxed first, so cascade composition is a free engineering win.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern proposal stages output many overlapping boxes whose union may cover diffuse referents well enough that the mask stage recovers them, making the topology filter leakier than hypothesized.
fastest_falsification: Thirty low-fill-ratio referents on one cascade with oracle-box controls, half a day; oracle boxes failing to rescue performance falsifies the stage attribution.

one_line: Query syntax steers output geometry: detection-flavored phrasing produces boxier masks from the same model on the same image
problem: Multi-task dense VLMs are trained on mixtures where phrasing correlates with annotation geometry (detection-style prompts with boxes, segmentation-style prompts with masks), creating a potential leakage from query syntax into output shape that nobody audits at inference time.
core_hypothesis: Models learn the correlation between prompt register and target geometry, so paraphrasing a request from segmentation register ('segment the...') to detection register ('detect the...', 'locate the...') will measurably shift output mask statistics toward box-like shapes (higher rectangularity, lower boundary complexity) with the referent and image held fixed, revealing that output geometry is partly a linguistic artifact.
falsifiable_prediction: Across paraphrase pairs differing only in task register, rectangularity of produced masks will be systematically higher under detection-flavored prompts, the shift will exceed paraphrase noise measured within-register, and it will be strongest in models trained on the most heterogeneous task mixtures.
why_important: Geometry-by-phrasing means downstream measurements (areas, boundary statistics) depend on how the request was worded, an unrecognized nuisance for scientific and industrial users, and it exposes how shallowly task instructions are integrated in multi-task dense training.
why_possibly_novel: Instruction sensitivity is studied for answer content in LLMs; register-to-geometry leakage in dense outputs appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct register minimal pairs for 300 referents, run 3 multi-task dense VLMs, compare shape statistics across registers against within-register paraphrase baselines, and correlate effect size with training-mixture heterogeneity where documented.
main_risk: Some models legitimately switch output modality (boxes vs masks) by instruction, requiring the analysis to restrict to cases where a mask was produced in both registers.
default_community_belief: The instruction verb selects the task; conditional on producing a mask, its geometry is determined by the image and referent alone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong mask-decoder priors may fully determine geometry once the referent is selected, leaving register effects only in the modality choice, not in shape statistics.
fastest_falsification: Fifty register pairs, one model, rectangularity comparison in three hours; no register effect beyond paraphrase noise falsifies.

one_line: Open-vocab detection performance is interpolation in embedding space: accuracy on 'novel' classes is predicted by their distance to seen classes, exposing how little is actually open
problem: Open-vocab detectors report strong numbers on benchmark novel classes without controlling how semantically close those classes sit to the training vocabulary, so the headline capability (detecting genuinely new concepts) is confounded with easy interpolation between seen neighbors.
core_hypothesis: Novel-class performance is a smooth decreasing function of text-embedding distance to the nearest seen classes; benchmark novel sets cluster in the near-seen regime, so measured open-vocab strength is dominated by interpolation, and extrapolation performance (far-from-seen concepts) is dramatically lower and rarely sampled by current evaluations.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-class novel AP on embedding distance to the k-nearest seen classes will yield strong negative slopes across detectors, standard benchmark novel classes will occupy the near end of the distance distribution, and re-weighting evaluation by distance strata will shrink claimed open-vocab gaps between methods substantially.
why_important: A distance-conditioned report card changes the meaning of open-vocab claims, prevents users from extrapolating benchmark numbers to genuinely new domains, and gives a cheap pre-deployment predictor of per-class reliability computable from text alone.
why_possibly_novel: Seen-unseen leakage is a known worry; a quantitative distance-stratified evaluation protocol with re-weighted method comparison appears not to be standard practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute embedding distances from each benchmark novel class to the training vocabulary for 3 detectors with documented vocabularies, fit distance-performance regressions, and re-score methods under distance-stratified weighting.
main_risk: Training vocabularies of some public models are incompletely documented, forcing conservative reconstructions that could bias distance estimates.
default_community_belief: Benchmark novel-class AP measures open-world capability; embedding proximity to seen classes is not a variable anyone needs to report.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Visual similarity, not text-embedding distance, may drive transfer, weakening the text-distance regression even if interpolation is real.
fastest_falsification: Distance-AP regression using published per-class results and reconstructed vocabularies, mostly CPU work in a day; a flat regression falsifies.

one_line: Synonyms sail through class-aware NMS: querying near-duplicate vocabulary items produces duplicate boxes that standard suppression logic cannot merge
problem: Class-aware NMS assumes class identities partition detections, but open-vocab querying makes classes user-defined and freely overlapping; nobody specifies what suppression should do when the vocabulary contains synonyms or near-synonyms.
core_hypothesis: When a vocabulary includes semantic duplicates (sofa and couch, cup and mug), each attracts its own detection on the same object and class-aware NMS retains both, so duplicate rates scale with vocabulary redundancy; measured precision becomes an artifact of vocabulary composition, and embedding-similarity-aware suppression will recover the loss without harming distinct-class recall.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding synonyms to a query vocabulary will inflate duplicate detections on identical objects at rates predicted by pairwise text-embedding similarity, aggregate precision will fall although the image set and model are unchanged, and replacing class-aware NMS with similarity-thresholded suppression will restore precision at negligible recall cost.
why_important: Practitioners build large vocabularies by merging lists, guaranteeing redundancy; an evaluation and a one-line suppression fix keyed to embedding similarity addresses a failure that every deployed open-vocab detector currently has.
why_possibly_novel: NMS variants are heavily studied for closed sets; the interaction of suppression logic with user-defined overlapping vocabularies appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one detector under vocabularies with 0 to 50 percent injected synonyms, measure duplicate and precision curves, then evaluate similarity-aware suppression across thresholds and report the operating characteristics.
main_risk: Some detectors score classes jointly through softmax, partially suppressing synonyms before NMS, so the effect size may be architecture-dependent in ways that complicate a general claim.
default_community_belief: Vocabulary composition is the user's business; detection plumbing like NMS is neutral infrastructure that works for any class list.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Softmax competition may already collapse synonym scores onto one winner in most architectures, leaving duplicates rare enough to ignore.
fastest_falsification: One detector, one split, vocabulary with and without 20 injected synonyms, duplicate-rate comparison in three hours; no inflation falsifies.

one_line: Vocabulary interference: adding irrelevant classes to the query list changes detections of unrelated classes through score renormalization
problem: Open-vocab detectors are treated as banks of independent per-class detectors selected by the query list, but softmax-style scoring couples all queried classes, and the magnitude of this coupling on real deployments is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Because scores compete through shared normalization, the detection set for class X depends measurably on which other classes are co-queried, even when those classes never appear in the images; interference will be largest when added classes are semantically near X, and it will move borderline detections across the threshold in both directions unpredictably.
falsifiable_prediction: Holding images and model fixed while varying only the co-queried vocabulary, per-class detection sets will change (measured by symmetric difference of detection sets at fixed threshold) far beyond run-to-run noise, with the change magnitude regressing on the added classes' embedding proximity to the target class, and sigmoid-scored architectures will show near-zero interference under the same manipulation.
why_important: Interference means open-vocab systems have no stable per-class behavior to certify: adding one query to a monitoring dashboard silently changes another query's alerts; the architecture-conditioned characterization also gives buyers a concrete selection criterion (sigmoid over softmax for stability).
why_possibly_novel: The softmax coupling is mathematically obvious but its deployment magnitude, semantic-proximity dependence, and use as an architecture selection criterion appear unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 2 softmax-style and 1 sigmoid-style detectors, evaluate 20 target classes under 10 co-query vocabularies of varying proximity, and report detection-set instability curves per architecture.
main_risk: Threshold placement interacts with interference (borderline-heavy classes show more instability), so results must be reported across threshold sweeps to avoid cherry-picked operating points.
default_community_belief: The query list is a filter on independent detectors; co-queried classes do not affect each other's outputs except by intended disambiguation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Many modern detectors score region-text pairs independently with sigmoids, so the coupling may be confined to older or specific architectures, reducing the finding's breadth.
fastest_falsification: One softmax detector, one target class, five vocabularies, detection-set differences in two hours; stability under vocabulary changes falsifies.

one_line: Hierarchical vocabularies break open-vocab detectors: querying 'animal' and 'dog' together splits scores and drops both below threshold
problem: Real query lists mix abstraction levels (vehicle and truck, animal and dog), but detectors treat vocabulary items as mutually exclusive competitors, and the behavior under hypernym-hyponym co-occurrence is unspecified and untested.
core_hypothesis: A dog region genuinely matches both 'dog' and 'animal', so competitive scoring splits its probability mass between them; under mixed-level vocabularies, true positives will be lost to score splitting (both labels falling below threshold) or arbitrary level assignment, and detection quality will degrade specifically for objects with a co-queried ancestor, a taxonomy-structured failure invisible in flat-vocabulary benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding hypernyms of target classes to the vocabulary will reduce recall of the target classes by an amount predicted by the hypernym's embedding proximity, the lost detections will show near-tied scores between levels, and taxonomy-aware post-processing (max over ancestor chains) will recover most of the loss without new training.
why_important: Mixed-level vocabularies are the norm in practical query lists assembled by non-experts; a predictable recall hole plus a cheap aggregation fix is immediately actionable, and benchmarks should add mixed-level tracks to reflect it.
why_possibly_novel: Taxonomy handling exists in closed-set hierarchical classification; its interaction with free-form open-vocab querying and competitive dense scoring appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 2 detectors on standard splits under flat vs hypernym-augmented vocabularies, measure per-class recall deltas and score-split statistics, and test the ancestor-max recovery.
main_risk: Hypernym embeddings may be visually diffuse enough that they rarely compete at detection strength, making the effect small outside contrived vocabularies.
default_community_belief: Users should just avoid redundant vocabulary levels; detectors behave sensibly enough under any reasonable class list.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sigmoid-scored detectors can assign high scores to both levels simultaneously, in which case mixed vocabularies cause duplicate boxes (a different failure) rather than recall loss.
fastest_falsification: One detector, ten classes, vocabulary with and without hypernyms, recall comparison in two hours; unchanged recall falsifies.

one_line: The learned background logit is a closed-set artifact: genuinely novel objects are absorbed into background more often than confused with any wrong class
problem: Open-vocab detectors retain a learned background/no-object score trained against the base vocabulary, quietly defining background as 'not one of the training classes' rather than 'not an object', a mismatch whose consequences for novel objects are unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Because background was optimized to reject regions unexplained by base classes, novel objects (which the base vocabulary cannot explain) match the background profile; the dominant error mode for far-from-base novel classes will be background absorption (no detection at all) rather than misclassification, an error split that current metrics do not report and that objectness-recalibration could fix.
falsifiable_prediction: Error decomposition on novel classes will show missed-entirely dominating misclassified, the miss rate will grow with embedding distance from the base vocabulary while the misclassification rate stays flat, and replacing the learned background score with a class-agnostic objectness signal will convert a substantial fraction of misses into correct detections.
why_important: Background absorption is the quiet killer of open-world claims: precision looks fine while novel recall silently dies; attributing it to the background head redirects fixes toward objectness recalibration rather than more vocabulary data.
why_possibly_novel: Background bias is discussed in open-vocab training papers; a distance-conditioned error decomposition isolating absorption as the dominant novel-class failure, with the objectness-swap test, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Decompose novel-class errors for 2 detectors into miss vs misclassification as a function of embedding distance to base classes, then swap in a class-agnostic proposal scorer and re-measure the decomposition.
main_risk: Class-agnostic objectness scorers bring their own biases (trained on similar base data), potentially reproducing the same absorption under a different name.
default_community_belief: Open-vocab detectors fail on novel classes mainly by confusing them with similar known classes; recall losses are a matter of embedding quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For visually salient novel objects, proposal machinery may fire regardless of the background head, concentrating the absorption effect on low-salience objects only.
fastest_falsification: Error decomposition for one detector on one novel split, half a day; misclassification dominating misses falsifies.

one_line: Softmax pixels cannot serve overlapping vocabularies: forcing one label per pixel breaks down when queries overlap ('person', 'shirt', 'blue'), and the sigmoid alternative changes rankings
problem: Open-vocab semantic segmentation evaluates with mutually-exclusive per-pixel labels inherited from closed-set tradition, but user vocabularies routinely contain overlapping concepts at different granularities that are simultaneously true of the same pixel.
core_hypothesis: Under overlapping vocabularies, softmax-per-pixel architectures must suppress true labels, and which one survives is determined by score-scale artifacts rather than semantics; the degree of vocabulary overlap (measured by co-true rates in ground truth) will predict per-class performance distortion, and independent sigmoid scoring will re-rank methods on overlap-heavy vocabularies relative to the standard benchmarks that hid the issue.
falsifiable_prediction: Constructing evaluation vocabularies with graded overlap, softmax pipelines will show performance dropping with overlap degree while sigmoid pipelines stay flat, method rankings will differ between low- and high-overlap vocabularies, and the suppressed-true-label rate will track text-embedding proximity between overlapping classes.
why_important: Multi-label truth at pixels is the actual semantics of open vocabularies (things have parts, attributes, and superclasses); an evaluation regime and architecture guidance for overlap-heavy use is missing infrastructure for the field.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-label segmentation exists as a niche; connecting vocabulary overlap statistics to open-vocab benchmark distortion and method re-ranking appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build overlap-graded vocabularies from part-whole and attribute annotations, evaluate 2 softmax-style and 2 sigmoid-style open-vocab segmenters, and compare performance-vs-overlap curves and cross-vocabulary rankings.
main_risk: Ground truth with reliable multi-label pixel annotations is limited, constraining the overlap grades that can be constructed honestly.
default_community_belief: Per-pixel argmax over the query list is the natural output format for open-vocab segmentation, as benchmark protocols assume.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For most practical vocabularies overlap may be rare enough that the distortion stays within noise, making the multi-label machinery unnecessary complexity.
fastest_falsification: One softmax segmenter on flat vs overlap-augmented vocabulary, performance delta in three hours; no overlap-dependent drop falsifies.

one_line: The single mask-token bottleneck: routing segmentation through one LLM embedding caps multi-instance and fine-boundary expressiveness measurably
problem: LLM-based segmenters emit a special token whose hidden state conditions a mask decoder, compressing the entire spatial answer into one fixed-dimension vector; the information-capacity consequences of this interface choice are asserted away rather than measured.
core_hypothesis: A single conditioning vector cannot simultaneously specify many disjoint regions or high-frequency boundary detail, so output complexity (number of recoverable components, boundary detail bandwidth) will saturate at a level set by the interface dimension; multi-token variants will show capacity scaling with token count on the same backbone, isolating the bottleneck from model quality.
falsifiable_prediction: As target complexity grows (more instances, higher boundary curvature), single-token models will plateau in achievable IoU while the same backbone with k mask tokens will plateau k-fold later, and reconstruction experiments (decoding masks from the token embedding alone) will show the embedding discarding component-level information beyond a small count.
why_important: The mask-token interface is being standardized across reasoning-segmentation models; a measured capacity law would inform whether the field is building on a bottleneck and how many tokens future interfaces need for realistic scene complexity.
why_possibly_novel: Interface capacity is discussed qualitatively; a controlled capacity-scaling measurement with token-count ablation on fixed backbones appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train small variants of an open reasoning-segmentation architecture with 1, 4, and 16 mask tokens on identical data, evaluate against complexity-stratified targets, and run token-embedding reconstruction probes.
main_risk: Training variance across variants may swamp capacity effects unless multiple seeds are run, raising compute cost beyond the minimal budget.
default_community_belief: One well-trained mask token suffices because the heavy lifting happens in the decoder conditioned on image features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder's cross-attention to image features may carry most spatial information, with the token acting as a mere selector, making capacity effectively unbounded and the plateau absent.
fastest_falsification: Complexity-stratified evaluation of an existing single-token model, half a day: no complexity-dependent plateau relative to a non-token baseline falsifies.

one_line: Chain-of-thought before the mask token changes the mask: reasoning length is an uncontrolled variable that moves dense outputs in reasoning-segmentation models
problem: Reasoning-segmentation models generate explanatory text before emitting the mask token, and the community reports only whether reasoning improves answer selection, not whether the amount and content of intervening text perturbs the spatial output for a fixed answer.
core_hypothesis: The mask token's hidden state depends on the entire preceding context, so injected verbosity (longer but semantically equivalent reasoning) shifts the conditioning vector; masks will drift measurably with reasoning length even when the identified referent is unchanged, meaning output geometry depends on a stochastic decoding variable nobody controls.
falsifiable_prediction: Forcing equivalent reasoning traces of different lengths (via prompting or constrained decoding) for identical queries will produce mask variance significantly above the deterministic baseline, drift will grow with token distance between the referent mention and the mask token, and anchoring the mask token immediately after the referent mention will reduce variance.
why_important: If dense outputs drift with verbosity, then temperature, prompt phrasing, and instruction-tuning style all leak into segmentation geometry, making reproducibility and regression testing of such systems ill-defined; the anchoring result would give an immediate architectural remedy.
why_possibly_novel: Reasoning-output coupling is studied for answer accuracy; its effect on the geometry of dense outputs through hidden-state drift appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 200 referents, elicit short and long equivalent reasoning on one open reasoning-segmentation model, measure mask IoU variance across conditions against greedy-decoding baselines, and test the token-distance regression.
main_risk: Controlling reasoning content while varying length is imperfect; content differences could explain drift unless equivalence is verified carefully.
default_community_belief: Reasoning affects which object is chosen; once chosen, the mask geometry is stable model behavior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The mask decoder may re-ground the token against image features strongly enough to wash out hidden-state drift, leaving geometry stable under verbosity.
fastest_falsification: Fifty referents, two reasoning lengths, IoU variance on one model in three hours; variance at baseline levels falsifies.

one_line: Alignment tax on pixels: safety tuning of the language backbone degrades dense outputs for sensitive-adjacent queries without any refusal being issued
problem: LLM backbones inside segmenting VLMs undergo safety alignment tuned on text behavior, and dense heads consume their hidden states; whether safety-induced representation shifts leak into spatial outputs for benign queries near sensitive topics has not been assessed.
core_hypothesis: Safety tuning reshapes representations for tokens and topics associated with people, medical content, and weapons, so benign dense queries touching these regions (segment the person's face, the syringe, the rifle in a museum photo) will show degraded grounding quality relative to matched neutral queries, without explicit refusals, because the conditioning vectors were displaced by alignment rather than gated by policy.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched query pairs (sensitive-adjacent vs neutral, controlled for visual difficulty) will show a consistent quality gap on safety-tuned backbones, the gap will shrink or vanish on the same architecture with a base (non-safety-tuned) backbone, and hidden-state analysis will show larger alignment-induced displacement for the degraded queries.
why_important: A silent quality tax on people-related segmentation affects mainstream applications (photo editing, medical annotation) and is invisible to safety evaluations (no refusal) and to benchmarks (which avoid sensitive vocabulary); measuring it informs how alignment should treat multimodal hidden states.
why_possibly_novel: Alignment taxes are documented for text task performance; their propagation through hidden-state interfaces into dense spatial outputs appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble visually-matched sensitive-adjacent and neutral query pairs, evaluate an open segmenting VLM with safety-tuned and base backbone variants, and compare quality gaps plus hidden-state displacement statistics.
main_risk: Base and safety-tuned backbone pairs that are truly comparable are scarce, and other differences between checkpoints could masquerade as alignment effects.
default_community_belief: Safety tuning affects what models say, not how well they see; benign queries are untouched by alignment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense heads are typically fine-tuned after alignment on grounding data that includes people, potentially re-anchoring the displaced representations and erasing the tax.
fastest_falsification: Sixty matched pairs on one safety-tuned model, quality-gap test in half a day; no gap falsifies.

one_line: Dialogue history contaminates grounding: the same query grounds differently after unrelated conversation turns, revealing spurious context sensitivity in segmenting VLMs
problem: Multi-turn segmenting assistants carry conversation history in context, and everyone assumes grounding of a new, self-contained query is invariant to that history; this invariance is never tested.
core_hypothesis: Because the mask-conditioning hidden state attends over the full context, semantically irrelevant history (previous unrelated queries, chit-chat, other images' descriptions) shifts dense outputs; contamination will grow with history length and with lexical overlap between history and the current scene, and history mentioning other objects present in the image will bias masks toward those objects.
falsifiable_prediction: Identical queries evaluated with empty vs padded-irrelevant histories will show mask disagreement well above decoding noise, disagreement will scale with history length and overlap, and adversarially-chosen benign history (mentioning a distractor category) will divert masks to the distractor at rates far above clean-history controls.
why_important: Assistants are deployed multi-turn by definition; history-dependent grounding breaks reproducibility, enables a prompt-injection-like attack via innocuous chat, and argues for architectural isolation of grounding turns, all currently unexamined.
why_possibly_novel: Context-length effects are studied for text QA; history contamination of dense outputs and the benign-history diversion attack appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 300 self-contained queries under empty, neutral-padded, and distractor-mentioning histories on one open multi-turn segmenter, measuring disagreement and diversion rates with decoding-noise baselines.
main_risk: Distinguishing legitimate context integration (history should sometimes matter) from contamination requires careful construction of certifiably-irrelevant histories.
default_community_belief: A well-formed new query is grounded on its own terms; irrelevant history is ignored by instruction-tuned models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention over long contexts may dilute history influence to negligible levels for strongly image-anchored tasks like segmentation.
fastest_falsification: Fifty queries under empty vs distractor histories on one model, three hours; diversion at control rates falsifies.

one_line: Pronouns break dense coreference: 'segment it' after establishing a referent fails disproportionately, exposing missing discourse-to-pixel binding
problem: Multi-turn interfaces invite anaphora (find the red car; now segment it), requiring the model to bind a discourse entity to pixels across turns; benchmarks test single-turn explicit reference only, leaving anaphoric grounding unmeasured.
