core_hypothesis: Segmenting VLMs resolve pronouns with text-side coreference machinery that is not linked to their spatial memory, so anaphoric queries will ground substantially worse than repeating the full expression, and failures will concentrate when the intervening turn mentions other entities (text-side interference) even though the image and referent never changed.
falsifiable_prediction: The anaphora penalty (full-expression accuracy minus pronoun accuracy on identical referents) will be large across current multi-turn models, will grow when distractor entities are mentioned between turns, and will not correlate with single-turn grounding quality, showing it is a distinct missing capability rather than general weakness.
why_important: Anaphora is the default register of interactive use; quantifying the penalty defines a capability gap that single-turn benchmarks structurally cannot see and provides a concrete target for discourse-aware grounding architectures.
why_possibly_novel: Coreference is mature in NLP and referring segmentation is mature in vision; their composition (discourse entities bound to masks across turns) appears essentially unbenchmarked.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 300 two-turn episodes (establish referent, then anaphoric request) with and without distractor mentions, evaluate 2 multi-turn segmenters against full-expression controls, and report the penalty decomposition.
main_risk: Some models re-run grounding on the concatenated text, effectively resolving the pronoun textually before grounding, which would shrink the penalty for architectures with strong text coreference.
default_community_belief: LLM backbones handle coreference natively, so pronoun queries inherit text-side competence and need no special evaluation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For simple two-turn cases, textual coreference plus re-grounding may genuinely suffice, confining failures to longer dialogues than the minimal design tests.
fastest_falsification: Fifty two-turn episodes on one model, penalty measurement in three hours; near-zero penalty falsifies.

one_line: Mutually exclusive queries are decoded independently: 'the left one' and 'the right one' produce overlapping masks, and joint decoding is free accuracy
problem: Batch querying of the same image with logically related expressions is universal in practice, yet each query is decoded independently, discarding hard constraints (mutual exclusion, exhaustiveness, containment) that the language makes explicit.
core_hypothesis: Independent decoding leaves measurable joint inconsistency (overlapping masks for exclusive referents, gaps for exhaustive partitions), and because the constraints are known from the query semantics, constrained joint inference over the existing outputs will convert inconsistency into accuracy at zero training cost, with gains concentrated exactly on the ambiguous cases where single-query decoding guesses.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured on query sets with known logical structure, pairwise-exclusive queries will overlap on a substantial fraction of images, applying joint assignment (optimal transport or ILP over instance candidates under exclusion constraints) will improve per-query accuracy over independent decoding, and gains will correlate with the single-query ambiguity level of each sample.
why_important: Joint decoding is a training-free wrapper deployable on any grounding model, and the inconsistency statistics double as a new evaluation axis (logical coherence of dense outputs) that current benchmarks never check.
why_possibly_novel: Structured prediction is classical, but exploiting inter-query logical constraints at inference time over modern grounding models, with coherence as a reported metric, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct exclusive and exhaustive query sets for 300 scenes, run 2 models independently, measure violation rates, then apply constraint-based joint assignment and report accuracy deltas.
main_risk: Joint inference needs candidate distributions per query; models exposing only hard masks require re-runs or approximations that may under-realize the theoretical gain.
default_community_belief: Each query is an independent inference problem; coherence across queries is not a property anyone measures or optimizes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If single-query outputs are already near-deterministic and correct on resolvable cases, violations may concentrate on hopeless samples where constraints cannot rescue accuracy.
fastest_falsification: Left/right exclusive pairs on 100 scenes with one model, overlap rate plus greedy joint assignment in half a day; negligible overlap or no gain falsifies.

one_line: Referring benchmarks teach discrimination, not description: expressions were authored against visible distractors, so models never learn what words mean, only what tells instances apart
problem: Standard referring datasets were collected by asking annotators to describe a target so another player could pick it among the image's annotated instances, an adversarial-discrimination protocol whose imprint on model semantics is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on discrimination-born expressions learn features that separate co-present instances rather than compositional word meanings, so they will underuse attributes that were redundant in training scenes (mentioning color only when distractors differ in color); their attribute sensitivity will be conditional on distractor structure, not intrinsic, and transfer to descriptive use cases (single-instance verification, absent-target detection) will be systematically poor.
falsifiable_prediction: Models will weight an attribute word strongly when the scene contains contrasting distractors and near-ignore the same word in single-instance scenes (measurable by attribute-perturbation sensitivity in both conditions), a context-dependence that descriptive semantics would not show and that predicts verification-task failure from the collection protocol alone.
why_important: If dataset game mechanics shaped what grounding means to these models, then porting them to verification, retrieval, and safety filtering (descriptive tasks) is unsound, and future data collection should mix descriptive protocols deliberately.
why_possibly_novel: Dataset biases in referring data are discussed for length and salience; tracing the discrimination-vs-description semantics distinction to the collection game and testing its behavioral signature appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure attribute-perturbation sensitivity (mask change when an attribute is altered) in distractor-present vs single-instance scenes for 3 models, and correlate the conditional-sensitivity gap with performance on a verification task.
main_risk: Instruction-tuned models trained on broader mixtures may have diluted the protocol imprint, requiring stratification by training data provenance.
default_community_belief: Referring data teaches grounded language understanding; how the expressions were elicited is a collection detail without semantic consequences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attribute usage conditioned on distractors is also rational pragmatics; models exhibiting it might be showing correct pragmatic inference rather than degenerate semantics, requiring careful separation.
fastest_falsification: Attribute-perturbation sensitivity in 30 paired scenes (with and without contrastive distractors) on one model, three hours; context-independent sensitivity falsifies.

one_line: IoU thresholds punish granularity disagreement as if it were error: 'the jacket' vs 'the person' mismatches dominate reported failures on referring benchmarks
problem: Referring evaluation counts a prediction wrong below an IoU threshold, conflating true grounding failure with legitimate disagreement about referential granularity (whether an expression denotes the garment, the person, or the person-with-garment), which language leaves underdetermined.
core_hypothesis: A substantial fraction of sub-threshold predictions are granularity disagreements (predicted mask is a superset or subset corresponding to a defensible reading) rather than wrong-object errors; standard metrics therefore overstate semantic failure, understate real progress, and penalize models that resolve granularity differently from annotator conventions rather than incorrectly.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing sub-threshold predictions into wrong-object, boundary-noise, and containment-consistent (super/subset) classes will show containment-consistent cases forming a large share, human judges will rate most containment-consistent predictions as acceptable readings, and model rankings will shift when containment-consistent cases are scored separately.
why_important: Benchmarks steer the field; if a big error share is metric artifact, effort is being spent fixing non-errors, and a granularity-aware protocol (accepting defensible containment readings or scoring them separately) would redirect progress toward real failures.
why_possibly_novel: IoU threshold arbitrariness is acknowledged; an error-decomposition tying sub-threshold mass to linguistic granularity underdetermination with human acceptability grounding appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Classify 1000 sub-threshold predictions from 2 models by the three-way decomposition using containment statistics, collect human acceptability ratings on the containment-consistent subset, and re-rank models under granularity-aware scoring.
main_risk: Automatic containment classification may mislabel sloppy masks as granularity choices, requiring conservative geometric criteria and human verification.
default_community_belief: Sub-threshold predictions are model failures; the IoU threshold is a fair, neutral arbiter of grounding correctness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Containment-consistent predictions may mostly be genuine confusions (grounding the person because the jacket word was not understood), which the human-acceptability check would expose as unacceptable.
fastest_falsification: Decompose 200 failures from one model, half a day; a small containment-consistent share falsifies.

one_line: Dense benchmarks are inside the pretraining crawl: grounding scores on standard test images are inflated by exposure, measurable with post-cutoff imagery
problem: Web-scale pretraining crawls plausibly contain the images (or near-duplicates) of standard dense benchmarks, but dense evaluation practice, unlike LLM practice, has no contamination-checking culture; the exposure inflation on grounding metrics is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Pretraining exposure to test images improves dense scores through instance-specific memorization (scene layouts, object identities), so models will perform systematically better on benchmark images that appear in accessible crawl indexes than on matched images that entered the web after the pretraining cutoff, with the gap constituting a direct estimate of contamination inflation for dense tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: Constructing an evaluation pair (benchmark-style annotations on crawl-present images vs post-cutoff images matched for category, size, and difficulty proxies), models will score measurably higher on crawl-present images, the gap will grow with model pretraining scale, and near-duplicate retrieval against open crawl indexes will predict per-image performance residuals.
why_important: If dense numbers carry exposure inflation, cross-model comparisons favor bigger crawls rather than better grounding, and the field needs post-cutoff refresh sets, a practice change this measurement would justify and calibrate.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination is intensively studied for LLM text benchmarks; a matched-pair exposure audit for dense grounding metrics appears not to exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate 500 post-cutoff images with referring and segmentation labels matched to a benchmark subset verified present in open crawl indexes, evaluate 3 models on both sets, and compare gaps across model scale.
main_risk: Matching difficulty across old and new imagery is imperfect (camera and content drift), so difficulty proxies and human-difficulty ratings must anchor the comparison.
default_community_belief: Dense benchmarks measure generalization; image-level contamination is an LLM problem, not a segmentation problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense supervision is annotation-specific (masks are not in the crawl), so exposure to pixels alone may confer little advantage, yielding a null gap.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate one model on 100 crawl-verified vs 100 post-cutoff matched images, one day including annotation of a small set; no gap falsifies.

one_line: Mask style is keyed to vocabulary: models reproduce each training dataset's annotation conventions per word, so 'person' masks include hair but 'pedestrian' masks do not
problem: Dense training mixes datasets with conflicting annotation conventions (include or exclude hair, handheld objects, clothing accessories), and since each dataset also has its own vocabulary register, models may resolve the conflict by binding convention to wording rather than harmonizing geometry.
core_hypothesis: Models learn dataset-specific mask styles indexed by the lexical items typical of each dataset, so near-synonymous queries whose usage differs across training sources will elicit systematically different mask conventions on identical instances, an absurd-but-learned behavior that reveals style-vocabulary entanglement in multi-dataset dense training.
falsifiable_prediction: Querying identical instances with dataset-typical synonym pairs will produce convention-level mask differences (hair inclusion, accessory inclusion) aligned with each word's source dataset conventions at rates far above within-word variance, and the effect will strengthen in models trained on more heterogeneous mixtures.
why_important: Style-vocabulary entanglement means dense outputs embed arbitrary curation history into the semantics of words, corrupting downstream measurement consistency and arguing for convention-normalization during multi-dataset training, a concrete data-engineering fix.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation inconsistency across datasets is known; the hypothesis that models key conventions to lexical items, testable by synonym probes on identical pixels, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify convention-divergent categories across major training datasets, construct synonym probes typical of each source, run 2 multi-dataset models on shared instances, and score convention adherence per word against source conventions.
main_risk: Synonyms also differ in embedding geometry for reasons unrelated to source datasets, requiring control synonym pairs from single-source vocabularies.
default_community_belief: Multi-dataset training averages annotation styles into a single harmonized convention per category.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Convention conflicts may resolve by dataset size dominance (the biggest source wins uniformly), producing word-independent styles and a null synonym effect.
fastest_falsification: Two convention-divergent synonym pairs probed on 50 shared instances with one model, three hours; word-independent conventions falsify.

one_line: Pseudo-label bootstrapping amplifies CLIP's salience bias generation over generation: self-trained dense models drift toward segmenting only what captions mention
problem: A dominant recipe trains dense models on pseudo-masks scored or selected by CLIP-style similarity, then sometimes iterates; the compounding of the scorer's known salience bias through these bootstrap loops is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: CLIP-scored pseudo-label selection preferentially admits salient, caption-typical instances, so each bootstrap generation trains on data increasingly depleted of non-salient instances; non-salient recall will decay measurably across generations while headline metrics (dominated by salient instances) hold steady or improve, hiding the drift.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking per-stratum recall (by size, centrality, and caption-mention probability) across 2 to 3 bootstrap generations will show monotone decay in the non-salient strata alongside stable aggregate numbers, and injecting a stratum-balanced admission rule into the loop will arrest the decay at equal compute.
why_important: Bootstrap pipelines are how open-vocab dense training scales; demonstrating a bias amplification law with a cheap correction (stratified admission) directly changes how the biggest training runs curate data.
why_possibly_novel: Confirmation bias in self-training is known abstractly; measuring salience-stratified drift across generations in dense VLM bootstrapping with an admission-rule fix appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a small-scale two-generation bootstrap with CLIP-scored pseudo-masks, evaluate stratified recall after each generation against the base model, and repeat with stratum-balanced admission.
main_risk: Small-scale loops may not reproduce the dynamics of production-scale pipelines, limiting external validity without industrial collaboration.
default_community_belief: Pseudo-label filtering by VLM score is a quality control step; iterating it refines the model rather than narrowing it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Diversity of web imagery may keep non-salient instances flowing in despite biased scoring, making the decay too slow to matter within realistic generation counts.
fastest_falsification: One bootstrap generation with stratified evaluation, a few GPU-days; no stratum decay falsifies.

one_line: Cumulative-IoU metrics are large-object metrics: standard referring scores are dominated by big masks, and instance-weighted re-scoring flips method rankings
problem: Referring segmentation commonly reports cumulative or overall IoU (pooled intersection over pooled union), which weights samples by pixel count; the community reads these numbers as general grounding quality without auditing the implied size-weighting.
core_hypothesis: Pooled-IoU metrics allow large-object performance to mask small-object failure, and methods differ enough in their size profiles that the choice between pooled and per-sample metrics changes method orderings; part of reported progress consists of large-object gains invisible to per-sample analysis, and small-referent grounding has improved far less than headline numbers suggest.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing published-style comparisons under per-sample mean IoU and size-stratified metrics will change at least some adjacent method orderings, the pooled-vs-per-sample gap per method will correlate with its size-performance slope, and progress-over-time curves will be visibly flatter for small referents than for the pooled metric.
why_important: Metric-induced misranking distorts which techniques the community adopts; a size-decomposed reporting standard is trivial to compute and would realign perceived with actual progress on the harder, smaller referents.
why_possibly_novel: Metric critiques exist for detection AP; a systematic size-weighting audit of referring segmentation's pooled-IoU convention with re-ranking evidence appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate several public checkpoints on standard splits under pooled, per-sample, and size-stratified metrics, and quantify ranking changes and per-method size slopes.
main_risk: Public checkpoints may differ from paper-reported models, so ranking-change claims must rest on the re-evaluated artifacts, stated clearly.
default_community_belief: Pooled IoU is a reasonable aggregate; metric choice among IoU variants does not change substantive conclusions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Method size-profiles may be similar enough (all trained on the same data) that rankings are stable across metrics, making the audit a confirmation rather than a correction.
fastest_falsification: Re-score 3 checkpoints under both metrics on one split, a few hours; identical orderings falsify the flip claim.

one_line: Grounding errors are predictable without the image: a text-only probe on query embeddings forecasts per-sample failure, showing benchmarks are partly language-solvable
problem: Per-sample difficulty in dense grounding is assumed to be dominated by visual factors (clutter, size, occlusion); how much failure is forecastable from the query text alone, before any image is seen, has not been quantified.
core_hypothesis: A large share of failure variance is carried by text-side features (construction type, word rarity, spatial-term presence, expression length), so an image-blind classifier on query embeddings will predict per-sample correctness with substantial accuracy; this both provides a deployment-time risk flag and reveals that benchmarks confound language difficulty with visual difficulty.
falsifiable_prediction: An image-blind probe trained on one model's outcomes will predict held-out failures well above base rate, will transfer across models (indicating shared language-side weaknesses rather than model quirks), and its top predictive features will match independently-documented weaknesses (negation, ordinals, laterality), validating it as a diagnostic instrument.
why_important: A text-only risk score costs nothing at inference (no image processing), enables routing hard queries to stronger models or humans, and its transferability across models would demonstrate that current dense failures are structural properties of the language interface, not incidental.
why_possibly_novel: Difficulty prediction exists for VQA; an image-blind failure forecaster for dense grounding used both as deployment tooling and benchmark critique appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a small probe on query embeddings to predict correctness for one model on a referring split, test transfer to two other models, and analyze feature attributions against known weakness categories.
main_risk: Text features correlate with visual difficulty through content (small objects get certain descriptions), so the benchmark-critique interpretation needs careful partialling of visual covariates.
default_community_belief: Grounding failure is mostly image-driven; you cannot know a query will fail without looking at the picture.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If failures are dominated by scene-specific distractor configurations, text-only prediction will barely beat base rates and the probe will not transfer.
fastest_falsification: Probe training and evaluation on existing outputs of one model, mostly CPU, a few hours; near-chance prediction falsifies.

one_line: Per-class dense performance is a language-statistics artifact: pretraining word frequency out-predicts visual difficulty measures for open-vocab segmentation quality
problem: Per-class results in open-vocab dense papers are interpreted visually (this class is hard because it is small or cluttered), while the text-side driver (how often and how consistently the class name appears in pretraining captions) is rarely entered into the same regression.
core_hypothesis: Class-name frequency and caption-usage consistency in pretraining corpora explain more variance in per-class dense metrics than standard visual difficulty measures (average size, boundary complexity, scene clutter), meaning open-vocab dense benchmarks function substantially as measurements of language exposure rather than of visual segmentation capability.
falsifiable_prediction: Across benchmarks and models, a regression of per-class quality on corpus statistics vs visual statistics will assign the dominant unique variance to the corpus side, the corpus coefficients will replicate across independently-trained models, and residual analysis will identify classes where visual factors genuinely dominate as a small minority.
why_important: If exposure dominates, then per-class gaps should be attacked with data interventions (caption augmentation for rare names) rather than architectural work, and cross-benchmark comparisons need frequency normalization to mean anything about vision.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency effects are documented for classification zero-shot accuracy; a variance-decomposition against visual difficulty measures at dense-prediction level appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble per-class metrics for 3 models on 2 dense benchmarks, compute corpus statistics from public caption datasets and visual statistics from annotations, and run commonality analysis to attribute unique variance.
main_risk: Corpus statistics from public proxies may misestimate the actual (private) pretraining mixtures, attenuating the measured language effect.
default_community_belief: Per-class dense difficulty is a visual property; language exposure matters mainly for exotic vocabulary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Visual and lexical difficulty are entangled through the world (rarely-photographed things are also rarely captioned), potentially defeating clean variance attribution.
fastest_falsification: Single-benchmark regression with both covariate families on existing per-class numbers, a day of CPU work; visual dominance falsifies.

one_line: The stuff-thing gap in open-vocab segmentation is caption-statistics debt: regions that captions rarely mention cannot be aligned, whatever the architecture
problem: Open-vocab segmenters consistently perform worse on stuff classes (road, sky, wall) than thing classes, which is attributed vaguely to stuff being amorphous; the alternative explanation, that web captions systematically fail to mention background stuff so alignment never forms, is untested.
core_hypothesis: The stuff-thing gap is primarily an alignment-data artifact: caption-mention rates for stuff regions are far lower than for things of equal image area, and per-class gap size will track mention-rate deficits rather than shape complexity; architectures cannot close a gap whose cause is missing supervision signal.
falsifiable_prediction: Estimating mention probability per class from public caption corpora, the stuff-thing performance gap will be largely explained by mention-rate differences in regression (with shape statistics adding little unique variance), and augmenting training with synthetically re-captioned data that mentions stuff will close a disproportionate share of the gap at fixed architecture.
why_important: Correct causal attribution decides investment: if the gap is data debt, dense re-captioning pipelines are the fix and architectural work on amorphous-region modeling is misdirected; the mention-rate framework also predicts which new domains will show the gap.
why_possibly_novel: The stuff-thing gap is universally reported but causally unattributed; the mention-rate accounting plus the re-captioning intervention appears to be a new decomposition.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class mention rates and shape statistics, regress the gap across 2 models, then fine-tune one model on stuff-mentioning re-captioned data and measure differential gap closure.
main_risk: Synthetic re-captioning quality could confound the intervention arm; caption noise may hurt things while helping stuff for unrelated reasons.
default_community_belief: Stuff classes are intrinsically harder for dense VLMs because they lack objectness and clear boundaries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Amorphous geometry may genuinely resist the query-based decoding used by modern segmenters, leaving a large architecture-attributable residual after mention-rate control.
fastest_falsification: Mention-rate vs gap regression on existing per-class numbers, one day of CPU; shape statistics dominating falsifies.

one_line: The residual error floor of referring benchmarks is mislabeled ground truth: top-model failures concentrate on ambiguous or wrong annotations, not model deficiencies
problem: Progress on referring benchmarks is slowing near an apparent performance ceiling, interpreted as remaining model deficiency; the composition of the residual error set (annotation errors, ambiguous expressions, multiple defensible answers) has not been audited at scale.
core_hypothesis: A majority of errors made jointly by all top models are benchmark defects: expressions with multiple valid referents, masks with wrong extents, or stale annotations; the true model-attributable error rate is substantially lower than reported, and model rankings within the defect-heavy residual are noise being over-interpreted by the community.
falsifiable_prediction: Human re-adjudication of the consensus-failure set (samples all top models miss) will classify most as annotation defects or genuine ambiguity, whereas samples missed by only some models will be predominantly valid, and cleaning the defect subset will compress reported method gaps while leaving the valid-failure ordering intact.
why_important: If the frontier is annotation noise, continued benchmark hill-climbing is measuring luck; a certified-clean residual split would refocus method development on real remaining failures (which the audit simultaneously identifies and characterizes).
why_possibly_novel: Label-error audits exist for classification test sets; a consensus-failure adjudication protocol for dense referring benchmarks with gap-compression analysis appears not to have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect consensus failures of 3 top checkpoints on one benchmark, have multiple annotators adjudicate 500 of them into defect, ambiguous, and valid categories, and re-score methods on the cleaned split.
main_risk: Adjudication itself is subjective for referring ambiguity, requiring clear guidelines and inter-annotator agreement reporting to be credible.
default_community_belief: Benchmark residuals represent hard, valid cases; the remaining gap to perfect scores is model capability waiting to be built.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Recent benchmark versions may already have been cleaned enough that valid hard cases genuinely dominate the residual, making the audit reassuring rather than corrective.
fastest_falsification: Adjudicate 100 consensus failures of two models, one day with two annotators; a large valid-failure majority falsifies.

one_line: Part-whole boundaries are training-unstable: pixels belonging to both 'person' and 'shirt' receive conflicting gradients, leaving a detectable noise signature along part seams
problem: Dense training mixes supervision at different granularities (whole persons, garments, body parts) over the same pixels, and the optimization consequence of these overlapping, formally-contradictory targets under single-label objectives is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Pixels in part-whole overlap zones receive alternating gradient targets across training batches, preventing convergence to stable features there; the learned representation will show elevated feature variance and prediction flicker specifically along part-whole seams (collar lines, waistlines), distinct from ordinary boundary uncertainty and reproducible across runs.
falsifiable_prediction: Feature-space variance under input jitter and prediction instability under retraining seeds will be significantly higher on part-whole seam pixels than on ordinary object-background boundaries matched for contrast, and switching to multi-label training objectives on the same data will selectively reduce the seam instability.
why_important: Part-whole seams carry disproportionate application value (garment extraction, body-region measurement); identifying a training-objective cause with an objective-level fix (multi-label targets) offers a concrete quality improvement and explains persistent flicker in video applications.
why_possibly_novel: Label conflict in multi-dataset training is discussed for classes; localizing its geometric signature to part-whole seams and testing the multi-label remedy appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure jitter-variance and cross-seed prediction disagreement on seam vs matched-control pixels for 2 models, then train small single-label and multi-label variants on identical part-whole data and compare seam stability.
main_risk: Seam pixels also have distinctive appearance statistics (fabric edges), so contrast-matched controls are essential to isolate the supervision-conflict contribution.
default_community_belief: Overlapping annotations average into sensible hierarchical features; boundary uncertainty is uniform in kind, differing only in degree.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern query-based decoders may compartmentalize granularities per query, sheltering shared features from the conflict and eliminating the seam signature.
fastest_falsification: Jitter-variance comparison on 50 seam and 50 control boundary segments for one model, half a day; equal variance falsifies.

one_line: Part queries default to the whole: 'the handle of the cup' returns the cup whenever the part boundary is not photometrically obvious
problem: Part-referring expressions are syntactically transparent, but dense models must translate the genitive construction into a within-object segmentation; when and why they fall back to whole-object masks is uncharted.
core_hypothesis: Models treat part expressions as weighted mixtures of part and whole concepts, with the whole dominating unless the part has strong photometric edges; fallback-to-whole will be the modal error, its rate will be predicted by the part's edge strength and the part-word's caption frequency, and it will persist even when the query is unambiguous, revealing that genitive syntax lacks a reliable compositional pathway to sub-object masks.
falsifiable_prediction: Across part-annotated categories, the error distribution for part queries will be dominated by whole-object masks rather than wrong parts or other objects, the fallback rate will regress on part-edge contrast and part-name corpus frequency, and prompt strengthening ('only the handle, not the cup') will reduce fallback far less than a visual-edge manipulation of equal informativeness.
why_important: Part-level grounding is the interface for manipulation, repair, and measurement instructions; characterizing the fallback law tells builders when part queries can be trusted and shows that the fix lives in supervision (part-contrastive pairs), not phrasing.
why_possibly_novel: Part segmentation exists as a supervised task; the compositional fallback analysis for open-vocabulary genitive queries with the language-vs-visual intervention comparison appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate part queries over part-annotated datasets on 3 models, classify errors, fit the fallback-rate regression, and run the matched prompt-strengthening vs edge-enhancement intervention comparison.
main_risk: Part annotations vary in convention (where the handle ends), which contaminates fallback classification near part borders.
default_community_belief: Part expressions work reasonably when parts are visible; failures are scattered rather than systematically biased toward the whole.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models heavily trained on part-annotated data may show wrong-part confusions as the modal error instead, indicating a different (discrimination) bottleneck than the mixture account.
fastest_falsification: Thirty part queries with error classification on one model, three hours; wrong-part errors dominating falsifies the fallback account.

one_line: Part grounding does not compose: models find 'the wheel of the car' but fail on 'the wheel of the boat', exposing memorized part-object pairs rather than part concepts
problem: Part vocabulary performance is reported on canonical part-object combinations, leaving open whether models possess transferable part concepts or a lookup table of frequent pairings.
core_hypothesis: Part grounding is stored as joint part-object statistics, not as compositional part concepts, so accuracy on unusual-but-real combinations (wheels on boats, handles on sculptures, screens on refrigerators) will collapse toward chance despite the part being clearly visible, and the collapse will be predicted by the pair's corpus co-occurrence rather than by visual clarity.
falsifiable_prediction: On a suite of visually-verified unusual part-object pairs, part-query accuracy will drop sharply relative to canonical pairs matched for part visibility, the drop will regress on pair co-occurrence statistics from public corpora, and the same part word will succeed and fail across hosts within a single image set, isolating the pairing as the causal variable.
why_important: Compositionality of part concepts is exactly what open-vocabulary promises for maintenance, robotics, and inspection in novel configurations; a lookup-table verdict caps the technology's applicability and defines the needed supervision (decorrelated part-host pairs).
why_possibly_novel: Compositional generalization is studied for attribute-noun pairs in classification; part-host decorrelation for dense grounding with the corpus-statistics regression appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate 80 unusual and 80 canonical part-host instances with matched part visibility, run 3 models, and fit accuracy against pair co-occurrence and visibility covariates.
main_risk: Unusual combinations are rare in natural imagery, and composited stimuli may introduce artifacts; careful sourcing from real oddity photos is required.
default_community_belief: Part words carry transferable meaning; a model that finds wheels on cars can find wheels anywhere they appear.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong shape-based part evidence (wheels are distinctive) may support genuine transfer for geometrically-salient parts, restricting the collapse to appearance-defined parts.
fastest_falsification: Twenty unusual-pair images on one model, three hours; canonical-level accuracy falsifies.

one_line: Occlusion language is evaluated incoherently: 'the partially hidden cat' has amodal semantics but modal ground truth, and models are punished whichever they output
problem: Referring expressions about occluded objects semantically denote the whole object (amodal extent), while segmentation ground truth almost always marks visible pixels only (modal extent); this unacknowledged mismatch makes occlusion-heavy evaluation internally contradictory.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on modal masks but described referents produce inconsistent intermediate behavior (mostly modal masks with sporadic amodal leakage into occluder regions), and measured performance on occluded referents is substantially an artifact of the semantics-annotation mismatch rather than grounding failure; making the target convention explicit in the query will move outputs measurably, showing the ambiguity is live inside the model.
falsifiable_prediction: On occluded-referent samples, prediction mass inside occluder regions will be nonzero and highly variable across samples (inconsistency signature), scoring the same predictions against modal and amodal ground truth will reorder models, and convention-explicit prompts ('visible parts only' vs 'entire object including hidden parts') will shift occluder-region mass in the instructed direction on at least some model families.
why_important: Occlusion is ubiquitous, and downstream users need to know which convention a model follows before trusting areas or extents; establishing convention-controllability via language would also be a novel, useful capability measurement.
why_possibly_novel: Amodal segmentation is a supervised niche; the referential-semantics mismatch in standard evaluation and prompt-based convention control for open models appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble occluded-referent samples with both modal and amodal ground truth (from existing amodal datasets), evaluate 3 models under neutral and convention-explicit prompts, and quantify occluder-region mass shifts and metric reorderings.
main_risk: Amodal ground truth is itself annotator-inferred and noisy, especially for large occlusions, capping the precision of the convention comparison.
default_community_belief: Occlusion difficulty is a visual reasoning problem; masks mean visible pixels and everyone knows it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may be so uniformly modal (zero occluder mass, no prompt sensitivity) that the mismatch is theoretically real but behaviorally inert.
fastest_falsification: Occluder-region mass measurement on 50 occluded referents under two prompt conventions, one model, three hours; zero mass and zero prompt effect falsifies liveness.

one_line: Language can probe amodal knowledge without amodal training: asking for 'the whole object including hidden parts' recovers completion that binary evaluation says models lack
problem: Dense models are assumed to lack amodal completion because their default outputs are modal, but the default output may reflect training convention rather than absent knowledge; no one has used language as the instrument to separate the two.
core_hypothesis: Occlusion completion is latently present in web-pretrained representations (captions describe whole objects), suppressed by modal mask supervision; explicit amodal instructions will elicit above-chance completion (predicted extent into occluded regions correlating with true amodal shape) despite zero amodal training, demonstrating knowledge-behavior dissociation controllable through the text interface.
falsifiable_prediction: Under amodal-explicit prompts, predicted masks will extend into occluded regions with better-than-chance agreement to amodal ground truth (measured against shape-prior baselines like convex completion), the effect will be present in language-heavy architectures and absent in pure dual-encoder pipelines, and no comparable extension will occur under neutral prompts.
why_important: If latent amodal knowledge is unlockable by phrasing, applications get occlusion-robust extents for free, and the finding recalibrates how the field infers capability absence from default behavior, a methodological correction with broad reach.
why_possibly_novel: Amodal completion is treated as requiring dedicated supervision; prompt-elicited zero-shot amodal behavior as a knowledge probe appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate amodal-prompted predictions on existing amodal-annotated datasets across 3 model families, scoring occluded-region prediction against amodal truth and geometric-completion baselines.
main_risk: Apparent completion could be low-level mask smoothing rather than knowledge; the geometric baselines and shape-specific agreement analysis must separate these.
default_community_belief: Without amodal supervision, dense models cannot and do not complete occluded shapes; their modal outputs reflect their knowledge.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask decoders may be architecturally biased toward visible-evidence support, making them incapable of expressing completion even if the backbone represents it.
fastest_falsification: Amodal-prompted masks on 40 occluded objects vs convex-completion baseline, one model, half a day; baseline-level agreement falsifies.

one_line: Non-object referents get object-shaped masks: shadows, reflections, and stains are segmented with a compactness prior that their physics violates
problem: Language can refer to photometric phenomena (the shadow on the wall, the reflection in the window, the wet patch), and dense models produce masks for them, but whether output geometry respects the physics of such regions (diffuse edges, non-compact supports, perspective-attached shapes) is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Mask decoders carry a thing-shaped prior (compact, closed, sharp-edged) learned from object-dominated supervision, so masks for photometric referents will be systematically too compact, too sharp, and too convex relative to ground truth, with error geometry differing in kind (not degree) from object-referent errors, revealing that referent ontology is flattened to objecthood at the decoder.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing predicted vs true shape statistics for photometric referents, residuals will show consistent compactness and sharpness surpluses across models, the surplus will be absent for matched object referents, and it will shrink in decoders trained with stuff-heavy supervision, tracking the prior's data origin.
why_important: Shadow, reflection, and spill segmentation matter for editing, safety (wet floors), and relighting; a characterized ontological bias tells users to distrust boundary and area estimates for this referent class and gives a supervision-mix lever for fixing it.
why_possibly_novel: Shadow detection exists as a supervised task; auditing open-vocabulary dense models for a thing-shaped prior on photometric referents appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble photometric-referent queries with careful ground truth from existing shadow and reflection datasets, run 3 open-vocab segmenters, and compare shape-statistic residuals against matched object-referent controls.
main_risk: Ground-truth conventions for diffuse phenomena are themselves contested (penumbra inclusion), demanding explicit annotation-protocol reporting.
default_community_belief: If a region is nameable, the segmenter's geometry machinery applies equally; referent type does not bias mask shape.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong photometric edges in typical shadow benchmarks may let models produce accurate sharp masks, hiding the prior except on genuinely diffuse cases.
fastest_falsification: Thirty shadow and reflection queries on one model with shape-residual analysis, half a day; unbiased geometry falsifies.

one_line: Negative-space referents are ungroundable: 'the gap between the buildings' asks for a region defined by absence, and dense VLMs have no representation for it
problem: Language routinely names interstitial regions (gaps, openings, spaces between, clearances), which have no positive appearance features; whether dense models can ground absence-defined regions has never been isolated as a capability question.
core_hypothesis: Pixel-text alignment is built entirely on positive appearance evidence, so absence-defined referents will fail in a characteristic way: masks will snap onto the bounding positive objects (the buildings, not the gap) or onto sky texture, and no phrasing will retrieve the interstitial region, revealing a representational hole rather than a difficulty gradient; geometric post-processing on the model's own object masks, by contrast, computes the region trivially, quantifying the gap between what the system knows and what its language interface can express.
falsifiable_prediction: On gap-referent queries, the modal output will overlap the flanking objects rather than the true interstitial region, accuracy will be near zero across phrasings and models, and a two-step baseline (ground the flanking objects, compute the between-region geometrically) will outperform direct querying by a dramatic margin, demonstrating the interface-expressiveness deficit.
why_important: Clearance and gap queries are core to navigation, docking, and assembly instructions; establishing that current interfaces cannot express them, while their components are computable, motivates language-to-geometry compilation layers as an architecture direction.
why_possibly_novel: Spatial-relation grounding is studied for object pairs; absence-defined region reference as a capability class with the compute-vs-express contrast appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate interstitial ground truth for 150 scenes, run direct queries across phrasings on 3 models, implement the two-step geometric baseline, and compare.
main_risk: Interstitial ground truth requires convention decisions (depth extent of a gap) that must be fixed and reported for reproducibility.
default_community_belief: Sufficiently trained VLMs ground any nameable region; interstitial space is just another spatial expression.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instruction-tuned models with strong spatial reasoning may compose the between-region internally, achieving moderate accuracy and softening the representational-hole claim.
fastest_falsification: Twenty gap queries on one model, overlap analysis in two hours; consistent interstitial grounding falsifies.

one_line: Image corruption strips language components in a fixed order: attributes fail first, then relations, then nouns, defining a corruption hierarchy of grounding
problem: Robustness studies report aggregate dense-metric decay under corruption, ignoring that a referring query bundles several linguistic components whose visual evidence degrades at different rates, and whose failure order determines what kind of wrong answer users get.
core_hypothesis: Attribute evidence (color, texture) lives in fragile high-frequency and chromatic channels while category evidence is redundant across scales, so as corruption increases, grounding degrades compositionally: attribute constraints stop working first (model picks the right category but wrong instance), spatial relations second, and noun-level category selection last, producing a predictable error-type trajectory rather than uniform decay.
falsifiable_prediction: Under graded blur, noise, and compression, error composition will shift in the predicted order (wrong-instance-right-category errors rising before wrong-category errors), component-specific probes (attribute-only, relation-only, noun-only queries) will show separated decay curves in the predicted order, and the order will be stable across corruption types that share the frequency profile.
why_important: The hierarchy tells deployed systems what failure to expect at given image quality (disambiguation dies before detection), enabling quality-gated query simplification, and it links dense-VLM robustness to interpretable evidence channels rather than opaque aggregate numbers.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption benchmarks exist for classification and segmentation; a linguistic-component-resolved decay analysis for grounding appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate component-isolated query sets under 5 corruption levels and 3 corruption types on 2 models, plot per-component decay curves, and test the ordering's consistency.
main_risk: Component-isolated queries differ in base difficulty, so decay must be normalized to clean-image performance per component to compare fairly.
default_community_belief: Corruption degrades grounding wholesale; the interesting variable is overall severity, not which parts of the query fail first.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attribute and category evidence may be more entangled in learned features than the frequency-channel story assumes, producing parallel rather than ordered decay.
fastest_falsification: Blur sweep with attribute-vs-noun query pairs on one model, half a day; parallel decay curves falsify.

one_line: Color words are silently catastrophic in false-color domains: querying 'the red region' in thermal or stained imagery grounds display palette, not physical meaning
problem: Specialized imaging (thermal, fluorescence, ultrasound overlays, satellite composites) uses false-color palettes where hue encodes measurement rather than reflectance, yet open-vocab tools are marketed into these domains without any account of what color language does there.
core_hypothesis: Dense models ground color words in display-space hue statistics learned from natural photos, so in false-color imagery color-containing queries will select palette regions with confident masks whose semantics are accidental (whatever the colormap painted), performance will be uncorrelated with the physical variable users intend, and nothing in the output flags the domain mismatch, a silent hazard specific to the language interface.
falsifiable_prediction: In palette-swapped versions of identical measurement data, masks for color queries will follow the palette (near-perfect swap-tracking) rather than the underlying measurement, while category queries on the same images remain palette-stable, isolating the hazard to color language; confidence will not differ between natural and false-color usage.
why_important: Medical and industrial users naturally reach for color words because their displays are colorful; demonstrating palette-tracking with unchanged confidence establishes a concrete misuse mode and motivates domain guards (palette metadata awareness) in deployed tools.
why_possibly_novel: Domain shift studies target feature distributions; the semantic misbinding of color vocabulary in false-color domains, isolated by palette-swap controls, appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public thermal and false-color scientific imagery, render each under 2 palettes, run color-word and category-word queries on 2 models, and measure palette-tracking rates and confidence distributions.
main_risk: Some false-color imagery co-occurs with natural-color context in training data, potentially teaching partial palette conventions that soften the effect for common colormaps.
default_community_belief: Color queries are among the most reliable attribute queries; color is a simple, robust visual feature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Users in these domains may rarely use color words with open-vocab tools, making the hazard real but operationally marginal.
fastest_falsification: Palette-swap test on 30 thermal images, one model, two hours; masks tracking measurement rather than palette falsify.

one_line: Language conditioning amplifies canonical-view bias: text-driven segmentation degrades more than class-driven segmentation on unusual viewpoints of the same objects
problem: Viewpoint robustness is studied for recognition, but language-conditioned dense prediction adds a second pathway (text embeddings encode how objects are typically described, which reflects how they are typically photographed) whose viewpoint sensitivity has not been separated from the visual pathway's.
core_hypothesis: Text embeddings anchor to canonical appearance statistics (web photos favor canonical views), so conditioning on language imports an additional canonical-view prior on top of the vision tower's; the viewpoint-induced performance drop for text-queried segmentation will exceed the drop for view-matched class-agnostic or mask-prompted segmentation using the same backbone, isolating a language-attributable robustness penalty.
falsifiable_prediction: On matched canonical and unusual-view instances, the degradation ratio will be significantly larger for text-conditioned than for geometry-prompted segmentation sharing the vision tower, and the per-category penalty will correlate with the viewpoint diversity of that category's web imagery, tracking the text prior's origin.
why_important: If language conditioning taxes viewpoint robustness, applications with unconstrained cameras (drones, manipulation, inspection) should prefer geometry-prompted pipelines for unusual views, and pretraining should diversify caption-image viewpoint pairing, both actionable consequences.
why_possibly_novel: Viewpoint studies treat the model as a whole; decomposing viewpoint sensitivity into vision-tower and language-conditioning contributions via prompt-modality controls appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble canonical and unusual-view instance pairs, evaluate text-conditioned vs geometry-prompted segmentation on shared backbones for 2 model families, and compare degradation ratios with category-level viewpoint-diversity covariates.
main_risk: Geometry prompts (boxes, points) carry different information than text, so the comparison needs careful information-matching to attribute the gap to the language prior rather than prompt informativeness.
default_community_belief: Viewpoint robustness is a property of the vision backbone; how the query is expressed does not change it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The vision tower's own canonical bias may dominate so thoroughly that the language pathway adds no measurable extra penalty.
fastest_falsification: Thirty view pairs under both prompt modalities on one model, half a day; equal degradation ratios falsify.

one_line: Dense VLMs are more sensitive to meaningless text perturbation than to meaningful image perturbation: a sensitivity-asymmetry metric nobody computes
problem: Robustness is evaluated per modality in isolation, so the field lacks any calibrated comparison of how much output change a semantically-null text edit causes versus a semantically-real image edit, though this asymmetry determines which input deserves engineering care in deployments.
core_hypothesis: Because text conditioning funnels through a low-dimensional bottleneck with high leverage over the decoder, dense outputs move more under paraphrase-level text noise than under image changes of matched semantic magnitude (object displacement, lighting change); this asymmetry is quantifiable as the ratio of output divergence per unit semantic change and will exceed one substantially for dual-encoder models.
falsifiable_prediction: Defining matched semantic units via human equivalence judgments (text edits rated meaning-preserving; image edits rated meaning-relevant), the divergence ratio will consistently exceed one across referring datasets for dual-encoder models, will be closer to one for LLM-decoder models, and will predict which real-world failure reports (phrasing complaints vs lighting complaints) dominate for each system.
why_important: The asymmetry metric gives deployment teams a principled answer to where to spend robustness effort (query normalization vs image standardization) per model, and it exposes an under-recognized design flaw: the input meant to be the stable specification (language) is the volatile one.
why_possibly_novel: Single-modality robustness is standard; a cross-modal, semantically-normalized sensitivity ratio for dense outputs appears to be an unmeasured quantity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched perturbation banks (50 meaning-preserving text edits, 50 meaning-relevant image edits) over 100 scenes, compute output divergences on 2 models per family, and estimate the ratio with human-anchored normalization.
main_risk: Semantic magnitude matching across modalities is inherently soft; the conclusion must be robust to reasonable re-weightings of the human equivalence anchors.
default_community_belief: Image robustness is the hard problem; the text input is discrete, clean, and comparatively trustworthy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For heavily text-augmented recent models the ratio may already be near parity, making the metric descriptive rather than corrective.
fastest_falsification: Ten scenes with 5 text and 5 image perturbations each on one model, divergence comparison in half a day; image-dominant sensitivity falsifies.

one_line: Region-text training never mines spatial near-misses: negatives are other images' captions, so adjacent-region confusions are structurally untrained
problem: Contrastive region-text objectives draw negatives from unrelated images or shuffled captions, an expedient choice whose consequence (the model is never penalized for grounding the region next to the right one) is invisible in loss curves but potentially decisive for localization precision.
core_hypothesis: Because near-miss negatives (descriptions of adjacent regions, or the right description paired with a shifted box) are absent from training, the learned score surface is flat in the spatial neighborhood of the true region; localization errors will concentrate at small offsets with near-tied scores, and a modest fine-tune adding synthetic spatial near-miss negatives will sharpen the score surface and disproportionately reduce adjacent-region errors without new data collection.
falsifiable_prediction: Score-vs-offset profiles around true regions will be measurably flat within small displacements for standard models (score dropping less than a few percent for displacements that halve IoU), the flatness will predict each model's adjacent-error rate, and near-miss fine-tuning will steepen profiles and cut adjacent errors on held-out data while leaving distant-error rates unchanged.
why_important: This locates a whole error class in a training-objective blind spot with a cheap, data-free remedy (synthetic offsets), and the score-profile flatness measurement provides a new diagnostic that any lab can run on frozen models.
why_possibly_novel: Hard-negative mining is studied for retrieval; the specifically-spatial near-miss gap in region-text training and its offset-profile signature appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure score-offset profiles for 2 frozen models over 500 regions, correlate flatness with adjacent-error rates, then run a short near-miss fine-tune on one open model and re-measure both quantities.
main_risk: Aggressive near-miss training could over-sharpen and harm robustness to annotation jitter, requiring an explicit precision-robustness trade-off analysis.
default_community_belief: Standard InfoNCE-style negatives suffice; localization precision comes from architecture and data scale, not negative composition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Box-regression and mask losses in modern pipelines may already supply the spatial gradient that contrastive negatives lack, making profiles sharp and the fine-tune redundant.
fastest_falsification: Score-offset profiles on 100 regions of one frozen model, three hours; sharp profiles falsify the blind-spot premise.

one_line: Vision-only fine-tuning silently unmoors the text tower: dense adaptation with a frozen text encoder grows the modality gap and quietly sacrifices off-vocabulary generalization
problem: The standard dense-adaptation recipe freezes the text encoder (to preserve open-vocab ability) and tunes the vision side, assuming the frozen text space remains a valid coordinate system for the drifting visual features.
core_hypothesis: Vision-side fine-tuning optimizes alignment only for the training vocabulary's directions, so visual features drift into a subspace matched to those words while the rest of the text space dangles unanchored; in-vocabulary metrics improve while alignment for unseen words decays in proportion to their distance from the training vocabulary, meaning the recipe's open-vocab preservation premise is inverted precisely where it matters.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking alignment quality during vision-only fine-tuning, in-vocabulary dense performance will rise while zero-shot performance on held-out vocabulary falls, the fall will correlate with embedding distance from training words, and measured modality-gap statistics restricted to off-vocabulary directions will grow monotonically with fine-tuning steps.
why_important: This recipe underlies most domain adaptations of open-vocab models (medical, aerial, industrial); if it trades away exactly the open-vocabulary property users think they are keeping, the community needs anchored alternatives (feature-space regularization toward pretrained geometry or joint light-touch text tuning).
why_possibly_novel: Catastrophic forgetting is studied for classes; the geometric account of off-vocabulary alignment decay under frozen-text dense adaptation, with distance-dependent predictions, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune an open-vocab segmenter's vision side on a narrow vocabulary, evaluate dense zero-shot on distance-stratified held-out words at checkpoints, and measure off-vocabulary gap statistics over training.
main_risk: Effects may depend on fine-tuning scale and learning rate, requiring a sweep to distinguish inherent geometry from hyperparameter pathology.
default_community_belief: Freezing the text encoder preserves open-vocabulary capability during dense adaptation; that is the whole point of the recipe.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Vision drift may be low-rank and near-isotropic in text-space coordinates, leaving off-vocabulary alignment essentially intact except at extreme fine-tuning budgets.
fastest_falsification: One narrow fine-tune with held-out-vocabulary checkpoints, a few GPU-days; stable off-vocabulary performance falsifies.

one_line: Referring video segmentation ignores temporal validity: 'the man running' keeps his mask after he stops, because expressions are treated as identity labels rather than time-indexed predicates
problem: Video referring expressions contain predicates that are true only during intervals (running, holding, glowing), but models and benchmarks treat the expression as a persistent identity tag for one object track, never asking when the description holds.
core_hypothesis: Training pairs each expression with a full-length track, so models ground once and propagate by appearance, making masks insensitive to the predicate's truth value over time; the mask will persist through predicate cessation (the man stops running) and will fail to acquire objects whose predicate becomes true mid-clip, both measurable as temporal-validity violations that current metrics cannot see.
falsifiable_prediction: On clips with annotated predicate intervals, mask presence will be statistically independent of predicate truth outside the first grounding window, persistence-after-cessation and failure-to-acquire rates will both be high across models, and per-frame re-grounding (an expensive control) will recover validity sensitivity, confirming the propagation shortcut as the cause.
why_important: Time-indexed language is the point of video queries (find the person falling, the machine overheating); identity-tag semantics silently substitutes a different, easier task, and quantifying the substitution defines what video grounding benchmarks must add (predicate-interval annotations).
why_possibly_novel: Referring video segmentation is an active area, but temporal-validity evaluation (when the expression is true, not just which object it picks) appears absent from its protocols.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate predicate intervals for 150 clips from existing video referring datasets, evaluate 2 models for persistence and acquisition violations, and run the per-frame re-grounding control on a subset.
main_risk: Some predicates are identity-like in practice (clothing descriptions), so the suite must isolate genuinely transient predicates to measure the effect cleanly.
default_community_belief: Video referring models track the described object; temporal dynamics of the description are a nuance handled implicitly by video training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Recent video-language models with dense temporal supervision may partially track predicate truth, showing moderate rather than negligible validity sensitivity.
fastest_falsification: Twenty cessation clips on one model, persistence measurement in three hours; masks that drop at cessation falsify.

one_line: Motion language is grounded from single-frame appearance: 'the car turning left' is answered by wheel angle and pose, not by motion, so still images fool video grounding
problem: Video grounding models accept motion-referential language and are assumed to compute the referenced motion from temporal features, but static appearance correlates of motion (pose, orientation, blur) provide a shortcut whose contribution has not been isolated.
core_hypothesis: Models ground motion words primarily via static correlates, so their selections will be largely reproducible from single frames, and adversarial cases where appearance and actual motion conflict (a car angled left but reversing, a person in running pose standing still) will be resolved by appearance at rates near the appearance-only baseline, demonstrating that motion semantics is not actually computed.
falsifiable_prediction: Single-frame ablation (feeding one frame repeated) will preserve most motion-query selections, and on appearance-motion conflict clips the model will side with appearance far above chance, with the two measurements together bounding the true temporal contribution to a small share.
why_important: Motion-referential queries are central to traffic analysis, sports, and safety monitoring; if grounding reduces to pose matching, systems will misidentify exactly the anomalous-motion cases (reversing, stalling) they exist to catch.
why_possibly_novel: Static-bias analyses exist for action recognition; transplanting the conflict-stimulus methodology to language-conditioned dense video grounding appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate motion queries under repeated-frame ablation on standard clips, curate 60 appearance-motion conflict clips, and measure appearance-siding rates on 2 models.
main_risk: Conflict clips are rare and often odd-looking; curation must avoid confounds that make them hard for reasons besides the conflict.
default_community_belief: Video models use temporal features for motion language; that is what distinguishes them from image models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models with strong optical-flow-like features may pass the conflict test for coarse motions, confining the shortcut to subtle cases.
fastest_falsification: Repeated-frame ablation on 50 motion queries, one model, three hours; selection collapse under ablation falsifies the static-shortcut claim.

one_line: State-referential masks do not update: 'the traffic light that is red' keeps its mask after the light turns green, exposing grounding as a one-shot event, not a maintained belief
problem: When a referring property changes truth value mid-video (lights change, doors open, screens turn off), the correct behavior of a grounded mask is undefined in current benchmarks and unexamined in current models: should the mask follow the object or the property?
core_hypothesis: Models ground at some effective decision time and then track appearance, so state changes leave masks frozen on the originally-selected object regardless of query semantics; neither object-following nor property-following behavior is chosen deliberately, and which occurs is an artifact of when the internal grounding happened relative to the state change, making behavior unpredictable by design.
falsifiable_prediction: On state-change clips, mask behavior after the change will be near-perfectly predicted by pre-change selection (object-following) with no sensitivity to whether the query is property-essential ('the light that is red') or identity-essential ('the light on the left'), a distinction humans respect in judgment studies on the same clips; grounding-time manipulation (starting inference mid-clip) will flip outcomes, confirming the artifact account.
why_important: Property-tracking versus identity-tracking is a semantic contract that video grounding systems silently fail to define; monitoring applications (alert while the valve is open) need property semantics, and this experiment forces the specification into the open with a clean behavioral test.
why_possibly_novel: Video grounding evaluates track quality; the semantics of reference under state change, and the grounding-time artifact prediction, appear undiscussed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate 80 state-change clips with property-essential and identity-essential query pairs, run 2 models with varied inference start times, and compare behavior against human judgments of intended reference.
main_risk: Human intuitions may themselves split on some items, requiring the analysis to use only high-agreement clips as ground truth.
default_community_belief: Tracking the initially-referred object is obviously correct; the query picks the object and the tracker follows it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For most applications identity-following may genuinely be the desired contract, making property-sensitivity a corner case rather than a core deficiency.
fastest_falsification: Fifteen state-change clips with both query types on one model, three hours; query-type-sensitive behavior falsifies the one-shot account.

one_line: Temporal-order reference is grounded by spatial heuristics: 'the car that arrived last' selects by position in frame, because event order is not represented in video grounding
problem: Expressions referencing event order (the last person to enter, the first box placed) require episodic memory over the clip, a capability video grounding models are presumed to inherit from temporal architectures but which is never isolated from spatial-configuration shortcuts.
core_hypothesis: Models lack usable event-order memory and substitute spatial heuristics correlated with order in typical footage (latest arrivals are nearest the entrance, first-placed objects are at the bottom of piles); on order-decorrelated clips where these heuristics fail, order-referential grounding will collapse to the heuristic's prediction rather than to chance, a signature that distinguishes shortcut substitution from mere incapacity.
falsifiable_prediction: On clips engineered so arrival order and final spatial position are decorrelated, model selections will match position-based predictions far above chance and order-based ground truth near chance, and reversing the clip (which flips true order but preserves final configuration) will leave selections unchanged, the decisive signature of order-blindness.
why_important: The clip-reversal test is a cheap, general-purpose audit of whether any video-language system represents temporal order at all, applicable beyond segmentation; order reference matters for forensic video review and assembly verification, where the spatial heuristic answer is exactly the wrong one.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal-order probing exists for video-text retrieval; a dense-grounding version with the reversal-invariance signature and decorrelated staging appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stage or curate 60 order-decorrelated multi-object clips, run order-referential queries forward and reversed on 2 models, and score selections against order truth, position heuristics, and reversal invariance.
main_risk: Staged clips may look unnatural; sourcing naturally-decorrelated footage (parking lots, package stacking) is slower but more convincing.
default_community_belief: Temporal architectures give video grounding models access to event order; order-referential queries are hard but not structurally broken.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some long-context video-language models process frame sequences with genuine order sensitivity and may pass the reversal test for salient events.
fastest_falsification: Ten decorrelated clips forward and reversed on one model, three hours; reversal-sensitive, order-correct selections falsify.
